Every item was drafted by AI from Eli's founder intake and frameworks and is waiting for Eli's review: set "reviewed": true on an item once he signs off, and the draft label disappears. resources.title: The Idea Test
resources.summary: Score up to 5 ideas on 6 questions, with proof rules that stop you flattering yourself, and pick the one to test this week.
resources.output: One chosen idea scored on all 6 questions, the proof behind every high score, your weakest score and its fix, a drop rule, and an insider booked this week.

sections.heading: Pick one idea in 30 minutes
sections.body:
Most first ideas don't fail because they're bad. They fail because nobody was paying for a fix, or because the founder had no way to reach buyers. This test checks both before you spend a dollar or a month.

Set a 30-minute timer. Spend 10 minutes putting up to 5 ideas in the grid and scoring each one 1 to 5 on 6 questions: Eli's 5, plus 1 more. Would you still care in 2 years? Spend the other 20 hunting proof for your top 2, then rescore. The calculator adds it up, out of 30.

Eli's rule: "No idea is perfect. Don't ideate for too long." You're not choosing your life's work today. You're choosing the one idea you'll test first. By the end you'll have a winner, the proof behind it, its weakest score and a message out to one insider.
bullets: Score 1 for no, or no proof. Score 3 for some signs you can name. Score 5 for yes, with proof you could show a stranger.
No proof, no score above 2. A guess is a guess, however good it feels.
Score fast. Your first honest answer is usually right. Come back to the unsure ones once the grid is full.
Only one idea? Score it anyway. A low score shows you exactly what proof to go find.

sections.heading: Fill the grid with ideas worth scoring
sections.body:
Good ideas are usually noticed, not invented. Paul Graham's essay How to Get Startup Ideas (2012) argues the best ones grow out of the founder's own life. Ideas made up on purpose tend to sound plausible and attract nobody.

If your list is thin, or full of apps for strangers, spend 10 minutes on these prompts first.
steps: Write down 3 communities you're already part of: your team, your job, your school, your gym, your game, your church. Sahil Lavingia's The Minimalist Entrepreneur (2021) says to start with a community you belong to, because you already know its problems and where it gathers.
Write down 3 things people around you already pay for and complain about. Haircuts, tutoring, car detailing, phone repair, video editing. A payment plus a complaint is the best raw material there is.
Write down 1 boring job people keep putting off. Graham calls the habit of ignoring tedious work "schlep blindness". Boring work keeps competitors away.
Rewrite each idea as one line: [what you do] for [who] so they [result]. "Pressure washing driveways for homeowners getting ready to sell" beats "a cleaning business".
Stuck? Paste your lists into Ask Eli's Playbook and ask for 10 ideas you could test this month for under $100. Keep only the ones tied to a real complaint on your list.
Keep the 5 you'd actually work on for a year. Cut the rest without guilt.
sections.example: Gymshark started in 2012. Ben Francis was 19, studying at Aston University in Birmingham and delivering pizzas. He was a gym-goer himself, so he knew what lifters wanted to wear. With his friend Lewis Morgan, he made early pieces in his parents' garage on a sewing machine and a screen printer. The lesson: he didn't need a survey to find the idea. He was already the customer, inside the community.

sections.heading: Questions 1 to 3: will they pay, can you reach them, why you
sections.body:
Score in this order. If an idea fails question 1, the others barely matter.

Question 1 is where most ideas die. Y Combinator's Jared Friedman asks how acute the problem is. Paul Graham's version: a few people who want it badly beat a crowd who'd probably like it.

Questions 2 and 3 are about money, reach and edge. MJ DeMarco's CENTS test in The Millionaire Fastlane (2011) adds 2 checks worth stealing. Time: does it only earn while you're working? Control: could one platform, landlord or supplier shut you down? He also warns that easy entry cuts both ways. If you can start it this afternoon for $0, so can everyone else, so question 3 has to carry more weight.
bullets: Question 1, people pay to solve it: do people already pay to fix this, or pay for this kind of value, like saved time, peace of mind or education? Score 5 if you can name 3 people or businesses paying for a fix today, with prices. Score 1 if you can't name anyone.

Question 2, economics and channels work: does one sale make money after costs, and where exactly will buyers see you? Score 5 if a sale clears a profit and you can reach 20 likely buyers this month through a channel you already have, like a group chat or door to door. Score 1 if you'd need shelf space, a big ad budget or a platform's approval first.

Question 3, clear differentiator: are you faster, cheaper, higher quality or running a better supply chain than what they use now? Score 5 if a customer could repeat your edge in one sentence, like "edits back in 24 hours, not a week". Score 1 if your edge is "I care more".

sections.heading: Questions 4 to 6: where it's going, who's inside, will you last
sections.body:
Question 4 looks ahead. Eli's example: someone could have a fantastic newspaper business, but that market is shrinking no matter how good the business is. Friedman looks for the opposite sign: did something change recently that makes this possible or needed now, like a new tool, rule or habit?

Question 5 is what YC calls founder-market fit: are you the right person, with real access to the problem? Question 6 protects you from your own boredom. The first mistake Eli names is trying to do too much. His fix: "pick one, get really good at it and focus on it for the next 5 years."
bullets: Question 4, market growing and AI-proof: is demand rising, and does AI make you faster or make you unnecessary? Score 5 if more people want this each year and AI speeds up your delivery. Score 1 if a free AI tool already does the whole job for the customer.

Question 5, insider access: did you live this problem, or can you talk to someone inside the industry this week? Score 5 if you lived it or a named insider already agreed to talk. Score 1 if you don't know anyone in that world, even through a friend.
Question 6, you'll care in 2 years: would you still want to work on this after 50 ignored messages? Score 5 if you already read, watch or talk about it for fun. Score 1 if you'd be bored by spring.

sections.heading: Score honestly: the proof rules
sections.body:
Most first-time founders score their favorite idea high on everything. That's normal, and it's the fastest way to waste 3 months.

Proof is behavior you can point to. Strongest first: someone paid you. People pay a competitor, and you know the price. People ask for it in public. People complain about it. "I'd buy that" isn't on the list.

Proof doesn't need a product. In 2007, Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia were roommates in San Francisco struggling to pay rent. A design conference had filled the city's hotels, so they put air mattresses on their floor, made a simple website and offered bed and breakfast. Three guests paid to stay. That was Airbnb's first proof, years before the app.
bullets: No proof, no score above 2. If you can't name a person, a post, a competitor or a price, it's a guess.
Write the proof next to every 4 or 5. Vague proof makes it a 3. No proof makes it a 2.
Treat a competitor as proof, not a threat. If nobody sells it, find out why before you get excited. Often nobody pays for it.
Count compliments as zero. Friends saying "cool idea" is kindness, not proof. Money, time and effort are proof.
Score the idea as it is today, not the version you picture after a year of work.
Treat any 1 as a red flag. Raise it, or write down exactly why it doesn't matter, before you move on.
sections.template:
PROOF HUNT: 10 MINUTES EACH FOR YOUR TOP 2 IDEAS

1. Prices (3 min)
Search: [service] [your town] price
Write down 3 prices.

2. People asking (3 min)
Search Facebook groups, Nextdoor or Reddit for:
"looking for a [service]" or "recommend a [service]"
Posts in the last 60 days: [count]

3. Complaints in their words (2 min)
Search Reddit, TikTok or YouTube comments for: [problem]
Copy 2 complaints word for word.

4. Sellers (2 min)
Check Etsy, Fiverr, Thumbtack or Facebook Marketplace.
Note 3 sellers, their prices and review counts.

Write each find next to the question it proves.
No finds for question 1? It scores 2 or less.

sections.heading: Read your grid and break ties
sections.body:
The calculator adds each idea's 6 scores into a total out of 30. Read it in this order.

Check question 1 first. If your leader scores 2 or less there, it isn't ready, whatever the total. Spend this week finding proof, or move to the next idea.

Then read the total. 22 to 30 is strong: take it to real buyers this week. 16 to 21 is promising with gaps: fix the lowest score before you build anything. Under 16 is weak: pick again, in one more sitting, not one more month.

If two ideas finish within 2 points of each other, use these tie-breakers in order. Stop at the first one that separates them.
steps: Higher score on question 1 wins. Proof that people pay beats everything else.
Shortest path to a first paying customer wins. Lawn care can get paid this weekend. A clothing brand needs designs, samples and traffic first.
Lowest cost to test wins. Pick the one you can test with your phone and under $100.
The one where you already know an insider wins.
Still tied? Flip a coin. If the result disappoints you, pick the other one. Then stop scoring and start.

sections.heading: Worked example: Maya picks in 30 minutes
sections.example: Maya, 19, scored 3 ideas. Math tutoring for 9th and 10th graders: proof 5 (4 posts in her town's parents group asking for math tutors last month, and local tutors list $40 to $60 an hour), economics 4, differentiator 3, market 4 (AI helps her prep, parents still want a person), insider 4 (her old algebra teacher), care 4. Total 24. Print-on-demand anime shirts: proof 2 (nobody she can name would buy hers), economics 2 (a few dollars a shirt after the printer's cut), differentiator 2, market 3, insider 1, care 5. Total 15. Video edits for local gyms: proof 3, economics 4, differentiator 3, market 2, insider 2, care 3. Total 17. Tutoring is strong and 7 points clear, so no tie-breakers. Her weakest score is differentiator, so she'll send parents a short progress note after every session. Drop rule: no paid session from 20 parent messages by the 30th, then she switches to gym edits. She texts her old teacher before closing the tab.

sections.heading: Message one insider today
sections.body: One insider conversation beats 10 hours of reading. An insider lives the problem or works inside the industry: a gym owner, a recruiter, a parent who hires tutors. Ask for 15 minutes and 5 questions, not to "pick their brain". Meet on a call or somewhere public. Send it before you close this page.
sections.template:
TEXT OR DM
Hi [name], it's [your name]. [How you know them, or where you saw their work.] I'm testing a small business idea: [your one-line idea]. You know this world better than I do. Could I ask you 5 quick questions this week, 15 minutes max? I'm free [day, time] or [day, time]. No pitch. Thanks either way.

THE 5 QUESTIONS
1. What's the hardest part of [problem] for [customer] right now?
2. How do they handle it today, and what does that cost them?
3. Who already does this well, and what do they charge?
4. What would make you doubt someone like me could do this?
5. Who else should I talk to?

WITHIN AN HOUR OF HANGING UP
Rescore questions 1, 2 and 5.
Write one sentence: what surprised you?

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Scoring for a week. You're picking a test, not a spouse. If it's taken more than one sitting, use the tie-breakers and stop.
Scoring 5 versions of one idea. Tutoring, SAT tutoring and a tutoring app are one idea. Score the strongest version once and use the other slots for real alternatives.
Scoring a crowd instead of a customer. "Gen Z" isn't a customer. "Parents of 10th graders struggling in Algebra 2 in my town" is.
Reading "no competitors" as a green light. Usually it means nobody pays. Search for sellers before you score question 1.
Picking the idea that needs the most building. An app or a product line can take months before the first sale. A service can get paid this week and teaches you the customer while you build.
Working on the winner and the runner-up at once. Park the runner-up in writing. Go back to it only if your drop rule triggers.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: How to Get Startup Ideas, Paul Graham (2012). Read it for why a few people who want something badly beat many who want it mildly, and for schlep blindness.
How to Get and Evaluate Startup Ideas, Jared Friedman, Y Combinator Startup School. Watch it for his questions on how acute the problem is and founder-market fit.
The Millionaire Fastlane, MJ DeMarco (2011). Use the CENTS test, Control, Entry, Need, Time and Scale, as a second check on questions 2 and 3.
The Minimalist Entrepreneur, Sahil Lavingia (2021). Read the chapter on starting with a community you already belong to.
Million Dollar Weekend, Noah Kagan (2024). Take his push to ask for money before you build anything.

sections.heading: Your output and next step
sections.body:
Fill in the worksheet below. The insider field matters most: a real name and a day this week.

Next, open Validation Interview Scripts and book 10 conversations with real buyers. Want a second opinion on your scores? Run the winner through the Idea & Offer Validator. Once your interviews say double down, map how it makes money in the Business Model Worksheet.

Make today day one. Send the insider message now.

resources.aiPrompt: Check that the chosen idea names what is sold and a specific customer someone could find this week, not a crowd like "Gen Z" or "small businesses". Compare the calculator scores with the proof field: every 4 or 5 needs named evidence of behavior (a post, a price, a competitor, a person who paid), and any high score backed only by opinions, compliments or "people would like this" should drop to 2, with one concrete way to find real proof in 48 hours using the proof hunt. If question 1 (people pay to solve it) is 2 or less, say plainly the idea isn't ready whatever the total, and if two ideas are within 2 points, check they broke the tie on question 1 first. Check that the lowest-score action and the drop rule each have a number and a date, and that the insider is a named person with a day this week, not "someone in the industry". End by sending them to Validation Interview Scripts to book 10 conversations, and to the Idea & Offer Validator if they want a second opinion on their scores.

resources.title: Validation Interview Scripts
resources.summary: Copy-ready outreach, a 2-question screener, a Mom Test interview guide and a 10-interview grid that tells you to kill, pause or double down.
resources.output: Notes from 10 interviews, your customers' top 3 phrases, what they pay today, the commitments you earned and a kill, pause or double down call backed by counts.

sections.heading: Book your first interview today
sections.body:
People are kind. Ask "would you buy this?" and most will say yes to protect your feelings. Then they don't buy. Rob Fitzpatrick's book The Mom Test (2013) fixes this with one move: ask about their life and what they've already done, never about your idea.

Your goal: 10 conversations in the next 14 days, 15 to 20 minutes each, by phone, video, voice notes or in person. Not a survey, not a poll in your story. Ten is enough to hear the same words repeat, and small enough to finish in about 3 hours a week.

Before you read on, send one message to one person who has the problem. Use the outreach messages below. Everything else here works better with a conversation on the calendar.

sections.heading: Who to talk to: the 2-question screener
sections.body:
Talk to people who had the problem recently and did something about it. Someone who paid a shop, searched for an hour or built their own fix has real stories. Someone who can only imagine the problem has opinions.

Talk to whoever pays, not just whoever uses it. For tutoring, that's usually a parent. For a gym's social media, it's the owner, not the members.
bullets: Skip your mom, unless she's the customer. Cap friends and family at 3 of your 10, and screen them like anyone else.
If your customer is under 18, interview their parents, coaches or teachers, not the minors themselves. Never cold-message minors.
Meet strangers on a call or in a public place, and tell someone you trust who you're meeting and when.
sections.template:
SCREENER (in the DM, or in the first minute of a call)

1. When was the last time you [dealt with problem]?
Book them if: it happened in the last 3 months.
(Seasonal problem? The last season counts.)

2. What did you do about it?
Book first: anyone who spent money, time or effort on a fix.
(Paid someone, bought something, searched, asked around, built a workaround.)
"Nothing really"? Still worth a call. Tally it.

Failed question 1? Thank them, and ask:
"Who do you know who deals with this a lot?"

TALLY
Screened: [ ]  Had it in 3 months: [ ]  Did something about it: [ ]
Most did nothing about it? That's your first warning sign.

sections.heading: Find 10 people in 7 days with no network
sections.body:
Two of Eli's rules: "Your network is your net worth." And: "Talk to everyone, everywhere, every time." You don't need a network to start. You build one by asking.

Send messages in batches of 10. If fewer than 2 of 10 reply within 3 days, rewrite your first line and try a different place.
bullets: Find people posting about the problem. Search TikTok, Instagram, X or Reddit for the complaint in their words, like "can't find a tutor". Comment something useful first, then DM.
Go where they gather: Facebook groups, subreddits, Discord servers, campus clubs. Read the rules first, since many ban promotion, and ask a moderator before you post.
Text 5 people who know lots of people: a coach, an old teacher, a boss, a family friend. Ask who they know with the problem.
Walk into local businesses during a slow hour, like mid-afternoon on a weekday. Owners often say yes to 10 minutes with someone polite and specific.
End every interview with "Who else should I talk to?" One good interview often turns into 2.
sections.example: DoorDash started with a conversation. Stanford students Tony Xu, Andy Fang, Stanley Tang and Evan Moore were talking to small business owners in Palo Alto. A macaron shop owner showed them a thick booklet of delivery orders she'd had to turn down. In 2013 they put up paloaltodelivery.com, one page with PDF menus and their own phone number, and delivered the first orders themselves. The lesson: one honest conversation showed them the pain, and a one-page test showed them the demand.

sections.heading: Outreach messages you can copy
sections.body: Short, honest and easy to say yes to. You're asking to learn, not to sell. Never pretend to be a student researcher if you aren't one. If you write "not selling anything", don't pitch on the call. Send one follow-up at most.
sections.template:
1. DM TO SOMEONE WHO POSTED ABOUT IT
Hey [name], saw your [post/comment] about [problem]. I'm [first name], I'm starting a small business around [problem area] and trying to learn how people handle it today. Would you be up for a 15-minute call or a few voice notes this week? Not selling anything. Totally fine if not.

2. TEXT TO SOMEONE YOU KNOW
Hi [name], it's [first name]. I'm testing a business idea around [problem]. Do you know 1 or 2 people who've dealt with [problem] in the last few months? I'd love 15 minutes to ask them how they handled it. No pitch, just questions.

3. EMAIL TO A LOCAL BUSINESS OWNER
Subject: 15 minutes on [problem]?
Hi [name],
I'm [first name], and I'm starting a small business around [problem area] here in [town]. I'm talking to [type of business] owners to learn how they handle [problem] today. Could I ask you 5 questions, 15 minutes, by phone or in person? I can do [day, time] or [day, time]. I'm not selling anything.
Thanks,
[first name], [phone]

4. POST IN A COMMUNITY (ask a moderator first)
Hi all, I'm [first name] and I'm learning how people here handle [problem]. If you've dealt with it in the last 3 months, could I ask you about it on a 15-minute call? Not selling anything. Comment or DM me. Thanks to the mods for allowing this.

5. ONE FOLLOW-UP, 3 DAYS LATER
Hey [name], bumping this once in case it got buried. Still keen to hear how you handle [problem]. No worries if now's not a good time.

sections.heading: 3 rules that stop people lying to you
sections.body:
Fitzpatrick's 3 rules, in short. Talk about their life, not your idea. Ask about specific things that already happened, not opinions about the future. Talk less and listen more.

He also names the bad data to catch: compliments, fluff and ideas. Fluff is the vague stuff: generic claims ("I usually"), future promises ("I would") and maybes ("I might"). His sharpest line: if they haven't looked for ways to solve it already, they won't buy yours. When you hear bad data, don't argue. Steer back to what actually happened.
bullets: Compliment: "That's such a cool idea." Say: "Thanks. How do you handle this today?"
Future promise: "I'd totally buy that." Ask: "When did you last pay for something to fix this? What was it?"
Generic: "I always..." Ask: "Tell me about the last time. What happened?"
Feature idea: "You should add..." Ask: "What would that let you do? How do you manage without it now?"
Your own leading question: "Don't you hate when...?" Swap it for "What's the hardest part of...?" instead.
Vague answer: dig with "Tell me more about that", "Why was that hard?" or "What did you do next?" Then wait.
Silence after their answer: count to 3 in your head before you speak. People fill silence with the honest part.

sections.heading: The 20-minute interview guide
sections.body:
Ask these in order, word for word the first few times, then make them yours. Before each call, write down the 3 things you most need to learn. Check them off after.

Eli's advice is the core of every interview. Ask customers how they are "currently solving for something or what they are doing to fill the gap". What people already do and pay for tells you more than anything they say they'd buy.

Teresa Torres, in Continuous Discovery Habits (2021), calls this story-based interviewing: ask about one specific time, then keep them inside that story. If they bought or switched something recently, add the timeline questions. They come from Jobs to Be Done switch interviews, which Bob Moesta teaches in Demand-Side Sales 101 (2020).
sections.template:
OPEN (1 min)
Thanks for doing this. I'm learning how people handle [problem]. There are no wrong answers, and I'm not selling anything today. Mind if I take notes?

CONTEXT (2 min)
1. Tell me a bit about you and where [problem area] shows up in your week.

THE LAST TIME (6 min)
2. Tell me about the last time you dealt with [problem]. When was it?
3. What happened? Walk me through it from the start.
4. What was the hardest part?
5. What did it cost you? Money, time, stress, missed chances.

WHAT THEY DO TODAY (5 min)
6. How do you handle it now? Show me if you can.
7. What else have you tried? Why did you stop?
8. What do you spend on it now, in money or hours a month?
9. What happens if you just don't deal with it?

IF THEY BOUGHT OR SWITCHED SOMETHING (4 min)
10. When did you first think, I need something better? What was going on?
11. What made you finally act that week?
12. What else did you look at? Why that one?
13. What almost stopped you?

CLOSE (2 min)
14. What should I have asked that I didn't?
15. Who else do you know who deals with this?
16. Your commitment ask. See the next section.

sections.heading: End with a commitment ask
sections.body:
Compliments cost nothing. Commitments cost something. Fitzpatrick's test is whether people give up time, reputation or money for what you're doing. Ask for one at the end of every interview, sized to the pain you heard. A no is useful data too.

Keep your promise. If your message said no pitch, don't sell on the call. Ask for time or an intro there. Send a money offer later, and only to people who described real pain. Never invent scarcity: if you say 5 spots, there are 5 spots.

Only take money for something you can deliver soon, and refund it if you can't.
bullets: Time: "Can I show you a rough version next week and get your honest reaction? 15 minutes."
Reputation: "Who's one person you know who deals with this? Would you introduce me?"
Money: a deposit or pre-order, offered in a follow-up message after the call. It's the strongest signal you can get. Price it near what they pay today, and use the Pricing Worksheet to go deeper.
Score every interview: 0 for compliments only, 1 for time, 2 for an intro, 3 for money.
sections.example: In 1999, Nick Swinmurn wanted to know if people would buy shoes online without trying them on. He photographed shoes at local stores and posted them on a simple website. When someone ordered, he went back to the store, bought the pair at full price and shipped it. He had proof that strangers would pay before he owned a single pair. That test became Zappos.
sections.template:
FOLLOW-UP OFFER (within 48 hours, only to people who described real pain)
Hey [name], thanks again for walking me through [their story]. You said "[their exact words]". I'm opening [real number] early spots for [what you'll do] at [price], ready by [date]. If I don't deliver, you get a full refund. Want one? If not, no hard feelings. Your answers already helped a lot.

sections.heading: Notes: one snapshot per interview
sections.body:
Fill this in within 10 minutes of hanging up, while it's fresh. Teresa Torres calls her one-page version an interview snapshot. Keep all 10 in one place, like a notes app, a Notion page or a Google Sheet. Lay them side by side and the patterns jump out.

If you use Granola on calls, it can take notes for you, but write the best quotes yourself. Ask before you record anyone. Recording laws differ by state and country, so check yours first.
sections.template:
INTERVIEW #[number], [date]
Who: [name, role, how you found them]
Last time it happened: [date]
Their story in 3 lines: [what happened, in order]
How they handle it today: [tools, people, steps]
What it costs them today: [$ a month] / [hours a month]
Spends money, or 1+ hour a month, on it today? [Y/N]
Dislikes or dropped what they use now? [Y/N]
Best quote: "[exact words]"
Other phrases worth stealing: "[ ]" / "[ ]"
What pushed them to act: [ ]
What held them back: [ ]
Pain, 1 to 5 (your judgment): [ ]
Commitment, 0 to 3: [none / time / intro / money, with details]
Referrals: [names]
What surprised you: [ ]

sections.heading: Kill, pause or double down: read your 10
sections.body:
After 10 interviews, fill in the grid. Count. Don't guess. Eli's test for product-market fit: "People will want to pay for your product without you needing to sell it to them." Ten interviews won't prove that. They tell you which way to walk.

The double down bar is 5-4-3-1. It's 127's rule of thumb, not science.

Ten interviews show you the loudest patterns, not every need. If your call is pause, keep going toward 20.
bullets: Double down at 5-4-3-1: at least 5 of 10 spend money, or an hour a month, on a fix today, and at least 4 dislike or have dropped what they use now. At least 3 gave you a commitment, and at least 1 put money down. Next stop: the Business Model Worksheet.
Kill: 2 or fewer spend anything on a fix today, or only 0 or 1 dislike what they use now. Go back to The Idea Test and score your runner-up. You just saved yourself months.
Pause: anything in between, including a near miss on 5-4-3-1. Change one thing, the customer, the problem or the angle, and run 5 more interviews.
Circle every phrase 3 or more people used. Those words become your headline, your offer and your posts.
sections.example: Jordan, 20, tested sneaker cleaning for students at his college. He screened 16 people to find 10 who had the problem in the last 3 months. In 12 days he ran all 10 interviews. 6 had paid a shop $25 to $40 a pair, and 2 more spent over an hour a month cleaning their own: 8 spend today. 7 hated the week-long wait or had ruined a pair at home. "I don't trust myself with suede" came up 4 times. Commitments: 3 booked a demo clean, 2 introduced friends and 2 paid a $10 deposit. That's 8-7-7-2, past 5-4-3-1. Verdict: double down. His headline came straight from the grid: suede cleaned by Sunday, no week-long wait.
sections.template:
THE 10-INTERVIEW GRID

Spends = money, or 1+ hour a month, on a fix today
Unhappy = dislikes or dropped what they use now
Commit = 0 none, 1 time, 2 intro, 3 money

#  | Spends | Unhappy | Commit | Pain 1-5 | Phrase
1  | Y/N    | Y/N     |        |          | ""
2  | Y/N    | Y/N     |        |          | ""
3  | Y/N    | Y/N     |        |          | ""
4  | Y/N    | Y/N     |        |          | ""

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Pitching during the interview. The moment you describe your idea, people start being nice. Save it for the follow-up offer.
Asking "how much would you pay?" Price opinions are fluff. Ask what they paid last time, then test your price with a real offer.
Writing your summary instead of their words. You need their exact phrases for your headline and offer later.
Interviewing a chatbot instead of people. AI can draft your questions and sort your notes. It can't tell you what real people did last month.
Stopping after 3 great calls. Three excited people are a start, not a market. Finish all 10 before you decide.

sections.heading: Go deeper
sections.body: Next step: if your call is double down, map the money in the Business Model Worksheet this week, then build The One-Page Offer. If it's kill, go back to The Idea Test and score your runner-up. Want a second read on your notes? Paste your grid into the Idea & Offer Validator.
bullets: The Mom Test, Rob Fitzpatrick (2013). The whole method behind this script. Reread the parts on commitment and on keeping conversations casual.
Demand-Side Sales 101, Bob Moesta (2020). Learn the four forces, push, pull, anxiety and habit, that decide whether someone switches.
Continuous Discovery Habits, Teresa Torres (2021). Take her story-based interviewing and the one-page interview snapshot.
The Startup Owner's Manual, Steve Blank and Bob Dorf (2012). Take the core of customer development: get out of the building and test your guesses with real customers.

resources.title: Business Model Worksheet
resources.summary: Put your idea on one page with real numbers: who pays, what one sale leaves you, how many customers you need and what each one costs to get.
resources.output: A one-page business model with your price, cost per sale, margin, customers needed, cost to get one customer and your hours ceiling, plus a go, fix or switch call.

sections.heading: Your model is one sentence and five numbers
sections.body:
A business model answers one question: who pays you, for what, and does the math work before you run out of money or hours. Write it as one sentence: [customer] pays [price] for [result] and finds you through [channel]. Then back it with five numbers. Your price. What one sale costs you to deliver. How many customers you need for your monthly goal. What it costs to get one customer. How many hours each one takes.

Most first ideas sound fine as a story and break on one of those numbers. With 3 spare hours a week, you have about 13 hours a month. Sell those hours at $25 and your ceiling is $325 a month, however good you are. A $40 product that costs $30 to make and ship leaves $10, and one ad that flops wipes it out. Find that on paper tonight, not after you spend your $100.

This worksheet takes steps 1 to 4 of The Idea Test and blends them with Ash Maurya's Lean Canvas, a one-page model built for founders who are still guessing. Below: the fill-in order, a napkin math template for your phone, capacity and margin checks, go or fix rules, and a worked example from start to finish.

sections.heading: Fill the boxes in this order
sections.body: Ash Maurya created the Lean Canvas, the core tool of his book Running Lean, by adapting Alexander Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas for startups. Osterwalder's boxes for key partners, activities, resources and customer relationships matter more once a business is running. Maurya swapped them for problem, solution, key metrics and unfair advantage: the things a new founder still has to prove. Fill it in this order, from evidence, and put a question mark next to anything you're guessing.
steps: Customer, 5 minutes. Write one specific kind of buyer you can reach this week. If you can't list 10 real names or businesses who match, narrow it until you can.

Problem, 5 minutes. Copy the pain in their words from your Validation Interview Scripts notes. Add how they solve it today and what that costs them. The Lean Canvas calls this the existing alternative, and it's your real competition.
Solution, 5 minutes. Write the result, not the category. "8 ready-to-post Reels a month from your own clips" is a solution. "Video editing" is a category. Never fill this box before the problem box.
Model and price, 5 minutes. Pick one way to make money from the next section and one price to test.
Napkin math, 10 minutes. Run the template below and put a number on every line.
Channels, 5 minutes. Pick two at most, rate each easy, medium or hard to reach, and estimate what one customer costs you there in dollars or hours.
Differentiator, market and AI, 5 minutes. Write one reason you win, the proof, and whether the market and AI help or hurt you.
Count your question marks. Three or more means go back to customer conversations before you build anything.
sections.template:
ONE-PAGE MODEL

One sentence: [customer] pays [price] for [result] and finds me through [channel].

Customer: [who, and how many I can name]
Problem: [their words]. Today they [current fix], which costs them [money / time]
Solution: [the result I deliver]
Model: [one-time / monthly / productized / product / pay-for-performance]
Napkin math: price $[ ], cost per sale $[ ], margin $[ ], goal $[ ] a month = [ ] customers
Channels: [channel 1, easy / medium / hard, cost per customer] and [channel 2]
Ceiling: [hours per customer], so [most customers I can serve]
Differentiator: [faster / cheaper / higher quality / better supply chain]. Proof: [who said it]
Market and AI: [growing / shrinking]. AI changes [what]
Question marks: [number]

sections.heading: Pick one way to make money
sections.body: Eli's advice, from his own mistakes: there are a million ways to make money, so pick one, get really good at it and focus on it for the next 5 years. Your first model should be one your customer already understands. With under 3 hours a week, pick one where a single sale doesn't eat your week: a productized service, a monthly plan or a simple product.
bullets: One-time sale: a cleaning, a logo, a resume rewrite. Easy to sell, but you need new buyers every month, so your channel carries the business.
Monthly plan: a fixed fee for ongoing results, like lawn care, tutoring or social posts. You need fewer customers for the same goal, and you lose them the month you stop delivering.
Productized service: one fixed scope, one fixed price, the same process every time, like "8 Reels a month for $200". No custom quotes, and templates cut your hours per customer.
Product margin: you buy or make something and sell it for more, like resale, a clothing drop or a digital download. Profit is the gap after every cost, and your cash sits in inventory until it sells.

Pay-for-performance: you get paid on results, like an ad agency that charges per booked client instead of a monthly retainer. Use it only when you can track results and can afford to wait to get paid.
Free for users, paid by sponsors or ads: newsletters and channels. It needs a big audience before it pays, so it rarely works as a first model.
sections.example: Designjoy, run by designer Brett Williams, sells design as a subscription instead of quoting projects. Clients pay one flat monthly fee for unlimited requests, worked one at a time, and can pause or cancel. The one-at-a-time rule is what makes it work: clients can ask for as much as they want, but each one only ever has one task in his queue. Same skill as a freelancer billing by the hour, very different ceiling.

sections.heading: Napkin math on your phone
sections.body:
There's no calculator on this page on purpose. Nine lines on your phone calculator tell you more than a 20-page plan. Use monthly numbers and round costs up, not down.

Kevin Kelly's 2008 essay 1,000 True Fans is the mental model. A creator with 1,000 true fans who each spend $100 a year brings in $100,000 a year. You don't need millions of customers. You need a specific number, and a plan for where the first 10 come from. Your version is smaller: your monthly goal divided by what one customer leaves you after costs.

Count payment fees in your cost. Stripe's standard US rate is 2.9% plus 30 cents per successful domestic card charge (Stripe, 2026), and other checkout tools and marketplaces charge their own rates or take a cut. Check the rate on whatever you use.
sections.template:
NAPKIN MATH (monthly numbers. Mark each line K for known or G for guess)

1. Price per sale: $[P]
2. Cost to deliver one sale: $[C]
   product or materials: $[ ]
   shipping and packaging: $[ ]
   payment and platform fees: $[ ]
   tools or help used per sale: $[ ]
3. Margin per sale: P minus C = $[M]
   Margin %: M ÷ P x 100 = [ ]%
4. Monthly goal, what you want left over: $[G]
5. Customers or sales needed: G ÷ M = [N], rounded up
6. Cost to get one customer: $[money spent] and [hours spent] hours ÷ [customers won] = $[CAC] and [ ] hours each
7. Payback: CAC ÷ M = [ ] sales (or months, on a monthly plan)
8. Hours per customer: [H]. Hours needed: N x H = [ ]. Hours you have this month: [ ]
9. Startup cost to make the first sale: $[ ]. Can you afford to lose it? [yes / no]

Verdict: [go / fix / switch], because line [number] breaks.

sections.heading: Services: your hours are the ceiling
sections.body:
If you sell your time, your income has a hard cap: hours available times your rate. Most first services hit it fast, because the same spare hours also have to cover finding clients, messages and redos.

MJ DeMarco's CENTS test in The Millionaire Fastlane scores a business on Control, Entry, Need, Time and Scale. Time asks whether the business can earn without trading your hours. Scale asks whether it can reach far beyond your neighborhood. A first service usually fails both, and that's fine. Build it so it can pass them later.

Eli hit this ceiling himself. He ran a health and wellness consulting business building custom workout and meal plans, then pivoted to e-commerce to scale beyond giving away his time. His rule: your business is only as valuable as it is when you aren't there to run it.
steps: Time one full delivery with a stopwatch, including messages and revisions. Write hours per customer per month.
Multiply by customers needed from your napkin math. If the total is more than your available hours, this price can't hit your goal.
Fix it in this order: productize (fixed scope, templates, checklists), raise the price, cut the scope, then change the model. Planning to find hours you don't have is not a fix.
Write your ceiling: the most customers you can serve well. That's honest scarcity you can tell buyers about later in The One-Page Offer.
sections.example: Brian Scudamore was 19 in 1989 when he spent $700 on an old Ford pickup and started hauling junk to pay for college. He called it The Rubbish Boys so one guy with a truck would look bigger. Every job needed him behind the wheel, so growth meant turning the work into a system other people could run. It became 1-800-GOT-JUNK?, adding franchise partners from 1999. The lesson for your scale box: write down the part of the job only you can do now, and how you'll hand it off at 10 customers.

sections.heading: Products: know your landed cost
sections.body:
Landed cost is everything it takes to get one unit into your hands, ready to sell: the item, shipping to you, duties or import fees, and packaging. Gross margin is price minus landed cost, divided by price. Then subtract what it costs to get the item to the buyer: shipping out, platform cuts and payment fees.

Retail's old rule of thumb is keystone pricing: a store sells at double what it paid you. A common rule for makers is to double your cost again to set that wholesale price. Put together, if stores might carry your product one day, your landed cost has to sit near a quarter of the retail price.

Eli's first business was sneaker reselling: $2,000 in, $3,000 out, before college. Eli's results aren't typical or a promise of what you'll earn. Resale is the fastest way to learn the product model. Your profit is the gap after fees and shipping, and your cash sits in inventory until it sells.
sections.example: Illustrative hoodie drop. Blank and print: $14. Shipping to you: $2. Bag and sticker: $1. Landed cost: $17. Price: $40, so gross margin is $23, or 58%. Free shipping to the buyer costs you $6, and a 2.9% plus 30 cent payment fee is $1.46. You keep $15.54 a hoodie, so a $500 monthly goal takes 33 hoodies. Keystone check: a store wants to buy at $20 to sell at $40, which leaves you $3. Sell direct first, or get your cost down before you pitch stores.

sections.heading: Differentiator, market and AI
sections.body:
Pick one of the four differentiators from The Idea Test: faster, cheaper, higher quality, or a better supply chain. Then write the proof from a real person, not your opinion. "Better quality" with no proof is a hope.

The Lean Canvas also has a box for an unfair advantage, something that can't easily be copied or bought. Most first businesses don't have one yet. Leave it blank before you write "passion" or "quality". Yours may grow into relationships, an audience, or speed nobody else will match.

MJ DeMarco's Entry commandment adds a warning: if anyone can start your business in a day for $0, so can your competitors. That doesn't kill the idea. It means you win on execution and trust, not on the idea.
bullets: Market direction: a great business in a shrinking market still shrinks. Growing looks like more people searching for it, competitors raising prices and buyers asking for more.
Shrinking looks like prices falling every year, buyers moving to a free option and fewer businesses offering it. If you see it, pick a growing slice of the market or a different idea.
AI check: if a buyer can type one prompt and get your result for free, change the offer. Sell what AI can't easily do: judgment, trust, local presence, accountability and taste.
Ask Perplexity or Claude for recent trends, check the sources it cites, then confirm with one insider who works in that market.

sections.heading: Go, fix or switch
steps: Name check: can you list 10 real people or businesses who match your customer box? If not, narrow the customer until you can.
Margin check: would one refund or one redo wipe out a week of profit? If yes, raise the price or cut the cost before you launch.
Hours check: does customers needed times hours per customer fit the hours you have? If not, productize or raise the price.

Channel check: is at least one channel easy, and does one customer cost less than one sale's margin? With under $100 to spend, you need payback on the first sale, so stay organic until a paid test proves otherwise.
Cash check: can you make the first sale for less than you can afford to lose? If not, shrink the first version to a pre-sale, a sample batch or one pilot client.
Proof check: does your differentiator have proof from a real person, and does it survive the AI check? If not, it's a guess.
Five-year check: would you still want to work on this in 5 years? If not, run it as a short test and keep looking for the one you would.
bullets: All yes: go. Build the offer in The One-Page Offer, then set the price in the Pricing Worksheet.
One or two no: fix those boxes this week and rerun the napkin math.
Three or more no: switch the model, or go back to The Idea Test and try your next idea.
Before you commit, paste your one-page model into the Idea & Offer Validator, then show it to one insider and ask: "What here do you think is wrong?" No one is self-made.

sections.heading: Worked example: Ava's barbershop Reels
sections.example:
Ava, 19 (illustrative). Goal: $600 a month. Time: 3 hours a week, about 13 a month.
Customer: barbershop owners within 20 minutes who post less than once a week. She can list 31.
Problem: "I know I should post. I never have time." Today they post once a month or pay a nephew when he remembers.
Draft 1, hourly at $25: 13 hours x $25 = a $325 ceiling. It fails the goal before she finds a client.
Draft 2, productized: 8 Reels a month from the shop's own clips, captioned and scheduled, $200 a month. Three editing templates get each Reel to about 15 minutes, so 2 hours per shop.
Napkin math: $6.10 in payment fees, so a $193.90 margin. $600 ÷ $193.90 = 3.1, so 4 shops, using 8 of her 13 hours.
Cost to get one: 40 DMs and 6 walk-ins led to 5 conversations and 1 yes. About 4 hours, $0.
Ceiling: 6 shops. At 10, she trains a friend on her templates.
Differentiator: faster. Reels back in 48 hours. 4 of the 6 owners she interviewed said a slow editor is why they stopped posting.
AI check: AI makes cutting clips cheap, so she sells the plan, the hooks and the posting.
Verdict: go. Next: The One-Page Offer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Leaving fees out. Payment fees, platform cuts, packaging and shipping add up. Count every one per sale.
Pricing your time at $0. A $50 job that takes 5 hours pays $10 an hour. Put hours in the math.
Planning on everyone. "Anyone who wants to look good" gives you no channel. Name the first 10.
Calling revenue profit. $1,000 in sales with $800 in costs is $200 of profit.
Running three models at once. Pick one way to make money. Add a second when the first runs without you.

Buying customers before the margin can carry it. A $15 margin can't survive a $20 cost per customer. Prove a channel for free first, then test paid with a capped budget in the Launch Budget Calculator.
Never updating it. Rerun the math after every 10 customer conversations and after your first 5 sales.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: Running Lean by Ash Maurya: the full Lean Canvas, and how to test your riskiest box first.
Kevin Kelly's essay 1,000 True Fans (2008, free on his site, The Technium): why a small, specific number of real customers can be enough.
The Millionaire Fastlane by MJ DeMarco (2011): read it for the CENTS test, especially Time and Entry.
The Minimalist Entrepreneur by Sahil Lavingia (2021): start with a community you're already in, build as little as possible, and get profitable early.
Business Model Generation by Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur (2010): the original Business Model Canvas, worth it once your business is running.

resources.aiPrompt: Recompute the napkin math: margin must equal price minus every per-sale cost (flag missing payment fees, shipping, packaging or platform cuts), and customers needed must equal the monthly goal divided by the margin, rounded up. Check that hours per customer times customers needed fits the hours the member actually has, and that the channels field gives a cost to get one customer in dollars or hours, with at least one easy channel. Flag a customer box that names a category instead of people they could list 10 of, a problem with no current alternative, a solution written as a category, and a differentiator with no proof from a real person or one AI could replace. The most common weak answer is a price with no cost line and a customer of "everyone": call it out directly, ask for numbers, and have them mark guesses as guesses. If the math or the proof fails, send them back to Validation Interview Scripts or The Idea Test; if it holds, send them to The One-Page Offer and then the Pricing Worksheet.

resources.title: The One-Page Offer
resources.summary: Build an offer so clear and so good it's hard to refuse, without a word of hype: outcome, stack, a guarantee you can keep and three versions to paste.
resources.output: A one-page offer, a 3-sentence DM version and a landing-page version, built on the value equation, with a guarantee you can afford and proof that's real.

sections.heading: An offer is the whole deal, not the product
sections.body:
Two people can sell the same resume edit. One gets ignored. The other books out. The difference is rarely the skill. It's the offer: who it's for, what they get, how fast, what happens if it doesn't work, and how the price is framed.

Alex Hormozi's $100M Offers (2021) breaks value into four levers. People pay more when the dream outcome is bigger and when they believe they'll actually get it. They pay more again when it's faster and asks less effort and sacrifice from them. Most first offers only talk about the outcome. The cheapest upgrades are usually speed, effort and belief.

Eli's version: make the offer so good it almost feels like it can't be true, because nobody would turn it down if it really does what you say. The catch is the word really. Every line has to be true, and every promise has to be one you can keep. Below: how to beat their current option, build the stack, pick a guarantee you can afford, use only real scarcity, and three versions to paste into a DM, a page or a pitch.

sections.heading: Beat what they'd do instead
sections.body:
Your competition is whatever they'd do if you didn't exist. April Dunford starts positioning there in Obviously Awesome (2019): list the competitive alternatives, find what you do that they can't, then find who cares most about that. For a first business, the alternative is rarely a big company. It's doing nothing, doing it themselves, asking a friend, or a cheap tool that half works.

Assume your first version is worse than the alternatives at most things. Better on one thing your customer cares about is enough, if you can prove it. Then say it in one line. Donald Miller's StoryBrand one-liner has three parts: the problem, your solution, and the result.
steps: List 3 alternatives your customers named when you asked how they solve this today. Include doing nothing.
For each one, write what it costs them: money, time, hassle or risk.
Circle the one thing you do better that they'd pay for. If you can't find one, fix the offer before you write it.
Write your one-liner and read it to one person who fits. If they ask "so what do you actually do?", rewrite it.
sections.template:
WHAT THEY'D DO INSTEAD
1. [alternative, e.g. do nothing]: costs them [money / time / hassle / risk]
2. [alternative, e.g. do it themselves]: costs them [ ]
3. [alternative, e.g. a friend or a cheap tool]: costs them [ ]
The one thing I do better, that they'd pay for: [ ]

ONE-LINER
[Customers] struggle with [problem, in their words]. I [solution, in plain words], so they [result] in [timeframe].

sections.heading: Build the stack: every problem becomes a solution
sections.body: Hormozi's method for building what he calls a Grand Slam Offer is mechanical, which is good news. You don't need to be creative. You need a list. Write every problem your customer hits before, during and after getting the result, then turn each one into something you deliver. Use the levers as prompts: what makes it feel slow, hard, risky or not worth it?
steps: Write the dream outcome at the top of the page, in their words: "interviews at finance firms", not "a better resume".

Set a 15-minute timer and list at least 10 problems, in their words from your Validation Interview Scripts notes. "I don't know what's wrong with my resume" and "I don't have time to tailor it for every job" are two.
Flip each problem into a solution. Don't judge them yet.
Pick how you'd deliver each one: done for you, done with you on a call, or a template they use themselves. Done for you is worth the most to them and costs you the most hours.
Trim: cross out anything that costs you a lot and matters little to them.
Stack: keep the 3 to 5 that matter most and cost you little to repeat. Templates, checklists and a short video walkthrough are cheap to deliver again and again.
Check the levers. You want one item that makes it faster, one that makes it easier, and one that raises their belief it will work. If a lever is empty, add one item for it.

PROBLEM TO SOLUTION GRID (list 10, keep 3 to 5)

Problem 1, in their words: [ ]
Lever: [slow / hard / risky / not worth it]
Solution: [ ]
Delivery: [done for you / done with you / template]
Cost to me: [low / high]. Keep? [yes / no]

Problem 2, in their words: [ ]
Lever: [ ]
Solution: [ ]
Delivery: [ ]
Cost to me: [ ]. Keep? [ ]

Problem 3, in their words: [ ]
Lever: [ ]
Solution: [ ]
Delivery: [ ]
Cost to me: [ ]. Keep? [ ]

[Repeat to 10]

sections.heading: Pick a guarantee you can afford to keep
sections.body:
A guarantee raises their belief that it will work, the hardest lever to move when you have no reviews yet. Hormozi sorts guarantees into four types. Pick the strongest one you could still honor if 1 in 3 buyers claimed it. That's a stress test, not a forecast.

The best guarantees remove the exact fear. Shoes bought online might not fit, so Zappos built its name on free shipping both ways and a 365-day return window. Glasses bought online might look wrong on your face, so Warby Parker grew with Home Try-On: 5 frames mailed to you to try for 5 days, free.
bullets: Unconditional: "Not happy? Full refund, no questions." The strongest, and only safe when your cost per sale is low.
Conditional: you refund or keep working if they did their part and still didn't get the result, like "Send it to 30 postings. No interviews, I rewrite it free." Write the conditions plainly.
Anti-guarantee: "All sales final", with the honest reason, like custom work you can't resell. Use it when a refund would cost you real money.

Implied or performance: they pay only for results, or per result. Eli's example is an ad agency that charges solely on performance instead of a retainer. Offer it only when you can track results and can afford to wait to get paid.

Know the rule. In the US, the FTC's guides on guarantee advertising treat a "money-back" or "satisfaction" guarantee as a promise of a full refund on request. Any conditions have to be stated clearly up front. Rules differ by place, so check yours.

Expect some refunds and read them as a signal. Online course sellers report refund rates of roughly 5 to 10% (Teachery, 2026). If more than 1 in 10 buyers ask for their money back, your offer is promising more than you deliver.
sections.example: Domino's promised pizza in 30 minutes, or money off. In December 1993 it dropped the guarantee in the US, after a St. Louis jury handed a multimillion-dollar award to a woman hurt in a crash with a Domino's driver. Critics had argued for years that the promise pushed drivers to rush. The lesson: a guarantee that depends on things you don't control, or tempts you to cut corners, can cost far more than the refunds.

sections.heading: Real scarcity, real deadlines, useful bonuses
sections.body: Scarcity and urgency work because they're usually true signals. Fake them and you trade one sale for your name, and buyers talk to each other. Win their trust, win their wallet.
bullets: Real scarcity is your actual capacity: "I edit everything myself, so I take 4 new shops a month." Use the ceiling from your Business Model Worksheet.
Real urgency is a real date: a group that starts Monday, a season like prom, or a price rise for new buyers on a date you'll honor.

A good bonus solves the next problem they'll hit right after the main result. It should be cheap for you to repeat and worth real money to them. If you list a value next to it, make it what you or others actually charge.

Out of bounds: countdown timers that reset, "only 2 spots left" when it isn't true, a deadline you quietly extend, and reviews you wrote or paid for. The FTC's 2022 staff report on dark patterns names fake countdown timers and false scarcity claims as deceptive design.

Also out of bounds: a crossed-out "regular price" nobody ever paid. In the US, a former-price comparison has to be a real price you charged for a real stretch of time (FTC guides, 16 CFR 233). Check local rules if you sell elsewhere.

sections.heading: Worked example: Maya's resume rewrite
sections.body: Maya, 21, is illustrative. She interviewed 9 seniors applying to finance internships. Their alternatives were the campus career center with a two-week wait, a $150 online service, or nothing. Her problem list had 12 items and her stack kept 4. Her weakest lever was belief, since she had no reviews, so she picked guarantees she can afford. Her real scarcity is her time: 5 rewrites a week.

sections.heading: Write your one-page offer
sections.body:
Name it so the right person knows it's for them. Hormozi's MAGIC naming formula packs in a reason to act now, who it's for, their goal, a time frame and a container word like sprint, kit or blueprint. "Finance Resume Rewrite in 48 Hours" says who it's for, what they get and how fast in six words.

Frame the price the way Eli does: cost as the smallest number, value as the largest. Dollar Shave Club launched in 2012 with a viral video and razors from $1 a month, plus shipping, and that small number was the hook. Do the math honestly. $49 over a 16-week semester is about $3 a week. Never hide the real total. Set the number itself in the Pricing Worksheet.

Fill every bracket. Cut any line that doesn't help them decide. It should fit on one phone screen with two scrolls.

sections.body: Nobody reads a full offer in a DM. Before you send anything, paste your one-page offer into the Idea & Offer Validator for a blunt second read. Then send the short version to people from your interview list first, and count what happens.
steps: Send the 3-sentence version to 10 people who match your "For" line, starting with the people you interviewed. If they don't know you, use an opener from Outreach Scripts.
Count replies that ask about price, timing or how to pay. Those are buying signals. Compliments are not.
If 3 or more of 10 ask how to buy, build the landing page next.
If 0 or 1 ask, change one thing and send it to 10 new people. Fix the "For" line or the outcome first. The price is rarely the first problem.
Ask every no: "What would stop you from buying this today?" Answer it in the offer or the FAQ.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Selling features. "Line-by-line edit" is a feature. "More interviews from the same applications" is the outcome. Lead with the outcome.
Stacking filler. Ten bonuses nobody asked for look desperate. Every item should solve a problem from your list.
A guarantee you can't pay. If 1 in 3 buyers claimed it, could you cover it? If not, make it conditional or smaller.
Fake proof. Invented testimonials, made-up numbers, or someone else's results presented as yours. Leave the proof line empty before you fake it.
Fake scarcity. A timer that resets or a spot count that never moves. Use your real capacity or a real date, or skip urgency.
Hiding the real cost. Framing is fine. A "$1 a day" line that hides a 12-month contract is bait-and-switch.
Writing it once. Rewrite it after your first 5 sales with real results, and cut what nobody cared about.

resources.title: Pricing Worksheet
resources.summary: Set a price you can defend: tie it to your buyer's return, check what they pay today, ask 4 price questions and test it on 5 real buyers.
resources.output: A price and model tied to a one-sentence ROI story, your margin and customers-needed math, three options, both framings, and a 5-buyer test with a written raise rule.

sections.heading: Price from the value, not your nerves
sections.body:
Most first prices come from fear. You pick the lowest number nobody could refuse, then work a full week for $200.

Your price decides how hard your month is. At $50 a month, you need 20 customers to bring in $1,000. At $150, you need 7. Each customer takes about the same work to find.

Eli's rule: "The best businesses or products can be tied back to an ROI model." Your buyer gets more revenue, more capacity, lower costs, time back or peace of mind. Work out roughly what that is worth to them. Then price so the deal is clearly good for them and still pays you well.

This worksheet does it in order. You put a dollar number on the value, check the price works for you, see what buyers pay today and ask buyers four price questions. Then you pick a model and three options, frame the number and test it on 5 real buyers. The built-in calculator does the math as you go.

sections.heading: Put a dollar number on the value
sections.body:
Value-based pricing starts from what the result is worth to the buyer, not from your costs or a competitor's number. Patrick Campbell built the pricing firm Price Intelligently, later ProfitWell, on that idea: measure what buyers value, then price from it instead of copying or guessing.

Selling to consumers, like a hoodie or a candle? There's rarely clean ROI math. Do steps 1 and 2 quickly, then spend your time on what buyers pay today and the four price questions. Those matter more for you.
steps: Write the outcome in the buyer's words from your interviews. "Reels that bring in trial sign-ups" beats "video editing".
Pick one or two value types: more revenue, time saved, cost avoided or risk removed.
Get the inputs from the buyer. Ask: "What does a new customer pay you, and how long do they usually stay?" and "How many hours a month does this take you now?"
Do the math per month. Revenue: extra customers a month times what one customer is worth to them. Time: hours saved times what their hour is worth.
Use the low end of every estimate. If the deal still looks good on low numbers, it's a real deal.
Enter the monthly value in the calculator and read the ROI multiple. It reads under 3x as thin, 3x to 10x as healthy, and over 10x as a sign you can charge more.
Claim only value you can show. Trust beats everything in sales, and an inflated ROI that wins the deal loses you the customer.
sections.example: Jordan, 19, edits Reels for local gyms. He asks one owner two questions. A new member pays $60 a month and usually stays about 8 months, so each new member is worth $480 to the gym. The owner also spends about 6 hours a month making his own videos and puts his time at $25 an hour. Jordan's low estimate: 1 new member a month ($480) plus 6 hours back ($150), so $630 a month in value. At $250 a month, that's a 2.5x return, and the calculator calls it thin. Jordan can't honestly promise more members yet, so he changes the model instead of the claim. You'll see how below. These numbers are illustrative.

sections.heading: Make sure the price works for you too
sections.body:
A price has to work on both sides. The buyer's ROI is half the check. The other half is yours: what each sale leaves you, what you earn per hour and how many customers your goal takes. Add your cost to deliver, your hours and a monthly goal, and the calculator shows all three.

Cost to deliver means cash you spend per sale or per customer per month: supplies, apps, paid help, shipping and payment fees. Your own time goes in the hours box instead.
bullets: Gross margin: the share of each sale you keep after delivery costs. Services and digital products usually keep most of each sale. Physical products keep less, and ads, refunds and discounts all come out of what's left.
Hourly rate: what you keep per sale divided by your hours. If it's below what a part-time job pays you, raise the price, cut the scope or deliver faster.
Customers needed: your monthly goal divided by what each customer leaves you. If that's more buyers than you can reach this month, the price is too low for the goal.
What one sale earns you: price minus cost to deliver. It's also the most you could pay in ads to win one sale and break even. Take it to the Launch Budget Calculator before you spend on ads.
sections.example: Jordan's cash cost is about $10 per gym per month for app subscriptions and stock clips. Each gym takes 8 hours of his time. At $250 a month he keeps $240 per gym, earns about $30 an hour and needs 5 gyms to clear $1,000 a month after costs. Five gyms is reachable from his interview list, so his side of the deal works. Illustrative numbers.

sections.heading: Check what buyers pay today, in 30 minutes
sections.body: Your buyer already has a number in mind, set by what they've seen and what they do now. Include the options people forget: doing it themselves, paying a friend, or doing nothing and living with the problem. Set a timer.
steps: Minutes 0 to 10: search Google, Instagram, TikTok and Reddit for the product or service near you. Ask Perplexity what [service] costs in [city], then open the sources it cites. An AI answer is a lead, not proof.
Minutes 10 to 20: list 5 competitors with their price, what's included and how they charge. Screenshot each offer.
Minutes 20 to 25: enter the lowest and highest price in the calculator, plus what buyers spend on today's fix.
Minutes 25 to 30: write what the cheap ones leave out and what the expensive ones include. That gap is where your offer wins.
Choose your position. Pricing below the cheapest needs a reason and a date to raise. Pricing above the highest needs proof of something buyers can't get elsewhere.
sections.example: Sneaker cleaning: a mall shop charges $35 with a 5-day wait. A local cleaner on Instagram charges $20 but has no reviews. A mail-in service charges $45 plus shipping. Low $20, high $45. A $30 price with 24-hour turnaround and before-and-after photos sits mid-range on price and wins on speed and trust.

sections.heading: Ask buyers the four price questions
sections.body:
Talk about price before you finish building. That's the core advice of Monetizing Innovation by Madhavan Ramanujam and Georg Tacke (2016): have the willingness-to-pay conversation early, then design the product around the price buyers will pay.

Use the four questions of the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter, introduced by Dutch economist Peter van Westendorp in 1976. The full method is a survey of many buyers. With 5 to 10 buyers, it's a conversation tool that shows you a rough range. Answers are opinions, not payments, so the real test comes when you ask for money.
steps: Pick 5 to 10 people who match your customer, ideally from your interview list.
Show the offer first: two sentences and what's included. Nobody can price something vague.
Ask the four questions in the template's order and write down each exact number.
Don't react, defend or hint at your price. Say thanks and move on.
Type each buyer's answers into the calculator's four buyer boxes, separated by commas.

Read the range. If your price is above most buyers' too-expensive number, add proof or offer a smaller version. If it's below most buyers' too-cheap number, raise it, because a price that low makes people doubt the quality.
sections.template:
Four price questions (ask after you've explained the offer)

Here's what you'd get: [OFFER IN 2 SENTENCES, PLUS WHAT'S INCLUDED].

1. At what price would this be so expensive you wouldn't consider it? $____
2. At what price would it start to feel expensive, but you'd still think about it? $____
3. At what price would it feel like a bargain, a great buy for the money? $____
4. At what price would it be so cheap you'd doubt the quality? $____

Then ask:
"What would you compare this to?"
"Who else would decide on spending like this?"

Log per buyer:
[NAME] | Too expensive $[ ] | Getting expensive $[ ] | Bargain $[ ] | Too cheap $[ ] | Compares it to [ ]

sections.heading: Pick a model and build three options
sections.body:
Sometimes the model matters more than the number. Eli's example is an ad agency paid solely on performance instead of a retainer. His point: a new model can scare the existing market, but if it's more favorable to the buyer, it can become hyper attractive.

Then offer three options instead of one. One price asks yes or no. Three ask which one. Blair Enns makes options central to his method in Pricing Creativity (2018), and Ramanujam and Tacke call it good-better-best.

Options help, but they're not magic. In Predictably Irrational (2008), Dan Ariely tested an Economist offer: web only $59, print only $125, print and web $125. With the pointless print-only option listed, 84 of 100 students chose print and web. Without it, 32 did. Yet the researchers who first described this decoy effect suspect it "occurs rarely in the marketplace today" (Huber, Payne and Puto, 2014). Build three options because buyers differ.
bullets: One-time: pay once, get the thing, like a resume rewrite or a logo. Easy to sell, but you keep finding new buyers.
Monthly: ongoing payment for ongoing results, like lawn care or editing. Use it when the value repeats every month.
Pay-for-performance: paid per result, like a fee per new client. Use it only when you can track the result yourself and can wait to get paid.
Base fee plus bonus: a small fixed fee covers your costs, plus a bonus per result. Safer than pure performance for a first offer.
Three options: build each for a different buyer, not just more stuff, and put the one you expect most people to pick in the middle.
Keep every option real: worth buying and something you'd happily deliver. A fake option you never plan to sell, or a made-up "was" price, is manipulation and out of bounds.
sections.example: Jordan's ROI was thin at $250, so he rebuilt the offer. Starter: 8 Reels a month for $150. Standard: 12 Reels for $150 plus $50 for each new member who joins with his tracked trial code. Full: 12 Reels, posting and a monthly results report for $300 plus $50 per new member. If Standard brings 1 member a month, the gym pays $200 for $630 of value, a 3.2x return. Jordan takes a little risk, and the owner takes almost none. Illustrative numbers.
sections.template:
Three options

Option 1, [NAME]: for [WHO IT'S FOR]
Includes: [2 TO 3 DELIVERABLES]
Price: $[ ] [PER MONTH / ONE TIME]

Option 2, [NAME]: for [WHO IT'S FOR]
Includes: everything in Option 1, plus [THE THING MOST BUYERS ASKED FOR]
Price: $[ ]

Option 3, [NAME]: for [WHO IT'S FOR]
Includes: everything in Option 2, plus [SPEED, SUPPORT, DONE-FOR-YOU WORK OR RESULTS REPORTING]
Price: $[ ]

Checks before you share it:
[ ] Each option is real, worth buying and something you'd happily deliver
[ ] The differences are obvious in 5 seconds
[ ] No "most popular" label until it's true

sections.heading: Frame the number: smallest for cost, largest for value
sections.body:
Eli's rule: "When selling cost, always frame it as the lowest possible number, when value the highest." Research backs the first half, with a limit. Harvard's John Gourville found that recasting a cost as pennies a day made people more willing to pay, because they compared it to small everyday spending (Journal of Consumer Research, 1998). It works when the daily number sounds petty.

Dollar Shave Club put its small number in its name: razors from $1 a month. Unilever bought the company in 2016 for a reported $1 billion.
bullets: Cost, small: "$5 a day" instead of "$150 a month". Use per day only when the daily number sounds like a small habit, like a coffee.
Value, large: "$5,760 a year in member revenue" instead of "1 new member a month".
Against today's fix: "Less than the mall shop, and back in 24 hours instead of 5 days."

Price endings: a price ending in 9 signals a deal. In catalog field tests, Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester found 9-endings lifted demand, and that price cues lose power the more a seller uses them (Harvard Business Review, 2003). Use 9-endings on value offers and round numbers on premium ones.
Never let framing hide the real cost. Show the full price, fees and terms before anyone pays.
sections.template:
Cost, smallest number
$[PRICE] a month is $[PRICE DIVIDED BY 30] a day, less than [SMALL DAILY THING].

Value, largest number
[ONE RESULT] is worth about $[VALUE PER YEAR] a year to you.

Against today's fix
[YOUR OFFER] costs less than [ALTERNATIVE] and [IS FASTER / BETTER IN ONE CLEAR WAY].

One-line pitch
For $[DAILY] a day, you get [OUTCOME], worth about $[YEARLY VALUE] a year.

sections.heading: Test it on 5 buyers, then raise on a rule
sections.body: A price is a guess until someone pays it. Test it on 5 real buyers within 7 days, and write your raise rule before the first conversation.
steps: Offer the price to 5 people who match your customer. Start with your interview list.
Say the price plainly, then stop talking. No apology, no discount on the spot.
Track each answer as paid, "let me think" or no. Ask every no: "What would make this a yes?"
If 5 of 5 say yes fast, the next 5 buyers hear a higher price.
If 0 or 1 of 5 says yes, check the buyer and the offer before you touch the price. It's usually the wrong person or an unclear outcome.
If someone says it's too expensive, offer the smaller option. Cut the scope, never just the price.
bullets: Raise when you're booked up, when almost nobody pushes back, when you have results to show or when you add real value.

Let demand set the pace. Creator Nick Saraev launched his paid community at $28 a month with a 400-member cap, then raised the price in steps as seats filled, reaching $128 within about 10 days by his own account.
Raise for new buyers first. Give existing customers notice, explain why, and honor anything you promised.
Warn, don't surprise. In 2011 Netflix moved people who wanted DVDs and streaming from $9.99 to $15.98 a month and lost about 800,000 US subscribers in one quarter.
sections.example: Jordan offers Standard to 5 gym owners from his interviews. Two sign up, two say "let me think" and one says no because he wants a fixed bill. Jordan keeps the price, offers the no Starter instead, and writes his rule: if the first 3 gyms average 1 new member a month for 60 days, new gyms start at $200 base. Illustrative numbers.
sections.template:
Hi [NAME], a quick heads-up. Starting [DATE, AT LEAST 30 DAYS OUT], my price for new clients goes from $[OLD] to $[NEW], because [REAL REASON: MORE INCLUDED, RESULTS, DEMAND].

You keep $[OLD] until [DATE OR "FOR AS LONG AS YOU STAY", WHATEVER YOU PROMISED]. Nothing changes in what you get.

Thanks for being one of my first customers. Reply with any questions.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Pricing from your costs or your nerves. Start from the buyer's value and what they pay today, then check your margin.

Being the cheapest because you're new. Be new and better at one thing. A founding price is fine if it's real: Membership.io, tied to membership coach Stu McLaren, suggests about 20% to 30% below the eventual price, raised once results are proven (2026).

Assuming cheap sells easier. In RevenueCat's 2026 subscription app report, high-priced apps had a median 2.8% of downloads become paid users, against 1.4% for low-priced apps. That's correlation, not proof, but cheap isn't automatically easier.
Asking "Would you buy this?" and counting the yes. Ask the four questions, then ask for payment.
Discounting the moment someone hesitates. Change the scope instead and offer the smaller option.
Charging by the hour for work you'll get faster at. Jonathan Stark's point in Hourly Billing Is Nuts: hourly pricing punishes you for getting better. Price the result.
Pay-for-performance on results you can't track. Agree in writing how a result is counted before you start.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: Monetizing Innovation by Madhavan Ramanujam and Georg Tacke (2016): read the willingness-to-pay chapters before you build anything else.
Pricing Creativity by Blair Enns (2018): how to present three options and stop selling your hours.
Hourly Billing Is Nuts by Jonathan Stark: a short read on moving service work from hours to value.
Predictably Irrational by Dan Ariely (2008), chapter 1: why every price gets judged against the options next to it.
Mind Your Pricing Cues by Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester (Harvard Business Review, 2003): what 9-endings and sale signs do, and why overusing them backfires.

sections.heading: Your output and next step
sections.body:
Fill in the fields below: your ROI story, competitor range, buyer answers, model, price or three options, both framings and your test rule. Your calculator results save with them, so you can ask Eli's Playbook for feedback on the whole picture.

Next, paste your framings and options into The One-Page Offer, then onto your page with the Landing Page Brief. Check the full model in the Business Model Worksheet, and track revenue per sale every week in the Founder KPI Dashboard. Planning to pay for ads? Take what one sale earns you into the Launch Budget Calculator first.

Sales tax, invoicing and payment rules vary by place, so check local rules or ask a licensed professional before you charge regularly.
