resources.title: Landing Page Brief
resources.summary: Turn your One-Page Offer and your customers' own words into a one-goal page that says what you sell, proves it honestly and asks for one action.
resources.output: A message mining sheet, a filled landing page brief, block-by-block page copy you can paste into Carrd, Shopify or Framer, and a test plan with a pass mark.

sections.heading: Your page has one job
sections.body:
A landing page is not a website. It has one job: get one kind of visitor to take one action. Anything that doesn't help that action is in the way.

Julian Shapiro's landing page guide sums it up as a formula: purchase rate equals desire minus labor and confusion. Desire is how much they want the result. Labor is every tap, field and scroll you ask for. Confusion is every second they spend wondering what you sell. Most first pages lose on confusion, not design.

So the fix is rarely a prettier template. It's a clearer headline in your customer's own words, and it's already sitting in your interview notes.

In about 75 minutes you'll mine those words and decide what visitors already know. Then you'll fill nine blocks in order, find honest proof with zero customers, build on a cheap tool and test the page on real people before you share it.

sections.heading: Steal your headline from your customers
sections.body:
Joanna Wiebe of Copyhackers teaches that you don't invent good copy. You find it. Her name for the method is message mining: collect the exact words customers use about their problem, then build the page out of them. Their words work because they're already in the reader's head.

You need 20 to 30 raw phrases. Five good conversations usually give you that. If you haven't had five yet, run Validation Interview Scripts first. A page built on guesses is a guess with a nice font.
steps: Set a 30-minute timer. Open your interview notes, DMs, comments and voice memos.
Add competitor reviews from Google, Amazon or the app store, and Reddit threads where your customer vents. Middle reviews, 2 to 4 stars, often say what's missing.
Copy 20 to 30 phrases word for word into the mining sheet. Don't fix their grammar.
Sort each into a row: pain, result, what they tried, objection, or their name for it.
Tally repeats. A pain or result phrase from 3 or more people is a headline candidate. A repeated objection goes in your FAQ.
If nothing repeats after 5 conversations, your customer is too broad. Narrow it and talk to 5 more people.

sections.heading: Decide who's arriving and what they know
sections.body:
In Breakthrough Advertising (1966), Eugene Schwartz argued that copy has to start where the reader's awareness already is. Copywriters now teach his idea as five stages: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware and most aware. The less someone knows, the more page you need before you mention a price.

Your first visitors will mostly come from one of three places. Pick the main one, then fill the brief below. Pull your voice words from the brand sheet in Brand Basics in an Afternoon, and the offer lines from The One-Page Offer.
bullets: Warm: people you've interviewed or DM'd. They're product aware. Lead with the offer and the price, and keep it short.
Followers who know you, not the offer: solution aware. Lead with the result, then how it works, then the offer.
Cold: strangers from a post or a search. Treat them as problem aware. Open with the pain in their words and earn the price with proof.
Skip the unaware for now. People who don't know they have the problem need content first. Start with 30-Day Content Calendar.
sections.template:

WHO

THEIR WORDS (from your mining sheet)

Headline draft: [built from the phrases above]

BUILD
Tool: [Carrd / Shopify / Framer / Gumroad / Stan / Notion / Claude-written page]
After the click: [confirmation they get] and [how you get notified]

sections.heading: The nine blocks, in order
sections.body:
Every first page needs the same nine blocks. On a phone, people read top to bottom, and each block answers the next question in their head. Shapiro warns that the further you stray from a standard layout, the more confused visitors get. Get creative with words, not structure.

Give the page one goal and one place to click. Unbounce calls the ratio of links to goals the attention ratio, and says it should be 1:1. Cut the menu, the social icons and any 'learn more' link that leaves the page. Keep a contact email and your policies in the footer.
steps: Headline: what you sell and the result, in their words. Shapiro's test: reading only this line, would they know exactly what you sell?
Subhead: one or two sentences on who it's for, how it works and how fast.
Button: a verb plus the result, like 'Book my rewrite', visible before any scrolling.
Proof strip: one true line under the button. 'Built from 14 interviews with nursing majors' counts.
How it works: 3 steps from paying to having the result, so nobody wonders what happens next.
Benefits: 3 outcomes they can picture. 'Your sneakers look new in 48 hours' beats 'premium cleaning solution'.
Offer: what's included, the price as the smallest true number and a guarantee you'll honor every time.
FAQ: your top 3 objections from the mining sheet, each answered in one or two plain sentences.
Final button: the same action and words as the first. Never a second, different ask.
sections.example:
Priya, 20, rewrites resumes for internship applicants. Illustrative.
Traffic: warm, from 12 interviews and her major's group chat, so the page stays short.
Headline: Get more interviews from the same applications.
Subhead: A line-by-line resume rewrite for internship applicants. Send it tonight, get it back in 48 hours.
Button: Book my rewrite
Proof strip: Built from 12 conversations with applicants and 2 campus recruiters.
How it works: Upload your resume. Get the rewrite plus a 10-minute call. Apply the same week.
Benefits: Recruiters see your best work in the top third. Every bullet shows a result, not a duty. You stop guessing what's wrong.
Offer: $49 once. One round of edits. Full refund if you don't think it's better.
FAQ: Is this just AI? Does it work for my major? What if I hate it?
Final button: Book my rewrite

sections.heading: Write the copy, then cut it
sections.body:
Draft the page in the template below, block by block. Then run every line through Harry Dry's three tests from Marketing Examples. A line that fails all three gets cut.

Eli's rule applies here: solve problems, don't sell products. Every line should be about their result, not your features.
bullets: "Can I visualize it?" 'Back in 48 hours' paints a picture. 'Fast turnaround' doesn't.
"Can I falsify it?" 'Every bullet shows a result' can be checked. 'World-class quality' can't, so nobody believes it.
"Can nobody else say this?" 'Built from 12 interviews with applicants at your school' is yours. 'We care about our customers' is everyone's.
Read it out loud. If a line sounds like an ad, rewrite it the way you'd text a friend.

Guarantee: [one plain sentence you will honor every time]

sections.heading: Honest proof when you have no customers yet
sections.body:
Trust beats everything else in sales. That's Eli's rule, and fake proof breaks it the second someone spots it. You don't need testimonials to launch. You need something true that lowers the risk of saying yes.

Dropbox had no public product when Drew Houston put up a short video of it working in 2008. He later said the beta waiting list jumped from 5,000 to 75,000 people. A demo is proof. So is a photo of real work, a number you can back up or a promise you'll keep.
bullets: Show the work: a 60-second screen recording, a before-and-after photo or a shot of your setup. Real beats polished.
Count your research: 'Built after 15 conversations with families on the north side.'
Write a founder note: 2 or 3 sentences on why you, and what you've already done with this problem.
Run a free pilot for 2 or 3 people in exchange for honest feedback and written permission to share the results.
Offer a guarantee you can afford to honor every time. Taking the risk off them shows you believe in it.
Make a real founding-customer offer: a lower price for your first 10 customers that ends when the 10th one pays. Show spots left only if the count is real.
Leave a block out before you fill it with something made up.

Out of bounds: invented testimonials, stock photos posed as customers, review counts you don't have, logos you haven't earned and timers that reset. The FTC's 2022 staff report on dark patterns names fake countdown timers and false scarcity as deceptive design. Rules vary by country, so check yours.

sections.heading: Ugly and live beats pretty and late
sections.body:
Buffer, 2010. Before writing code, Joel Gascoigne put up two pages. The first explained the app and had a 'Plans and pricing' button. The second said it wasn't ready yet and asked for an email. Once sign-ups came in, he added a page of paid plans in between to see if people still clicked with a price attached. His write-up is called 'Idea to Paying Customers in 7 Weeks'. Lesson: test the click on the price, not just interest.

DoorDash, 2013. Stanford students put up a bare page called PaloAltoDelivery.com with PDF menus from local restaurants and their own phone number. When orders came in, they drove the food over themselves. Lesson: a plain page that takes real orders beats a polished one that takes none.

Harry's, 2013. Before launch, the razor brand ran a two-page site: an email signup, then a referral page. Rewards grew with each friend who joined, from shave cream at 5 referrals to a year of free shaving at 50. Co-founder Jeff Raider wrote on Tim Ferriss's blog that it gathered more than 100,000 emails in one week, 77% of them through referrals. Most of the fraud hit the top tier. Lesson: if your goal is a waitlist, give a real reward for sharing, keep the top prize modest and make sure every reward ships.

sections.heading: Build it in an afternoon
sections.body:
Pick the tool that matches what you sell and build today. You can rebuild once you have customers. Prices and plans change, so check each pricing page before you pay.

Speed beats polish on a phone. Google's research found that as mobile load time goes from 1 second to 10 seconds, the chance a visitor bounces rises 123% (Google/SOASTA Research, 2017). Compress your images, skip autoplay video and use one font.

Set up your checkout in your own name a few days before launch. Payment platforms verify your identity and bank details before they pay you out, and that can take a few days.
bullets: A service or a waitlist: Carrd. One page with a form or a booking link. As of late 2026, its free plan covers 3 one-page sites on a Carrd address, and your own domain plus forms start at Pro Standard, $19 a year. Confirm on carrd.co before you pay.
Physical products: Shopify. One product page holding your nine blocks is enough. Check its pricing page for the current plans and trial.
Digital products like templates or guides: Gumroad or Stan, which handle checkout and delivery for you.
More design control: Framer.
A fast first test: a Notion page published to the web.
Want it coded for you: paste your brief and page copy into Claude and ask for a single-file HTML page, or build and host it on Replit.
sections.template:
You are helping me write and build a one-page landing page for my first business. Use only the facts below. Never invent testimonials, numbers, reviews, logos or urgency.

BRIEF
[paste your filled Landing Page Brief]

MY CUSTOMERS' WORDS
[paste your best 10 phrases from the mining sheet]

1. Write the page copy in this order: headline, subhead, button, proof strip, how it works, 3 benefits, offer, FAQ, final button. Plain, short, mobile-first. Reuse my customers' phrases.
2. Give me 5 more headlines built from their exact words, and pick the one that says most plainly what I sell.
3. Flag any line a competitor could also say, and rewrite it so it's specific to me.
4. When I say 'build it', make a single-file HTML page: one button to [your checkout, booking or form link], no menu, one font, fast on a phone.

sections.heading: Test it before you share the link
sections.body:
How you do one thing is how people think you do everything. That's Eli's rule, and a broken button proves it. Test on your own phone first, then on real people.

For a rough yardstick, the median landing page converted about 6.6% of visitors across 41,000 pages (Unbounce Conversion Benchmark Report, 2024 data). Most of those pages were built by marketing teams for paid traffic, so treat it as a loose range, not a target. Under 100 visitors, count people and ask why. Percentages lie at small numbers.
steps: Five-second test: show the page for 5 seconds to 3 people who've never seen it. Ask what you sell and who it's for. If 2 of 3 can't say, rewrite the headline and subhead.
Phone check: open it on mobile data. Nothing cut off, the button easy to tap, loaded before you can count to 3.
Click test: make a real purchase or booking yourself, then refund or cancel it. Confirm the buyer got a confirmation and you got notified.
Honesty check: delete any claim you couldn't prove if a customer asked.
Ask 5 people from your interviews: 'Would you buy this, and if not, what's stopping you?' Fix the block their answers point to.

Share it with 20 to 50 warm contacts and wait 72 hours. 0 actions: rework the offer or the who in The One-Page Offer. Clicks but no finish: fix the checkout or form. 2 or more buyers: keep the page and open First Launch Checklist.
sections.example: Illustrative. Priya mined 12 interviews and heard 'I apply everywhere and hear nothing' from 7 people. Her first headline was 'Resume Rewrites by Priya'. In the five-second test, 2 of 3 people thought she sold templates. She switched to 'Get more interviews from the same applications', and both new testers got it right. She sent the page to 40 people from her major's group chat. 9 clicked the button, 3 booked at $49 and 2 asked if it works for grad school applications. She added that question to the FAQ, kept the page and opened the First Launch Checklist.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Using your business name as the headline. Nobody knows it yet. Say what you sell and what changes.
Asking for two things. 'Book a call' plus 'Follow us' splits attention. Pick one goal and cut the other link.
Listing features instead of outcomes. 'Premium materials' says nothing. Say what they'll see, save or stop worrying about.
Writing a clever headline. If it needs explaining, it fails the five-second test.
Faking urgency. A timer that resets or 'only 3 left' that isn't true breaks trust for good. Use real deadlines only.
Polishing for a week before anyone sees it. Ship a plain version today and fix what real visitors tell you.

sections.heading: Go deeper
sections.body: Next: plan launch week with First Launch Checklist, and write the posts that send people to your page with Hook & Caption Bank. Paste your 5 headline drafts into Ask Eli's Playbook and ask which one says most plainly what you sell, then test the winner on real people.
bullets: Julian Shapiro, 'Landing Pages', in the free growth guide on julian.com: the purchase rate formula, the header test and a page template.
Joanna Wiebe, Copyhackers: search 'Copyhackers message mining' to see how to pull headlines out of reviews.
Eugene Schwartz, Breakthrough Advertising (1966): the stages of awareness from the source. Dense, but it explains why warm and cold pages differ.
Harry Dry, Marketing Examples: short teardowns of real copy. Use his three tests on every headline.
Unbounce, 'attention ratio': a short read on why one page gets one goal.

resources.title: Brand Basics in an Afternoon
resources.summary: Set your positioning, name, voice, two colors, one font, a wordmark and matching handles in one afternoon, for $0 and without an agency.
resources.output: A one-page brand sheet: an onliness line, a name that passed 5 checks, three voice rules, two contrast-checked colors, one font, a wordmark in two sizes and one handle everywhere.
resources.framework: How you do one thing is how people think you do everything

sections.heading: Your brand is a gut feeling you earn
sections.body:
Marty Neumeier's The Brand Gap (2003) defines a brand as a person's gut feeling about a product, service or company. Not your logo. Not your colors. The feeling people get from every interaction with you.

Eli's rule says the same thing from the other side: how you do one thing is how people perceive you do most things. A sloppy DM, a blurry profile photo or a page with three fonts tells people your work is probably sloppy too.

So a first brand doesn't need to be impressive. It needs to be clear and consistent. Make a few simple choices today and repeat them everywhere for at least 6 months.

This playbook runs in five timed blocks, about 2 hours, for $0. You'll pick who it's for and write a line nobody else can claim, test a name, set three voice rules, choose two colors and one font that pass a contrast check, and lock one handle everywhere. If you're still choosing colors at hour four, stop. Done and consistent beats perfect and late.

sections.heading: Block 1, 25 minutes: who it's for and why you're the only one
sections.body:
Seth Godin's This Is Marketing (2018) argues for the smallest viable audience: the smallest group you could serve and still keep the business alive. Small feels risky. It's the opposite. A narrow who makes every other choice on this page easy, from your name to your first post.

Then write an onliness statement, the test from Marty Neumeier's Zag (2006). Finish the sentence: our brand is the only [category] that [benefit]. If you can't finish it, or a competitor could say the same thing, you're not different yet. Eli puts it bluntly: your product likely sucks, so prove it's better than your competition.

Liquid Death is the loud version. Founder Mike Cessario sells canned water with heavy metal branding and the line 'Murder your thirst'. Water is about as boring as a category gets, and nobody confuses Liquid Death with anyone else.
steps: Write your customer in one line with 3 details: who, where and what situation. 'Night-shift nurses in Des Moines who meal prep on Sundays' beats 'busy people'.
Name 2 places they gather, online or off. If you can't, narrow the who or pick a different one.
Fill in the onliness line: our [business] is the only [category] that [benefit] for [who].
Run the swap test: put a competitor's name in your line. If it's still true, change the how or narrow the who until it isn't.
Write the plain line you'll say when someone asks what you do: "I help [who] get [result] without [pain]."
Read both lines to 2 people who fit the who. If neither says 'that's me' or asks how it works, rewrite.
sections.example:
Lawn care. Onliness: Northside Lawn Co is the only lawn crew on the north side that texts you a photo when the job's done. Plain line: I help busy north-side families get a clean yard every week without chasing a contractor.
Print-on-demand. Onliness: the only running shirt brand written by college runners, for college runners. Plain line: Shirts for college runners who want gear that's actually funny.
Tutoring. Onliness: the only SAT math tutor in town who teaches from your own practice-test mistakes. Plain line: I help high school juniors raise their SAT math score without boring prep books.

sections.heading: Block 2, 35 minutes: a name you can say out loud
sections.body:
A name doesn't make a business. Plenty of names sound strange until the business behind them is good. Spend 35 minutes, not 3 weeks. Eli's rule: no idea is perfect, so don't ideate for too long.

Alexandra Watkins, author of Hello, My Name Is Awesome (2014), gives two filters. A strong name passes SMILE: suggestive, meaningful, imagery, legs and emotional. A weak one trips SCRATCH: spelling-challenged, copycat, restrictive, annoying, tame, curse of knowledge and hard to pronounce. You don't need all five SMILE traits. You need zero SCRATCH problems.
steps: Write 20 options in 10 minutes. Mix plain (Northside Lawn Co), descriptive (Fresh Kicks Cleaning), your own name (Maya Tutors) and one-word ideas.
Cross out anything that trips SCRATCH. Say each survivor once to a friend. If they can't spell it, cut it.
Cross out anything too narrow to grow into, unless you want to stay narrow.
Search each finalist on Google, Instagram, TikTok and the app store. Drop any name a business in your space already uses.

Search trademarks for free on the USPTO website if you're in the US, or at your country's trademark office. A live mark on a similar name for similar products means pick another. This is awareness, not legal advice, so ask a licensed attorney before you spend real money on a name.
If you plan to register the business, check your state's business name search, usually on the Secretary of State's site.
Say your top pick out loud to 3 people. If anyone asks you to repeat it, keep looking.
sections.example: Illustrative. A short-form video editing service tried 'Kinetic Frame Studio', 'CutReady' and 'Edits by Jordan'. Kinetic Frame was hard to remember. CutReady's handle was taken on TikTok. Edits by Jordan won: easy to say, leads with personal brand, nothing similar in Trademark Search, and the handle was free on every platform.

sections.heading: Block 3, 15 minutes: three voice rules
sections.body:
Voice is how you sound in captions, emails and DMs. Mailchimp's public Content Style Guide is a good model: its voice stays the same everywhere, while its tone shifts with the reader's situation. You can joke in a caption. You don't joke in a refund email.

Donald Miller's Building a StoryBrand (2017) adds one rule for every bio and caption: your customer is the hero and you're the guide. Lead with their problem and the result they want. Bring yourself in second, as the person with the plan.

Glossier shows what a known voice is worth. Emily Weiss started the beauty blog Into the Gloss in 2010 and launched Glossier in 2014, to readers who already knew how the brand talked.
bullets: Direct, not rude. Say 'Here's what's holding your resume back', not 'Your resume is bad'.
Friendly, not fake. Say 'Glad you reached out', not 'OMG we LOVE you!!!'.
Confident, not hype. Say 'Back in 48 hours', not 'The fastest service on the planet'.
Write your own 3 words with a this-not-that line for each. Pick words a customer would use about you, not words from a motivational poster.
Read your last 5 captions or DMs out loud. Rewrite any that break a rule.
sections.template:
BIO (customer first, you second)
[Result they want] for [who].
[How you help, in 5 to 8 words].
[One true proof line].
[One call to action: link, DM keyword or booking]

VOICE RULES
[word 1]: [this], not [that]
[word 2]: [this], not [that]
[word 3]: [this], not [that]
Tone: [where jokes are fine] / [where you're always plain and calm]

sections.heading: Block 4, 30 minutes: two colors, one font, a wordmark
sections.body:
Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow (2010) argues that being distinctive matters more than being different. People buy brands they can recognize in a second. Distinctive assets are the colors, characters, sounds and phrases that say 'this is you' before anyone reads your name. They only work if you repeat them.

Duolingo's green owl, Duo, is the famous case. The same owl stars in its TikTok, sits in the app and shows up in its reminders. One asset, repeated everywhere, for years.

Keep your system tiny so you can actually keep it consistent.
steps: Pick one main color and one accent. The accent goes on buttons and highlights. Everything else stays white, black or gray.
Write down the exact hex codes so you never eyeball them again.

Check contrast on anything with text on it. WCAG, the web's accessibility standard, asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Paste your codes into the free WebAIM Contrast Checker. If a pair fails, darken the color or switch the text to black.
Pick one font from Google Fonts. Bold for headings, regular for everything else.
Make a wordmark: your name typed in your font and main color. That's a real logo, and it's free.
Export a square version for profile photos and a wide one for your page header in Canva's free plan. Shrink the square to thumbnail size. If you can't read it, simplify.
Pick one distinctive asset you'll repeat in every post: a color, a catchphrase, a sound, a character or a video format.

sections.heading: Block 5, 15 minutes: one handle everywhere
sections.body: Matching handles make you easier to find and make a tiny business look established. Grab the same one everywhere today, even on platforms you won't use yet.
steps: Search your handle on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and the one other platform your customers use most.
If your exact name is taken, add a simple word: get, hq, co or your city. Keep it identical on every platform.
Claim it on all of them in one sitting.
Use your square wordmark or a clear photo of your face. If you lead with personal brand, your face usually wins.
Paste your bio line into every profile and add one link: your landing page or booking link.
Post one piece of content that says what you do, so a new visitor never lands on an empty profile.

sections.heading: Your one-page brand sheet
sections.body:
Put everything on one page. Save it in Notion or your notes app and send it to anyone who makes something for you, from a friend designing a flyer to a freelancer editing a video. That's how you stay consistent without thinking about it.

Write a do-not-change date at the bottom, 6 months out. Change your brand when customers give you a reason, not when you get bored.
sections.example:
Illustrative. Jordan, 19, edits short-form video for local gyms.
Who: owners of independent gyms within 30 minutes of Columbus who post less than once a week.
Onliness: Edits by Jordan is the only video editor in town who films and edits inside your gym in one visit.
Bio: Reels that fill your classes, for local gyms. Filmed in one visit, posted for a month. Link below.
Voice: direct, not rude. Hyped, not fake. Short, not cold.
Look: main #111111, accent #FF5A1F, font Inter. White text on #111111 scores 18.9:1. White on the orange only scored 3.1:1, so his buttons use near-black text at 6.1:1.
Distinctive asset: every Reel opens on the same 1-second whistle.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Spending the afternoon on the logo. It's the least important line on the sheet. A typed wordmark is enough for year one.
Choosing 'everyone' as the audience. If you can't reach 10 of them this week, the who is too broad.
Picking voice words nobody can act on. 'Professional' and 'quality' don't change a caption. Write the this-not-that line or pick another word.
Using colors that fail contrast. Pale text on a bright color looks fine on a laptop and disappears on a phone in sunlight. Check 4.5:1.
Running different handles on different apps. People search once. Make it identical everywhere.
Copying a big brand's look. You'll read as a knockoff, and you could step on their trademark.
Redesigning when you're bored. Distinctive assets work through repetition. Change only when customers give you a reason.

resources.title: First Launch Checklist
resources.summary: A day -14 to day +7 plan: set up payment safely, pre-sell to people who know you, open and close a real launch, then make the call.
resources.output: A dated launch calendar, a tested checkout, launch messages ready to send, feedback questions for every buyer and a written kill, pause or double down call.

sections.heading: Launch to people, not to the internet
sections.body:
A first launch isn't a big reveal. It's a short sales sprint aimed at people who already know you. It has a real open date, a real close date and a goal you set before any numbers come in.

The people who teach launches agree on the order. Jeff Walker's Launch builds interest before the cart opens, then closes it on a deadline. Alex Hormozi's $100M Leads puts warm outreach first, because people who know you answer. Noah Kagan's Million Dollar Weekend and Pat Flynn's Will It Fly? both push you to get paid before you build more. This checklist shrinks all of it to a phone, under $100 and under 3 hours a week.

Inside: a day -14 to day +7 calendar, setup checks that keep you out of trouble and launch messages to copy. Then a worked example and a day +7 debrief that ends in one call: kill, pause or double down.

Eli's biggest early mistake was "thinking it wasn't possible for me for way too long." The fix starts with a date.
steps: Pick day 0, your launch day, 14 days from today. Pick a close day 5 days after it.
Write your goal as one number, like 10 paying customers or $300 in pre-orders.
Put day -14, day 0, day +5 and day +7 in your calendar with reminders.
Text 3 people your launch date and ask them to check on you that day.

sections.heading: Set the goal, the window and the rules
sections.body:
Decide what counts as a win before launch day. Without a number, every result feels like a win or a disaster, and you learn nothing.

A launch needs a window: a day it opens and a day it closes. A deadline gets people to decide now instead of someday. When Pat Flynn launched his Smart From Scratch course, 44 percent of sales came on the final day (Pat Flynn launch report, 2017). His second-best day was the day the cart opened. Expect the same shape. Your two big days are day 0 and close day.

The deadline only works if it is real. Real reasons to close: you can only make 20 this batch, the intro price ends for good, pre-orders close before you order stock, or you only have 4 client spots. Out of bounds: countdown timers that reset, "only 3 left" when there are 30, and a "last chance" you plan to repeat next week. The FTC's 2022 staff report on dark patterns calls out fake countdown timers and false scarcity claims.

A drop is the cleanest real deadline for a product: a limited batch, released on a set date, gone when it's gone. Eli's e-commerce brand sold in drops. The result: $50K in gross sales from a part-time e-commerce brand; first drop sold out; customers in 35 of 50 states. Eli's results aren't typical or a promise of what you'll earn.
bullets: Goal: one number by close day, such as 10 customers or $300.
Window: open on day 0, close on day +5. Write the true reason it closes in one sentence.
Double down if you hit the goal, or if 3 or more people bought without you pushing.
Kill this version if 30 or more warm asks, each with one follow-up, produced zero buyers and zero questions.
Pause and fix if you land anywhere in between. Change one thing and relaunch.

sections.heading: Day -14 to -8: make sure people can pay and you can deliver
sections.body: This week has one job: a stranger could pay you and get what they paid for without you fixing anything live. Quality before growth. A broken first order costs more than a late launch.
steps: Day -14: Finish The One-Page Offer and the Landing Page Brief. If you can't say who it's for, what they get and the price in one sentence, fix that first.
Day -13: Pick one checkout. A Stripe or PayPal payment link works for a service with no website. Shopify fits physical products. Set up one, not three.
Day -13: Finish your checkout's account setup in your own name. Payment platforms verify your identity and bank details before they pay you out, and that can take a few days.
Day -12: Buy from yourself with a real card, then refund it. Check the receipt, the confirmation message and the payout date.
Day -12: Write a 3-line refund policy: the time limit, the condition and how to ask. Put it on your page and in your confirmation message.

Day -11: If you collect emails, add one line under the signup box: what you'll send, how often, and that they can unsubscribe anytime. In the US, CAN-SPAM expects marketing email to have an honest sender and subject line and a valid postal address (a registered P.O. box counts). Unsubscribes must be honored within 10 business days. Details: the FTC's CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business.
Day -10: Write your delivery steps from "paid" to "done". Run one full test delivery with a friend and fix what breaks.

Day -9: Check registration and sales tax for where you live and what you sell. Physical products usually bring sales tax rules. If you sell through a marketplace, check whether it collects the tax for you. Use your state or country's official small business site, or ask a tax professional. This isn't legal or tax advice.
Day -8: Set up separate money tracking: a separate account, or at least one sheet with every sale and cost.
Day -8: Go or move. If the test purchase or test delivery failed, push day 0 back one week. A late launch beats a broken one.

sections.heading: Day -7 to -1: warm up your people
sections.body:
Your first buyers will come from people who already know you. When Monica Lent opened her paid community, Blogging for Devs, 69 people paid in the first week (Indie Hackers, 2020). All but 3 traced back to her newsletter, her waitlist or her Twitter followers. Almost every buyer already knew her.

Walker calls this stretch the prelaunch: before you sell, show people the problem, why you care and the work behind it. Shrunk to one week, that's two posts and a lot of one-on-one messages. Ask permission before you send a link. Someone who says "yes, send it" on day -5 is your warmest lead on day 0.
steps: Day -7: Build a warm list of 50 names: phone contacts, DMs, followers who reply, teammates, classmates, coworkers, clubs and everyone you interviewed. Star your top 10 likeliest buyers.
Day -7: Send the early-access DM below to your top 10, one at a time. Log every reply.
Day -6: Post the problem: one story or post about the problem you solve and why you care. No link yet.
Day -5: Send the early-access DM to the next 20 names.
Day -4: Post the work: making it, packing it, a test delivery or a before-and-after.
Day -3: Count the yeses. If fewer than 3 of your top 10 said "send it", ask 3 of them what would make it a yes, and fix that before day 0.
Day -2: Load everything: launch post, launch DMs, buyer welcome message and feedback questions.
Day -1: Send a one-line reminder to every yes: "Link comes tomorrow at [time]."

sections.heading: Day 0 to day +7: open, follow up, close
sections.body:
Launch day is a sales day, not a posting day. Personal messages first, posts second. Most of your sales will come from the people who said "send it".

Keep the cart open 5 days. That is long enough for busy people and short enough to stay real.
steps: Day 0: DM the link to everyone who said yes, one by one, by name. Never a group message.
Day 0: Post your launch post and story. Reply to every comment and DM the same day.
Day 0: Before bed, log messages sent, replies and sales.
Day +1: Message the rest of your warm list. Ask each day 0 buyer: "Know one person who'd want this?"
Day +2: Post proof: a first delivery, a customer reaction shared with permission, or the work in progress.
Day +3: Send one follow-up to every "maybe" and every no-reply. One message, friendly, easy to say no to.
Day +4: Answer the top objection in a post and in your page's FAQ.

Day +5: Close as promised. Send "closing tonight" only to people who showed interest, then actually close. If someone's payment failed before the deadline, honor the price. Flynn had buyers hit technical problems right before his close.

Day +6: Deliver the first orders with extra care. Paul Graham's essay Do Things That Don't Scale tells how Wufoo sent early users handwritten thank-you notes. A note costs nothing and gets remembered.
Day +7: Send every buyer the feedback questions, then run the debrief below.

sections.body: Rewrite each one in your own voice before day -2. Keep the personal first line. If a message sounds like an ad, rewrite it like a text to a friend. Outreach Scripts has more for every situation.

sections.heading: Day +7 debrief: kill, pause or double down
sections.body:
Numbers first, feelings second. Fill in the debrief, then apply the rules you wrote on day -14.

Eli's test for product-market fit: "People will want to pay for your product without you needing to sell it to them." One launch won't prove that, so look for early signs. Someone paid before you finished explaining. A buyer sent a friend. A stranger asked how to pay. When something works, ask why, then follow Eli's rule: "Do more of what works, not just more in general."
steps: Count: warm list size, messages sent, replies, buyers, revenue and refunds.
Work out two rates: replies divided by messages sent, and buyers divided by replies.
Find your best source: the message, post or person that brought the most buyers. Write one sentence on why it beat the rest.
Write the top 3 objections in buyers' and non-buyers' exact words.

Make the call with your day -14 rules. Double down: launch again in 2 to 4 weeks to the next ring of people, using what worked. Pause: change one thing (offer, price, audience or message) and relaunch. Kill this version: go back to Validation Interview Scripts before you build more.
Move your numbers into the Founder KPI Dashboard and pick next week's one priority in your Weekly CEO Review.
sections.example: Illustrative: Tyler, 19, cleans sneakers on campus for $25 a pair, $30 after launch week. On day -14 he sets a goal of 12 pairs and opens a Stripe payment link. His test delivery shows pickups take too long, so he adds two set pickup times. On day -7 he lists 48 names and DMs his top 10: 7 say send it. Day -5 adds 9 more yeses. On day 0, 6 of the 16 yeses buy, and his launch post brings 2 people he never messaged. The top question is "Will it ruin my suede?", so on day +4 he posts a before-and-after of his own suede pair. Follow-ups and the close-day message add 5 buyers. Debrief: 13 buyers, 15 pairs, $375. His best source was his top 10, because he had seen their shoes. The call: double down. He relaunches in 3 weeks to referrals from his first 13 and drops the flyers that brought nobody.

Following up five times. During launch, send one follow-up, then let it go.
Changing four things after launch. Change one, relaunch and compare.

resources.title: Launch Budget Calculator
resources.summary: Plan a capped first ad test: your break-even cost per sale, the platform rules that apply, and when to stop or double down, all decided before you spend.
resources.output: A capped test budget, your break-even cost per sale, a daily budget and test length that fit platform rules, and stop and double-down rules written before you spend.

sections.heading: Your first ad budget buys information
sections.body:
Paid ads can teach you a lot fast, and burn your money just as fast. Eli lists marketing money lost on ads among the years of lessons behind his wins. So treat your first test as buying information, not profit.

Cap it. Pick an amount you could lose completely without stress, without skipping a bill and without borrowing. That's a one-time test budget, not a monthly one.

Know what a small budget can and can't do. Meta's long-standing guidance is that an ad set needs about 50 results in 7 days to get through its learning phase, and that falling short can raise your cost per result. At $10 a day you won't get close to 50 sales a week. What you can buy is a clear read on what a click costs, whether strangers click and whether your page turns them into buyers.

Then decide, before you spend, what result means stop and what means keep going. The rest of this page gives you a go or no-go check, your break-even number, the platform rules that apply, a test you can read and exact stop and double-down rules.

sections.heading: Earn the right to spend: organic first
sections.body:
Paid traffic amplifies something that already works. It doesn't fix something that doesn't. Alex Hormozi's $100M Leads (2023) names four core ways to get customers: warm outreach, free content, cold outreach and paid ads. Paid ads are the only one where every lesson costs cash, so start with the free three.

Run this check before you spend a dollar. If any line fails, skip ads for now. Warm outreach and content cost time, not money, and they teach you faster.
steps: You've sold at full price to at least 3 people who aren't close friends or family.
People you sent to your page bought or booked, and you know roughly what share of them did.
You know your top three objections, and your page answers them.
You have one post or message that clearly beat the rest. That's your first ad.
You know your break-even cost per sale. The next section shows you how.
The ad account and the card are in your name, and the card's limit is no more than you can afford to lose.
sections.example: Gymshark is the classic case. Ben Francis started it in 2012, at 19, and its early growth came from fitness YouTubers wearing the clothes in front of exactly the buyers Gymshark wanted. The brand borrowed attention through people and content before it paid for attention at scale. Do the same: earn attention first, then buy more of it once you know what converts.

sections.heading: Know your break-even cost per sale
sections.body:
Your price is not what a sale earns you. Take the price, subtract everything it costs to deliver that order, and what's left is the most you can pay in ads for one sale and still break even.

Count everything: product or supplies, packaging, shipping you cover, app fees and payment processing. Card payments usually cost around 3% plus a small fixed fee per sale, and your payment app's pricing page shows the exact rate. Below break-even, every sale loses money, and more ad spend just loses it faster.
steps: Write your price.
Subtract your cash costs per order: supplies, packaging, shipping you pay and payment fees.
What's left is your break-even cost per sale. Write it in the worksheet, and enter your cost to deliver in the calculator.
If customers often buy again within 30 days, enter purchases per customer in the calculator. Count only repeat buys you've actually seen.
Aim for ads that cost half your break-even or less. That leaves room for refunds, returns and a bad week.
sections.example: Maya, 19, sells hand-poured candles for $28. Wax, jar, wick, label and box cost her $9.50, and payment fees about $1.50, so each candle costs $11 to deliver. Break-even is $17 a sale. Ads that cost more than $17 per candle sold lose money on every order. So before any ad, she adds a 3-candle set for $72 that costs her $30 to deliver. Break-even on the set is $42, which gives an ad far more room to work. Illustrative numbers.

sections.heading: Run the calculator with honest numbers
sections.body: Start with cautious guesses, then swap in real numbers after day 2 of your test. Treat the benchmarks below as rough ranges, not promises. Your niche, ad and audience can land far outside them.
bullets: Total test budget and days: your cap and how long the test runs. The calculator turns them into a daily budget. Plan for at least 7 days.

Cost per click: WordStream and LocaliQ's 2026 Facebook ads benchmarks put the average click at about $0.60 for traffic campaigns and $1.80 for lead campaigns. A TikTok link click averaged about $0.49 in Focus Digital's 2026 report. Plan with $1 until you have your own number.

Optional: if your dashboard shows cost per 1,000 impressions and click-through rate instead, enter those and the calculator works out your cost per click. Meta's median was about $15 per 1,000 impressions in Triple Whale's 2026 data.

Page conversion: of 100 visitors, how many buy or book. WordStream and LocaliQ's 2026 Meta lead campaigns converted about 8.5% of clicks into leads. Sales usually convert lower than sign-ups: Focus Digital's 2026 TikTok median conversion rate was about 1.6%. Plan as if strangers convert at half the rate your followers did.
Price, cost to deliver and purchases per customer: from the last section. The calculator compares every result to your break-even, not your price.
Read the outputs: expected visitors, sales and cost per sale, your daily budget, a learning-phase check, your pause point, and the chance of zero sales even if your guesses are right.
sections.example: Maya enters an $80 cap over 8 days, so $10 a day. She guesses $0.90 a click. Her page converted 4% of followers, so she plans for 2% from strangers. For the $72 set with a $30 cost, the calculator shows about 89 visitors, about 1.8 sales and $45 per sale against a $42 break-even. Verdict: near break-even, fine for learning, not for scaling. It also shows a 17% chance of zero sales even if every guess is right, so one empty week won't prove the idea is dead. Illustrative numbers.

sections.heading: Platform rules that change your plan
sections.body: Check these before you build a single ad. They decide whether you can run the test at all, and how small it can be. Rules change, so confirm each one in the platform's help center the day you launch.
bullets: Accounts: Google Ads requires account owners to be at least 18, and TikTok only lets account owners over 18 link to its ads tools. Check Meta's current terms before you start. Platforms may also ask you to verify your identity or business before ads run, so set the account up a few days before your test.

Minimum budgets: TikTok Ads Manager needs more than $50 a day per campaign budget and more than $20 a day per ad group, so a $100 TikTok test lasts 5 days at most. On Meta, Ads Manager shows the minimum daily budget for your goal while you set up the ad set.

Learning phase: expect your ad set to show "learning limited" and don't treat it as failure. Since 2024 some advertisers have seen Ads Manager ask for fewer results, as low as 10 in 3 days (Jon Loomer; Ben Heath), but a $10-a-day test misses even that for sales.

Teen audiences: since February 2023, Meta only lets advertisers target under-18s by age and location. When a TikTok audience includes under-18s, interest targeting, the Lead Generation objective and TikTok Shop sales campaigns are off the table.

Ad review: every ad is checked against the platform's advertising policies. Claims about results, health, money or before-and-after photos get extra scrutiny, so read the policy for your category before you write the ad.

sections.heading: Set up a test you can read
sections.body: A test you can't read is just spending. Keep it simple, so each number points to one cause.
steps: Run one offer, one landing page and one audience. Test two things at once and you won't know which one worked.
Make 2 or 3 ads from your best organic posts. Same offer, different hooks.

Pick what the platform optimizes for. If your checkout can report purchases back to the platform, optimize for purchases and expect learning limited, as Ben Heath advises. If it can't, optimize for landing page views and count sales yourself.
Set the daily budget from the calculator and run at least 7 days. Review on a 3-day cycle, and make no edits before day 3 unless something is broken.
Add a tracking link or a discount code, so you know which sales came from the ad.
Write your stop rule and double-down rule in the worksheet before you press publish.
sections.example: Before The 4-Hour Workweek had its name, Tim Ferriss ran small Google search ads, each with a different candidate title, and kept the one people clicked most. He wasn't selling anything yet. He was buying information cheaply, which is exactly what your first test should do.

Offer and price: [OFFER], $[PRICE]
Break-even cost per sale: $[PRICE MINUS COST TO DELIVER]
Cap: $[TOTAL] over [DAYS] days = $[DAILY] a day
Platform and account owner: [PLATFORM], verified and in my name
Audience: [WHO, WHERE, AGE RANGE]
Optimizing for: [PURCHASES / LANDING PAGE VIEWS]
Ads: [BEST POST 1], [BEST POST 2], [BEST POST 3]
Tracking: [LINK OR CODE]

Pause an ad when: it has spent $[2 x BREAK-EVEN] with zero sales
Stop the test when: the $[CAP] is spent and cost per sale is over $[BREAK-EVEN]
Double down when: cost per sale is under $[BREAK-EVEN] on 2 tests in a row
One change if it fails: [HOOK / AUDIENCE / HEADLINE / OFFER]
Review dates: day 3 [DATE], day 7 [DATE]

sections.heading: Read the numbers together
sections.body: Don't react to one number. Each pattern points to a different fix, so find the pattern first.
bullets: Low click-through and pricey clicks: the ad isn't stopping the scroll. Test a new hook or a new first 2 seconds before you touch the page.
Cheap clicks, almost no sales: people are curious, but the page or offer isn't convincing. Go back to the Landing Page Brief and The One-Page Offer.
Add-to-carts but no purchases: something at checkout is off, like surprise shipping, a broken button or missing trust signals. Buy from your own page on your phone and find it.
Cost per sale under your price but over break-even: you lose money on each sale. Raise order value or cut delivery cost before you spend more.
Cost per sale well under break-even: you found something. Don't scale yet. Confirm it on a second test first.

sections.heading: Kill, pause or double down
sections.body: Write these rules before the test starts, and don't edit them mid-test. When something works, Eli's rule is to ask why. What did this do that the things before it didn't? Then double down until it stops working. "Do more of what works, not just more in general."
bullets: Pause an ad once it has spent about 2 times your break-even cost per sale with zero sales. If the ad were truly selling at break-even, zero sales by then would happen about 1 time in 7 by bad luck, and about 1 in 20 at 3 times. So 2x is the impatient rule and 3x the patient one.

Know the pro standard. Media buyer Taylor Sicard judges an ad only after about 5 to 10 sales, or 5 to 10 times the target cost per sale in spend (2026). A $100 test can't get there, so compare ads on click-through and cost per click, and judge the offer on total sales.
Stop the test when the whole cap is spent and cost per sale is above break-even. Stopping is not failing. A stopped test with clear notes beats a lucky one you can't explain.
Change one thing, then rerun with the same cap: the hook, the audience, the page headline or the offer.
Double down only when cost per sale stays under break-even on two tests in a row. One good week can be luck.

Scale in small steps. TikTok's own guidance is to raise a budget by at most 40% at a time while an ad group is learning and 30% after, with at least 2 days between changes. Recheck cost per sale after every step on any platform.
Reuse the winning hook in your organic posts, and keep delivery quality up as orders grow. Eli's rule: a bad product kills a company faster than great marketing can grow it.
sections.example: After 8 days, Maya has spent $80 on 104 clicks at about $0.77 each. Six people added the set to their cart, and 1 bought. Clicks came in cheaper than her guess, so the ads work. The leak is checkout. On her phone, she sees an $8.50 shipping charge appear only at the last step. She changes one thing, showing shipping on the product page, and reruns the same $80 test. Illustrative numbers.
sections.template:
My rules for this test (written [DATE], not edited mid-test)

Pause: any ad that spends $[2 x BREAK-EVEN] with zero sales.
Stop: when $[CAP] is spent and cost per sale is over $[BREAK-EVEN].
Double down: cost per sale under $[BREAK-EVEN] on 2 tests in a row. Then raise the budget in small steps and recheck after each one.
The one thing I'll change first if it fails: [ONE CHANGE].
What I'll do if it works: [REUSE THE HOOK IN ORGANIC / RAISE BUDGET / ADD A SECOND AD].

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Boosting a random post and hoping. Advertise only the post that already beat your others for free.
Judging after one day. Wait until day 3 and about 100 clicks before you change anything.
Comparing cost per sale to your price. Compare it to break-even, after every delivery cost.
Editing ads every day. Meta's own advice is to avoid unnecessary edits that send an ad set back into learning.
Setting a monthly ad budget before you've run one test. Run one capped test, then decide.
Putting ad spend on a card you can't pay off in full. Spend only money you already have.
Scaling before delivery can keep up. Make sure you can fill twice the orders at the same quality first.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: $100M Leads by Alex Hormozi (2023): read the warm outreach and paid ads chapters to see where ads fit once an offer already sells.
Traction by Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares (2015): the Bullseye method for testing channels cheaply before you commit money to one.
The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss (2007): the section on testing demand with small ad spends before you build.
Meta Business Help Center, About the learning phase and About learning limited: the official rules on results, edits and budgets.
Jon Loomer's blog on Meta ads: plain-English tests of how Meta's ad delivery actually behaves, written by a long-time practitioner.

sections.heading: Your output and next step
sections.body:
You now have a capped test budget, a break-even cost per sale, a daily budget and test length that fit the platform rules, and stop and double-down rules written before you spend. Your calculator results save with the worksheet. After the test, enter your real numbers and compare.

Next, build the ads with the Campaign Planner tool, fix leaks with the Landing Page Brief and log results in the Founder KPI Dashboard. If the math doesn't work at any realistic cost per click, go back to the Pricing Worksheet or The One-Page Offer before you go back to ads, and recheck your channels in the Business Model Worksheet.

This is a planning tool, not financial advice. Only spend money you can afford to lose.

resources.aiPrompt: Check that the test cap is a one-time amount they could lose without stress, and that they have organic proof first: at least 3 full-price sales to people outside close friends and family and one post that beat the rest; if not, tell them to skip ads for now and send them to Outreach Scripts. Check that the break-even cost per sale subtracts every delivery cost, including payment fees and shipping they cover, and call any plan whose expected cost per sale is above break-even a learning test, not a profit test. Check that the daily budget and test length meet the platform's minimums and run at least 7 days, that the optimization choice fits what their checkout can track. Check that the stop rule names a dollar amount (about 2 times break-even with zero sales, or the full cap) and a date, and that the double-down rule needs cost per sale under break-even on two tests and scales in small steps. The most common weak answer is a vague rule like 'stop if it isn't working': rewrite it for them with their own numbers. Send them to the Landing Page Brief if clicks are cheap but sales are not, and to the Campaign Planner tool to build the ad concepts.

resources.title: The Simple Operations Stack
resources.summary: The fewest tools and the simplest money setup to run a first business: one tool per job, $0 to start, business money kept apart from yours.
resources.output: Your stack on one page (six jobs, one tool each, cost and upgrade trigger), a tested checkout and a money setup: separate account, receipts folder and a taxes bucket.

sections.heading: Six jobs, one tool each, $0 to start
sections.body:
Software feels like progress. It isn't. Every new tool is another login, another bill and another place a customer's details get lost. A first business needs six jobs covered: getting paid, tracking people, keeping notes, email, booking and tracking money. Use one tool per job, and pay $0 a month until a free plan actually stops you.

Start with what you already own. Sahil Lavingia, who built Gumroad, argues in The Minimalist Entrepreneur (2021) for building as little as possible: do the work by hand, with tools you already have, until the work proves it needs more. Your phone, a Gmail account, Google Sheets and Google Calendar already cover four of the six jobs.

Money is the one job to set up properly on day one. Keep business money apart from personal money from your first sale. It makes pricing, taxes and every decision after easier.

Eli's rule: your business is only as valuable as it is when you aren't there to run it. Simple, written-down systems are the first step toward that.

Inside: the $0 tool for each job and the exact trigger to upgrade, the payment setup that fits what you sell, what payment platforms ask you for, a one-afternoon money setup and your stack on one page.

sections.heading: Start with what you already have
sections.body:
Ben Francis started Gymshark in 2012 at 19, sewing and screen-printing gym wear in his parents' garage, while delivering pizzas. The software and the warehouse came later, once orders demanded them.

Pieter Levels runs several products alone, including Nomad List and Photo AI, on deliberately plain tech: simple PHP and jQuery pages on a single server. Boring tools let one person run a lot. The lesson from both: start with what you have, and let real demand decide what you buy.
steps: List the apps on your phone that already do one of the six jobs: Gmail, Google Calendar, Sheets, Notes, your bank's app.
Give each job its $0 default from the next section, unless something you already use does it.
Spend nothing on software this week. Write down every moment a free tool slows you down. That list picks your first paid tool, if you need one at all.

sections.heading: The six jobs and your $0 default
sections.body: Each job gets one default tool and one upgrade trigger. The trigger is a specific event, not a feeling. Plans below are as of late 2026, so check current pricing before you sign up.
bullets: Getting paid: a payment link or checkout from Stripe, Square, PayPal or Shopify. Pick by what you sell, in the next section.
Tracking people: a Google Sheet with the columns below. Attio, from Eli's stack, has a free plan. Move when you track 30 or more open conversations, or you've missed a follow-up twice in a month.

Notes and docs: Google Docs or Notion, with one page called HQ. Notion's free plan is enough for one person. Add Granola for call notes once you have customer calls every week. Check Granola's current free plan limits.
Email: a free Gmail address used only for the business. Move to Google Workspace when you buy a domain and email customers every week. Workspace is a paid plan per user, so check current pricing.
Booking: Google Calendar's appointment schedule or Calendly's free plan. One link, two or three fixed time blocks a week.

Tracking money: a separate account plus an income and expense sheet, or Wave's free plan. Check that Wave serves your country. Move to QuickBooks when an accountant asks for it or bookkeeping takes more than an hour a week. QuickBooks is a monthly paid plan, so check current pricing.
sections.template:
CUSTOMER TRACKER COLUMNS (Google Sheet)

Name | How we met | Contact | Problem in their words | Stage (talked / interested / paid / follow up) | Last contact date | Next step | Next step date | Notes

Rule: sort by Next step date every morning. Anything dated today or earlier gets a message before noon.

sections.heading: Pick your payment setup
sections.body:
Choose by what you sell. Stripe, Square and PayPal charge no monthly fee for their basic setups. They take a cut of each sale instead. Shopify charges a monthly plan fee plus a cut of each card sale. Check each pricing page for the current rate in your country, as of late 2026.

Then test it before anyone else pays. A broken link costs you the sale and the trust.
bullets: Services, like tutoring, editing or lawn care: a Stripe Payment Link or a Square invoice. Send it after the call, or put it on your page.
In person, like pop-ups or detailing jobs: Square's free plan with Tap to Pay on your phone.
Physical products online, like merch or print on demand: Shopify. Start on its cheapest plan that fits, and check current pricing.
Buyers who only trust PayPal: add PayPal as a second option later, not first.

Never take business payments as a personal or friends-and-family transfer. PayPal's user agreement tells sellers not to ask buyers to pay that way, and says a personal account used mainly for business can be closed. Check the rules of any payment app before you use it for sales.

sections.heading: What payment platforms ask for
sections.body:
Payment platforms verify who you are before they pay you out. Expect to give your legal name, date of birth, home address, a tax ID such as your Social Security number (or an EIN once you have one) and a bank account for payouts. Set it up a few days before your first sale, because verification can take time, and use your real details: a mismatch can pause your payouts.

Shopify and PayPal require the account holder to be at least 18, or the age of majority where you live, and a few states set that higher (19 in Alabama and Nebraska, 21 in Mississippi). If that's you, read the platform's terms before you sign up. These are the terms as of late 2026, and banks and other tools set their own rules, so check each one before you apply.

sections.heading: Set up your money in one afternoon
sections.body:
This is awareness, not tax, legal or financial advice. Rules depend on where you live, so check them with a licensed tax professional before you decide anything.

Mike Michalowicz's Profit First (2014) is one cash method worth taking to an accountant. Instead of profit being whatever is left at the end, you split every deposit into separate accounts on a set schedule: profit, owner's pay, taxes and running costs. The idea is behavioral. Money you can't see in your spending account is harder to spend. Whether it fits you is a question for a professional.
steps: Open an account used only for the business. Every sale goes in. Every business cost comes out. Nothing personal touches it.

In the US, if you need an EIN, get it straight from the IRS website. It's free and takes minutes. The IRS's own warning: "Beware of websites that charge for an EIN." Whether you need one at all depends on your setup, so ask a tax professional.
Make a Receipts folder in Google Drive. Photograph every receipt the day you get it and name it date, vendor, amount. Ask a tax professional how long to keep them.

Open a second savings bucket called Taxes. Ask a tax professional what share of each payment to move there. Nobody withholds tax from business income for you, so this bucket is how you avoid a surprise bill.
Block 20 minutes on the same day each month: match sales to deposits, file receipts and move the tax amount.

Keep this page in your Notion HQ or a Google Doc. Before you add any tool, find its row. If a tool already does that job, you don't need another one.

Protect the accounts that touch money or customers. Turn on two-factor sign-in for your payment, email and bank accounts, and keep logins in a password manager, not a note on your phone.

sections.heading: Worked example: Jordan's $0 stack
sections.example: Illustrative. Jordan, 19, details cars on weekends at $60 a car. He verified his Stripe account in his own name and opened a separate checking account for the business. Getting paid: a Stripe Payment Link he texts after each job. Tracking: a Google Sheet with one row per customer and a next-step date, enough for his 12 regulars. Notes: one Google Doc called HQ with his prices, checklist and supply list. Email: a Gmail address used only for the business. Booking: a Google Calendar appointment schedule with Saturday and Sunday mornings open. Money: every payout lands in the business account, receipts go in a Drive folder, and a share of each payment moves to a Taxes bucket, the share a local tax preparer suggested. In October he details 14 cars: $840 in, minus card fees, with $0 spent on software. His next tool: none, until the same booking problem happens three times.

sections.heading: When to add a tool
sections.body: Let real pain pick your next tool, not a video about productivity apps. The rule: add a tool only when the same problem has hurt three times. Then add one, set it up fully and cancel whatever it replaced.
bullets: Sheet to Attio: you track 30 or more open conversations, or you've missed a follow-up twice in a month.
Gmail to Google Workspace: you've bought a domain and customers email you every week.
Free booking to paid: you need a feature the free plan doesn't have, and you've hit that wall three times.
Sheet to QuickBooks: an accountant asks for it, or bookkeeping takes more than an hour a week.
Over-tooled signs: you pay for something you haven't opened in 2 weeks, or you can't say where a customer's details live. Cancel anything without a row on your stack page.
Once the same task repeats 3 or more times a week, the Automation Starter Pack shows how to connect your tools.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Paying a website for an EIN. The IRS gives EINs out free, online.
Mixing money. One personal account for everything turns tax time into guesswork. Separate it before your first sale.
Two tools for one job. Customer notes in Notion and a sheet means one of them is wrong. Pick one.
Skipping the test purchase. A broken checkout link loses the sale and the trust.
Spending the tax money. The Taxes bucket isn't revenue. Leave it alone.
Sharing passwords over text, with no two-factor sign-in on the accounts that touch money.
Forming a company because a video said to. Learn the options, then ask a professional where you live.

sections.heading: Go deeper and next steps
bullets: The Minimalist Entrepreneur by Sahil Lavingia (2021): build as little as possible, and do things by hand until the work proves it needs software.
Profit First by Mike Michalowicz (2014): the bucket method for business cash. Read it, then talk it through with an accountant before you change your accounts.
IRS Publication 583, Starting a Business and Keeping Records: the plain-English US guide to which records to keep. Outside the US, find your tax authority's guide for new businesses.
Next: The 127 Stack lists every tool in Eli's toolkit with the trigger to adopt it. Once tasks repeat, use the Automation Starter Pack. Track what your stack produces in the Founder KPI Dashboard.

resources.title: Automation Starter Pack
resources.summary: Cut the busywork, then automate what still repeats: five starter automations and AI prompts, each with a trigger, a test and a human handoff.
resources.output: A 7-day repeat tally, two tested automations with a card each (trigger, steps, test, handoff, time saved) and a Claude Project that drafts your weekly repeat work.

sections.heading: Eliminate first, then automate
sections.body:
Automation makes a process faster. It doesn't make it better. Tim Ferriss sets the order in The 4-Hour Workweek: eliminate first, automate second, and delegate only what's left. Automating a task you should have cut just makes waste run faster.

A task is ready to automate when it passes three tests. It happens 3 or more times a week. The steps are the same every time. One mistake costs you little. Sending your price list passes. Handling a refund request fails, and anything that needs judgment goes to Delegate Your First Task instead.

Eli runs his own systems on what he calls AI coworking agents, tied into tools like Notion, Granola and Attio. You start smaller: one trigger, a few steps, one test. And you automate the repeat, never the relationship. Eli's rule: trust beats everything else in sales. A bot can send your prices. You answer the real questions, review every AI draft and keep every promise the bot makes.

Inside: a 7-day repeat tally and five starter automations, each with a trigger, steps, a test, a human handoff and the time it saves. Plus the Meta and email rules that keep your accounts safe, and a Claude Project that drafts your weekly numbers.

sections.heading: Count, cut, then pick two
sections.body: You can't automate what you haven't counted. For 7 days, log every business task that repeats. The notes app on your phone is enough. Dan Martell's Buy Back Your Time (2023) starts the same way: audit where your hours go before you change anything.
steps: Log every repeat task for 7 days: what it was, how many times it happened and how many minutes each took.
Multiply times by minutes to get a weekly total. Sort the list from the biggest total to the smallest.
Cut any task that produced no lead, sale or learning. Stop doing it for a week and see if anyone notices.
Mark a task Automate only if it passes all three tests: 3 or more times a week, the same steps every time, and a low cost if it goes wrong once.
Mark a task Human if it touches money problems, complaints, custom quotes or a relationship you're building.
Pick the 2 Automate tasks with the biggest weekly totals. Those are your builds. Everything else waits a week.

sections.heading: How every automation works
sections.body:
Every automation is a trigger plus one or more actions. In Zapier, the simplest workflow is one trigger and one action. Make calls the same idea a scenario. Many tools have automations built in: ManyChat replies on Instagram, Kit and Klaviyo send welcome emails, and Google Forms writes responses to a Google Sheet. Use the built-in option first. Add Zapier or Make only when two tools can't connect on their own.

Free plans cover your first builds. Zapier's gives you 100 tasks a month, two-step workflows only, checked every 15 minutes. Make's gives you 1,000 credits a month. Those are the limits as of late 2026, so check current pricing.

Write a card before you build. It forces the two parts people skip: the test and the human handoff. Keep every card on one Notion page called Automations.

AUTOMATION CARD

Name: [what it does, in 5 words or fewer]
Replaces: [repeat task] | [times per week] x [minutes each] = [weekly minutes]

Trigger (when this happens): [event] in [tool]
Steps (then do this):
1. [action] in [tool]
2. [action] in [tool]
3. [action] in [tool]

Test: [how I fake the trigger] | Passed on: [date]
Human handoff: [what it can't handle] goes to [me, by notification or email] | I reply within [time]

Check it: every [Monday] in my Weekly CEO Review

sections.heading: Automation 1: Instagram keyword replies
sections.body:
Build this when the same DM question arrives 3 or more times a week. ManyChat watches for a keyword in a comment or DM and replies for you, from a professional Instagram account. Its free plan covers only 25 active contacts a month and 4 active automations, so treat it as a test drive. Essential starts at $14 a month for 250 active contacts, and Pro at $29 for 2,500 (ManyChat pricing page, as of late 2026, check current pricing).

Meta's rules apply whatever tool you use. You get one private reply to a comment, within 7 days of it. After that, you can message again only once the person replies, and only within 24 hours of their last message. Meta's Human Agent tag lets a real person reply by hand within 7 days. Meta recommends saying when a chat is automated, and some places, like California, require it, so say it in your first reply. Teen Accounts have built-in limits on who can message them, so a teen who comments may not get your DM. Only message people who commented or messaged you first.
steps: Trigger: a comment or DM with your keyword, like PRICE, on one post or reel. Start with one post, not your whole account.
Action 1: a public reply to the comment, like "Sent, check your DMs."
Action 2: a DM with the answer, your link and one question back, so a real conversation can start.
Handoff: any reply the flow doesn't recognize sends you a notification. You answer it yourself the same day.
Test: comment the keyword from a friend's account. Then type a random question to check that the handoff fires.
Time saved: count last week's keyword DMs. 15 DMs at 3 minutes each is 45 minutes a week back.
sections.template:
KEYWORD FLOW: [KEYWORD]

Post call to action: "Comment [KEYWORD] and I'll send you [the price list / the guide / the link]."

Public reply (automatic): "Sent! Check your DMs, [first name]."

DM 1 (automatic): "Hey [first name], here's [the thing]: [link]. This first reply is automatic, but a real person reads every answer. Quick question so I send the right info: are you looking for [option A] or [option B]?"

If [option A]: "[one-line answer]. Book here: [booking link]"
If [option B]: "[one-line answer]. Details: [link]"

Anything else (handoff): "Good question. I'll answer this one myself by [time today]." Then notify me.

Never: fake countdowns, "only 2 spots left" when it isn't true, or chasing people who stopped replying.

sections.heading: Automation 2: Every lead lands in one place
sections.body: Leads leak when they live in DMs, texts and three inboxes. Send every form, booking and signup to one list: a Google Sheet or Attio. The Simple Operations Stack helps you pick. Google Forms can save every response to a Google Sheet with no extra tool. For anything else, a Zapier or Make automation adds the row.
steps: Trigger: someone submits your form or books a call.
Action 1: add a row or record with their name, contact, the problem in their words, where they found you and the date.
Action 2: send a confirmation that says exactly when you'll reply.
Handoff: you reply personally within 24 hours. Block 10 minutes a day on your calendar to clear new leads.
Test: submit a fake lead with your own email. Check the row, the confirmation and how long it took to arrive.
Time saved: about 3 minutes per lead you no longer copy by hand, plus the leads you stop losing.
sections.template:
LEAD CONFIRMATION (email or DM)

Subject: Got it, [first name]

Thanks for reaching out about [problem in their words]. I read every message myself and I'll reply by [day and time].

If it's easier to talk, grab a time here: [booking link].

[Your name]
[Business name]

sections.heading: Automation 3: A welcome email that sends itself
sections.body:
When someone joins your list, the first email should land in minutes, not whenever you remember. Automated emails earn more clicks: Klaviyo's 2026 ecommerce benchmarks put automated flows at about a 5.6% click rate, against about 1.7% for one-off campaigns. Treat that as a rough range for online stores, not a promise.

Kit and Klaviyo both have free plans to start. Kit fits creators and service businesses. Klaviyo fits Shopify stores, since it connects to your orders. Pick one.

In the US, the CAN-SPAM Act sets the basics for marketing email: honest sender details and subject lines, a working unsubscribe link and your physical mailing address. If you don't want your home address in every email, check which addresses count in the FTC's CAN-SPAM guide. Other countries have stricter consent rules, so check yours. Only email people who signed up.
steps: Trigger: a new subscriber joins your list.
Email 1, right away: deliver what you promised and ask one question they can reply to.
Email 2, two days later: one useful lesson or story about the problem you solve.
Email 3, four days later: your offer, with the price stated plainly and one link.
Handoff: replies land in your inbox. Answer each one yourself. Those replies are free customer research.
Test: subscribe with a second email address. Check the timing, every link, the unsubscribe link and how it reads on your phone.
Time saved: about 5 minutes per new subscriber you'd otherwise email by hand, plus the ones you'd forget.

WELCOME SEQUENCE

EMAIL 1 (right away)
Subject: Here's [the thing you promised]

Start with [one action that takes under 5 minutes].

Subject: The mistake I see most with [topic]
