Every email's footer: [business name] | [mailing address] | [unsubscribe link]

sections.heading: Automation 4: Call notes that file themselves
sections.body:
Every customer call is research, but only if the notes get used. Granola writes notes from your call, so you can listen instead of type. Check its current plan limits before you rely on it.

Tell people before the call that you use an AI notetaker, and ask if that's okay. Recording and transcription consent laws differ by state and country, and some require everyone on the call to agree. Check your local rules. If someone says no, take notes by hand.
steps: Trigger: a customer or sales call ends with Granola running.
Action 1: the notes go to a Calls database in Notion. Use Granola's sharing or integrations if your plan has them. If not, paste them in. It takes 60 seconds.
Action 2: run the summary prompt below on the notes.
Action 3: copy the next step and its date into your Sheet or Attio.
Handoff: you send the follow-up yourself within 24 hours, using the summary as your notes.
Test: run it on a 5-minute practice call with a friend. Check that the notes land in the right place.
Time saved: roughly 10 to 15 minutes per call that you'd spend typing and tidying notes.
sections.template:
CALL SUMMARY PROMPT

Here are my notes from a call with [name], a [type of customer]: [paste notes]

Pull out:
1. The problem in their exact words (quote them)
2. How they solve it today and what that costs them in time or money
3. Any objection or hesitation
4. Anything they said they'd pay for, and how much
5. The next step we agreed and its date
6. One question I should have asked but didn't

Keep it under 150 words. Quote them where you can. Don't add anything that isn't in the notes. If something is unclear, write UNCLEAR instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Automation 5: The weekly metrics email, drafted by Claude
sections.body:
The Founder KPI Dashboard asks for the same seven numbers every Monday. Automate the pull. A recurring reminder brings your number sources to you, and a Claude Project turns the numbers into a short read on what changed. The same Project turns one video into a week of captions.

A Claude Project keeps your instructions and files in one place, so every chat starts already knowing your business. Check that your plan includes Projects.

Claude drafts. You decide. Nothing it writes reaches a customer until you've read it, and you check every number against your own records.
steps: Trigger: a recurring Monday calendar event called Weekly numbers, with your number sources list from the Founder KPI Dashboard pasted into it.
Action 1: a Gmail filter that labels report emails from your tools as Numbers, so they're waiting in one place.
Action 2: pull the 7 numbers into the dashboard, then paste them into prompt 1 in your Claude Project.
Action 3: save Claude's answer on your Notion Weekly Review page.
Handoff: you make the kill, pause or double-down call yourself in your Weekly CEO Review. Claude only points at what changed.
Test: run it once on last week's numbers. Check every figure in Claude's answer against the dashboard.
Time saved: roughly 10 minutes a week of hunting for numbers, plus the Mondays you'd otherwise skip.
sections.template:
PROJECT SETUP (once)
Create a Project named after your business. Paste the instructions below into its custom instructions.
Upload 4 files: your offer, an FAQ with 10 real questions and answers, your price list and 3 posts that worked.
Test: ask a question your FAQ doesn't answer. A good setup says it doesn't know. If it invents an answer, tighten rule 1.

PROJECT INSTRUCTIONS
You help me run [business], which sells [offer] to [customer] for [price].
My voice: [three words, like direct, warm, plain]. Short sentences. No hype.
Rules:
1. Use the files in this project as the source of truth. Never invent facts, prices, results, reviews or promises.
2. Everything you write is a draft for me to review. Mark anything I must check with [CHECK].
3. If a message touches refunds, complaints, money disputes or anything legal, write HUMAN ONLY and stop.
4. If you don't know, say so and tell me what you'd need.

PROMPT 1: WEEKLY NUMBERS
This week vs last week:

Name the step where the biggest share of people dropped off, the one thing to do more of and the one thing to stop. Be blunt. Under 120 words. Use only the numbers above.

PROMPT 2: ONE VIDEO, FIVE POSTS

Give me 3 to 5 clip ideas under 45 seconds with start and end times, a hook under 10 words for each, on-screen text, and one caption each ending with: [call to action]. Use only what I said in the video.

sections.heading: Worked example: Leo's first two builds
sections.example: Illustrative: Leo, 20, edits short-form videos for local gyms at $300 a month per gym. His 7-day tally: 18 "what do you charge?" DMs at 3 minutes each (54 minutes), 6 website leads copied into his sheet at 4 minutes each (24 minutes), 4 discovery calls with 15 minutes of note cleanup after each (60 minutes), and 40 minutes rewatching old posts for ideas. He cut the rewatching, since it produced no lead or sale. He built two automations: a ManyChat keyword, RATES, on his three best reels, and a Google Form that writes to his sheet and sends a confirmation. He tested both from a friend's phone. In week 2 the flow hit the free plan's 25-contact cap, so he moved to Essential at $14 a month. An hour a week back was worth more than $14. The two builds save about 78 minutes a week, minus 10 minutes of checking, and he spends that hour calling gym owners. Call notes wait until he's doing 6 calls a week.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body: In 2024, a Canadian tribunal ruled against Air Canada over its website chatbot (Moffatt v. Air Canada). The bot told a grieving customer he could claim a bereavement discount after booking. The airline's real policy didn't allow that. Air Canada argued the chatbot was responsible for its own words. The tribunal disagreed and made the airline pay. Your automation speaks for you, so it only gets to say what you'd stand behind.
bullets: Automating a mess. If the steps change every time, simplify first. Delegate Your First Task shows how to write them down.
Building before counting. A task you do twice a month isn't worth an automation.
Skipping the test. Fake the trigger yourself before any customer sees it, and again after every change.
No way out to a human. Every flow ends with a person when the bot doesn't know.
Auto-sending AI drafts. AI writes the draft. You press send.
Messaging people who never contacted you, or emailing people who never signed up. It burns trust and can get your account restricted.
Set and forget. Automations break quietly when a tool changes. Check each one in your Weekly CEO Review.
Paying too early. Upgrade only when a limit blocks an automation that's working, like Leo's ManyChat cap.

sections.heading: Go deeper and next steps
bullets: The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss (2007): the order of its steps, especially cutting tasks before you automate them.
Buy Back Your Time by Dan Martell (2023): its time and energy audit, then handing off the draining, low-value work first.
The E-Myth Revisited by Michael E. Gerber (1995): why a business needs systems that run without the owner, the root of working on the business, not in it.
Next: when a task needs judgment, not a trigger, use Delegate Your First Task. Track what your automations change in the Founder KPI Dashboard, and check every one in your Weekly CEO Review.
Not sure what to automate first? Paste last week's tasks into the Workflow Recommender and compare its top three with your tally.

resources.aiPrompt: Check the tally: every automated task should repeat 3 or more times a week, follow the same steps and cost little if it goes wrong once; flag any build aimed at a rare or judgment-heavy task, and ask what they cut first, since eliminating comes before automating. Check each build has a specific trigger, ordered steps, a dated test that also fired the handoff, and a named human handoff with a reply time; the most common weak answer is "set up ManyChat" with no test or handoff, so call it out. Check the keyword flow only messages people who commented or messaged first, says the first reply is automatic, and uses no fake scarcity or promises they can't keep. Check time saved is times per week multiplied by minutes, minus checking time, not a guess, and that refunds, complaints, custom quotes and the final review of every AI draft stay human. If a task needs judgment, send them to Delegate Your First Task; if they can't pick what to automate, to the Workflow Recommender; and tell them to check every automation in their Weekly CEO Review.

resources.title: Delegate Your First Task
resources.summary: Find the task that eats your week, write it down so a tool or person can run it, and hand it off with a plan to check it.
resources.output: A one-week time audit, your Buyback Rate, a one-page SOP with decision rights, your first task handed to a tool or person, and a review plan for the first 3 runs.

sections.heading: If it lives in your head, it isn't a business yet
sections.body:
Eli's rule: your business is only as valuable as it is when you aren't there to run it. His own proof is $50K in gross sales from a part-time e-commerce brand. Eli's results aren't typical or a promise of what you'll earn. Asked how, he starts with people: an ambassador network of 100+ creators and a creative team driving content. Part-time only works when the work doesn't all run through you.

Test yours. If you vanished for a week, what would stop? Every answer is a task that lives only in your head.

You don't fix that by hiring. You fix it by writing the work down. Your first handoff is not your hardest task. It's your most repeated one, written so clearly that a saved reply, an automation, an AI tool or a friend can run it without texting you.

At your stage, money buys very little time. The math in this playbook usually says your first handoff should cost $0. People come later, through a small paid trial, once the steps are on paper.

In about an hour you'll have a one-week time audit, your Buyback Rate and one task picked by score. You'll also have a recorded one-page SOP with clear decision rights, the right tool or person to run it, and a review plan for the first three runs.

sections.heading: Audit one week of your time
sections.body:
Dan Martell's Time and Energy Audit, from Buy Back Your Time (2023), has you log everything you do in 15-minute blocks for two weeks. Each task gets a value from $ to $$$$, plus green if it gave you energy or red if it drained you.

You have under 3 hours a week for the business, so start smaller. Rebuild last week from your calendar, screen time, DMs and notes. List every business task with the minutes it took. If last week is a blur, log this week live instead. Give each task a tag from the list below and a plus or minus for energy. The low-value tasks that drain you are the first to go.
bullets: Only me: needs your judgment, your face or your relationships. Selling, key decisions, being on camera.
Repeat: done the same way every time. Answering the same DMs, posting, invoicing, scheduling, packing orders.
Waste: didn't need doing at all. Cut it today. Deleting a task is the cheapest handoff there is.

sections.heading: Do the buyback math
sections.body:
Martell's Buyback Rate is what you can afford to pay someone to take a task off your plate. Divide your yearly income by 2,000 working hours, then divide by 4. The 4 builds in a four-times return on every hour you buy back. His own example: $100,000 a year works out to $12.50 an hour. Any task someone could do for less than your rate shouldn't stay on your calendar.

You may not have a yearly income to plug in yet. Use the higher of two numbers: what your job pays per hour, or last month's business revenue divided by the hours you put in. If you earn $15 an hour, your Buyback Rate is $3.75. That isn't bad news. It tells you the first handoff should be free or close to it: delete it, template it, automate it or give it to AI.

Pay a person when the task blocks revenue, or when your Buyback Rate covers the cost. Redo the math every 90 days. As revenue grows, the answer changes.
sections.example: Illustrative: Jordan, 18, runs a sneaker cleaning service and works a $15-an-hour job. The business made $360 last month on 24 hours of work, which is also $15 an hour. Jordan's Buyback Rate is $15 divided by 4: $3.75 an hour. A freelancer at $15 an hour costs 4 times that, so Jordan doesn't hire yet. The first two handoffs are saved replies for pricing questions and a free booking link for drop-off times. Total cost: $0.

sections.heading: Pick your first task
sections.body:
Don't start with the hardest thing. Start with the task that is repeated, rule-based and low-risk if it goes wrong once. Martell's Replacement Ladder gives the order for handing work off. Admin goes first (his first hire is an assistant). Then delivery: fulfillment, onboarding, payments and customer support. Then marketing, then sales, and last, leadership.

Keep the sales conversations yourself for now. Early buyers are buying you as much as the product. Hand off selling only once you have a script that wins without you.

Score each repeat task from your audit.
steps: Frequency: weekly or more scores 2, monthly scores 1, rarely scores 0.
Rules: you can explain it without saying 'it depends' more than once. Yes scores 2, sort of scores 1, no scores 0.
Risk: if it's done a bit worse once, nothing breaks. Yes scores 2. If a mistake means a refund, an angry customer or lost money, score 0.
Time: it takes 60 minutes or more a week. That scores 2. From 20 to 59 minutes scores 1. Less scores 0.
Pick the highest total out of 8. On a tie, pick the one that drains you most. Anything under 5 waits.
sections.example: Jordan's audit shows two repeat tasks. First, answering 'how much for a deep clean?' and 'how long does it take?' in DMs. It happens daily, the answers never change, a slow reply loses nothing, and it takes 2 hours a week. Score: 8. Second, editing before-and-after photos: weekly, 40 minutes, low risk, but every photo needs an eye for what looks good, so it fails the rules test. Score: 5. The DMs go first. The photos wait for the next rung.

sections.heading: Record it, then write the SOP
sections.body:
SOP means standard operating procedure: steps anyone can follow. Don't write it from memory, because you'll skip the steps you do on autopilot. Martell's Camcorder Method starts with a recording: film yourself doing the task, then turn the video into written steps. Use your phone's screen recorder and talk out loud as you work. Paste the transcript into Claude, ask for a numbered checklist, then fix what it got wrong.

Atul Gawande's The Checklist Manifesto (2009) makes the case for short checklists that cover the steps people skip. His best-known example: Peter Pronovost's 5-step checklist for putting central lines into ICU patients. Doctors knew every step, yet nationally they followed them only about 30 percent of the time. When Michigan ICUs adopted the checklist, compliance rose close to 100 percent and infections fell by 66 percent, Gawande told NPR in 2007. If doctors need a checklist, your helper does too.

The part most SOPs skip is decision rights. In The 4-Hour Workweek, Tim Ferriss describes letting his outsourced customer service reps fix any problem costing under $100 without asking him. Your SOP needs a line like that, with your own number.

sections.heading: Choose who or what runs it
sections.body:
Match the task to the cheapest option that does it well. Work down this list and stop at the first one that fits. Dan Sullivan and Benjamin Hardy's Who Not How (2020) is the mindset: before you ask how you'll do something, ask who, or what, could do it.

With people, choose slowly. Eli's warning from his own list of mistakes: bad partnerships can cost you a ton, and more than just money. Choosing the right people to build with is crucial.
bullets: Delete it: if no customer would notice, stop doing it.
Saved replies and templates: free, and best for answers that never change.
Automation: ManyChat for Instagram DM keyword replies, a booking link for scheduling, Shopify for order emails, Klaviyo for email follow-ups. Best for 'when X happens, do Y' tasks.
AI: Claude or ChatGPT for first drafts of captions, emails and replies, Granola for call notes, Perplexity for research. You approve anything before it goes out.
Someone you know: a friend, sibling or classmate. Agree the task, the pay and the deadline in writing before they start.
A freelancer: Upwork or Fiverr for editing, design or support. Marketplaces also add fees, so check the current fee page before you budget.
Paying anyone regularly comes with rules: contractor or employee, minimum wage, tax forms. Check your local rules or ask a professional first.

sections.heading: Start with a small paid trial
sections.body:
Don't hand someone your operation after one chat. Give one small, real task and pay for it. Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, has long hired this way: candidates do paid trial work on real projects before anyone gets an offer. One trial tells you more about quality, speed and communication than an hour of talking.

Keep the trial to 1 to 3 hours of work. Pay for it whether or not you continue. Decide before it starts what a pass looks like, so you judge the work, not the vibe.
sections.template:
PAID TRIAL TASK
Hi [name], thanks for your interest. Before we work together, I'd like to pay you for one small trial task.

The task: [one sentence, e.g. edit 3 before-and-after photos to match the attached example]
What you get: [SOP link, a finished example, the files]
Deadline: [day and time]
Pay: [$ amount], paid when you deliver, whether or not we continue
A pass looks like: [e.g. matches the example, needs 1 round of fixes or fewer, delivered on time]
Questions: send them all in one message before you start.

If it goes well, the next step is [e.g. 10 photos a week at $X each]. Does that work for you?

sections.heading: Review three runs, then let go
sections.body:
Andy Grove's High Output Management (1983) sets how closely to check: it depends on the person's experience with this exact task, which Grove calls task-relevant maturity. New to it means close checks. Proven means you check results only. Grove is blunt that handing off a task and never checking it isn't delegating. It's abdicating.

When your helper gets stuck, use Martell's 1-3-1 rule: anyone who brings you a problem also brings 3 workable options and the 1 they'd pick. You answer yes, or choose a better option. They learn to decide, and you stop being the bottleneck.

Then let go. It won't be done exactly your way. If it's done well and consistently, that's a pass. Treat whoever helps you the way you'd want to be treated: clear instructions, fair pay on time, credit when it goes well.

Martell's Buyback Loop has three stages: audit, transfer, fill. You've done the first two. Fill is the point: book the hours you got back for one task on the business, or they'll leak into scrolling.
steps: Run 1: check everything. Note each place they got stuck or the result was off.
Fix the SOP, not just the result. If the same question comes up twice, the answer goes in the document.
Run 2: check the finished result only. Give 1 or 2 specific notes.
Run 3: spot check. If 8 of 10 outputs need no fixes, it passes. If not, do one more run with the improved SOP.
After run 3, switch to a 5-minute weekly check inside your Weekly CEO Review.
sections.example: Illustrative, start to finish: Jordan's audit shows 9 hours of business work last week, 3.5 of them on repeat tasks. Buyback Rate: $3.75 an hour, so tools first. Pick: pricing and turnaround DMs, score 8 of 8. Jordan screen-records a day of replies, Claude turns the transcript into a 6-step SOP, and the answers become 4 saved replies plus a ManyChat keyword, PRICE. Decision rights: refunds and damaged shoes come to Jordan. Run 1: Jordan reads every reply and adds 2 missing answers to the SOP. Run 2: checks 5 conversations. Run 3: spot-checks 2. Result: about 90 minutes back each week, booked as a Saturday block to pitch two local shoe stores on a pickup partnership. Next rung: photo editing, as a $20 paid trial with a friend.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Delegating a mess. If the task has no clear steps, you hand off confusion. Record it and write the SOP first.
Starting with the hardest task. Your first handoff should be boring. Win small, then climb the ladder.
No decision rights. If every refund needs you, you're still the bottleneck. Write a dollar limit into the SOP.
Hovering, or vanishing. Check run 1 closely, then step back on schedule.
Hiring a friend on a handshake. Put the task, the pay and the deadline in one message before they start.
Paying a person for what a saved reply could do. Run the buyback math first.
Letting the freed hours leak. Book them for one named task on the business, or they disappear.

bullets: Buy Back Your Time by Dan Martell (2023): the full Time and Energy Audit, the Buyback Rate and the Camcorder Method.
The E-Myth Revisited by Michael Gerber (1995): why a business that needs you for everything is a job, and how to build it to run from a manual.
High Output Management by Andy Grove (1983): read the part on task-relevant maturity before you supervise anyone.
The Checklist Manifesto by Atul Gawande (2009): how to write a checklist that people actually follow.
Who Not How by Dan Sullivan and Benjamin Hardy (2020): the habit of asking who could do this before you learn how.

resources.title: The 127 Stack
resources.summary: Every tool in Eli's own toolkit, grouped by job, with what it does, the trigger to adopt it, the first action and free plan facts.
resources.output: A Now list of three or four tools with a first action done, a Later list with a trigger for each tool, and a prompt pack for Claude, Perplexity and ChatGPT.

sections.heading: Three tools now, the rest when a trigger hits
sections.body:
This is Eli's toolkit, taken from his own list: Claude, Perplexity, ChatGPT, Notion, Miro, Granola, Attio, ManyChat, Shopify, CapCut, Higgsfield, Replit, Klaviyo, Google Workspace, Mercury, QuickBooks and Calendly. That's 17 tools. You need three or four this month.

The first mistake Eli names is trying to do too much. His advice on ways to make money: "pick one, get really good at it." Treat software the same way.

A tool goes on your Now list only if it passes three checks. This month's work needs it. Its free plan covers you. You can do its first action in under 30 minutes. Everything else goes on your Later list with a trigger: the exact event that means you need it, like "30 open conversations" or "bought a domain".

Each entry below gives you what the tool does, its trigger, the first action and whether there's a free plan. Plans change often, so check current pricing before you sign up. After the directory: what Eli means by harnesses and agent pipelines, in plain words, and a prompt pack you can copy.

sections.heading: Think and research: Claude, Perplexity, ChatGPT
sections.body: Pick one main AI assistant and use it every day. Add Perplexity when you need sources you can check.
bullets: Claude. Does: thinking partner, writing, planning and simple web pages built from a prompt. Free plan: yes, with usage limits. Paid plans add more use. When: now. First action: run prompt 1 in the pack below on your idea.

Perplexity. Does: AI search that shows its sources, for competitor prices, reviews and market trends. Free plan: yes. Paid plans add more advanced searches. When: now, while you validate. First action: run prompt 2 on your top 3 competitors, then open every source and confirm it yourself.

ChatGPT. Does: a general assistant with voice and image tools. Free plan: yes. Paid plans add more use and features. When: now if you prefer it as your main assistant, otherwise later as a second opinion on drafts that matter. First action: run prompt 5 on your offer.

sections.heading: Plan and organize: Notion, Miro, Google Workspace
bullets: Notion. Does: your business HQ for docs, processes, to-dos and content plans. Eli builds his content scheduling frameworks in Notion. Free plan: yes, enough for one person. When: now. First action: make one page called HQ with sub-pages for Offer, Customers, Content Plan, Money and Weekly Review.

Miro. Does: visual boards for mapping ideas, customer journeys and templates. Eli builds templates on Miro boards. Free plan: yes, with a cap on editable boards. When: later, unless you think in pictures. First action: map your customer's path on one board, from first seeing you to paying and coming back.

Google Workspace. Does: email on your own domain, plus Docs, Sheets, Drive and Calendar under your business name. Free plan: no. It's a paid plan per user, with a free trial. When: later, once you've bought a domain and email customers every week. A free Gmail account covers the same apps until then. First action: set up you@yourbusiness.com with a signature that holds your booking link.

sections.heading: Sell and follow up: Attio, Granola, Calendly, ManyChat, Klaviyo
sections.body: Your network is your net worth, Eli's principle, but only if you remember who's in it. These tools make sure no conversation gets lost and no follow-up gets forgotten.
bullets: Attio. Does: a CRM that tracks every person you talk to, their stage and the next step. Free plan: yes. When: later, once a Google Sheet can't keep up: 30 or more open conversations, or two missed follow-ups in a month. First action: import your sheet and set four stages: talked, interested, paid, follow up.

Granola. Does: AI meeting notes, so you listen instead of typing. Free plan: check current limits before you rely on it. When: now, once you have 2 or more customer calls a week. First action: use it on your next call, with permission, then pull out the problem in their words and the next step.

Calendly. Does: a booking link that ends the back-and-forth over times. Free plan: yes, for basic booking. When: now, if you sell calls or appointments. First action: one meeting type, two or three time blocks a week, link in your bio.

ManyChat. Does: automatic Instagram replies when someone comments or DMs a keyword. Free plan: yes, but only 25 active contacts a month. Essential starts at $14 a month and Pro at $29 (ManyChat pricing page). When: later, once the same DM question arrives 3 or more times a week. First action: one keyword on one post, tested from a friend's account. The Automation Starter Pack has the script.

Klaviyo. Does: email and text marketing, strongest when connected to a Shopify store. Free plan: yes, with a small cap on contacts and sends. When: later, once you have a store and people asking to hear about drops. First action: a signup form and a 3-email welcome flow. No store yet? Kit and beehiiv both have free plans built for creators. They aren't in Eli's stack, but they cost nothing to start.

sections.heading: Create content: CapCut, Higgsfield
sections.body: Real footage of you and your work builds trust first. Eli built 25M+ views across social, and his method was simple: be authentic, be consistent, and when a video works, reuse that format. AI video comes after you know what works.
bullets: CapCut. Does: phone video editing with cuts, auto captions and templates. Eli edits on iPhone with it. Free: yes, with a paid Pro tier. If it's not in your app store, Instagram's free Edits app does the same basic job. When: now, if content is how customers will find you. First action: film a 30-second tip or before-and-after and add on-screen captions.

Higgsfield. Does: AI video and image generation for shots you can't film. Pricing: paid plans, so check current pricing. When: later, once a format works with real footage. First action: generate one supporting shot for a proven format and label it as AI-made. TikTok and Instagram both have AI labels. Use them.

sections.heading: Sell online, build and bank: Shopify, Replit, Mercury, QuickBooks
sections.body: Shopify itself started as a fix for a real problem. In 2004, Tobi Lütke wanted to sell snowboards online through his shop, Snowdevil, and couldn't find store software he liked. So he built his own, and that became Shopify. You don't need to build anything: the tools he wished he had now exist. Pick by what you sell, and only pay for a store when you have products and buyers.
bullets: Shopify. Does: an online store with products, checkout and payments in one place. Free plan: no. A low-cost Starter plan sells through social and links, and full store plans sit above it. Check current pricing. When: now if you sell physical products. Later or never for most services, where a payment link and a simple page are enough. First action: one product page, then a real test purchase.

Replit. Does: builds and hosts small web apps from a plain-language description. Free plan: yes, with limits. Paid plans add more building and hosting. When: later, when you need a tool a page builder can't make, like a quote calculator or a client portal. First action: describe one small tool in two sentences and let it build a first version.

Mercury. Does: online business banking. Check its pricing and eligibility pages before you apply. When: later, once you've registered a business. First action: compare it with a local bank or credit union business account before you apply.

QuickBooks. Does: bookkeeping, invoices and reports an accountant can read. Free plan: no. It's a monthly paid plan, often with a trial. When: later, when an accountant asks for it or books take more than an hour a week. First action: connect your business account and categorize one month of transactions.

sections.heading: Tie it together: harnesses and agent pipelines
sections.body:
Eli calls his next level AI coworking agents: AI tied into specific tools like Notion, Granola and Attio. He also builds what he calls harnesses to run a business off of, and agentic pipelines for his technical projects. Here's the idea in plain words. It's a general picture, not his exact setup.

A harness is an AI assistant plus three things: instructions about your business, access to your tools, and rules for what it may do without asking you. A pipeline is a chain of steps where each output feeds the next. Granola's call notes become a Notion summary. The summary becomes a follow-up task in Attio. You approve the follow-up before it goes out.

The plumbing for this exists now. Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol in 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI to other software, and Claude can link to tools like Notion, Attio and Granola through connectors. That means an assistant can read your call notes or update a record, if you give it access. Give the least access that works, and keep a human approval step on anything a customer sees.

Start simple anyway. Anthropic's guide Building effective agents (2024) tells builders to find the simplest solution that works and add complexity only when it clearly helps. For you, that's the ladder below. Don't skip levels. Each one shows you what the next one should do.
steps: Level 1: one tool per job, used by hand. You learn what actually repeats. The Simple Operations Stack covers this.
Level 2: saved prompts and a Claude Project that holds your business files.
Level 3: trigger-and-action automations between tools. The Automation Starter Pack covers this.
Level 4: an AI assistant connected to your tools that drafts work and waits for your approval.
At every level, a human approves anything that reaches a customer, moves money or makes a promise.

sections.heading: The 127 prompt pack
sections.body: Save these in a Notion page called Prompt Pack. Fill the brackets, paste, then edit the answer by hand. Check every fact an AI gives you before you act on it or show it to a customer.
sections.template:
PROMPT 1: IDEA TEST (Claude or ChatGPT)
Here's my business idea: [idea, customer, price].
Run it through these questions, one at a time, and be blunt:
1. Does it solve a problem people already pay to solve, or add value they'll pay for? What proof do I have?
2. What are the economics? Through which channels could it scale, and how hard is it to reach them?
3. What's my differentiator: faster, cheaper, higher quality or a better supply chain?
4. Is this market growing or shrinking, and how is AI changing it?
5. Who is an insider I should talk to before I build anything?
Then name my weakest assumption and the cheapest way to test it this week.

PROMPT 2: COMPETITOR PRICES (Perplexity)
Find 5 businesses selling [offer] to [customer] in [city / online]. For each: name, price, what's included, review rating and count, and the source link. Put it in a table. Say which sources are older than 12 months. If you can't find a price, write NOT FOUND. Don't estimate.

PROMPT 3: MARKET DIRECTION (Perplexity)
Is demand for [product or service] in [market] growing or shrinking? Give me 3 data points with their source, publisher and year, and one way AI is changing this market. Flag anything from a company that sells into this market.

PROMPT 4: ONE-PAGE WEBSITE (Claude)
Build a single-page website for my business as one HTML file with inline CSS. Mobile-first, fast, clean.
Business: [name]. Positioning: I help [customer] get [result] without [pain].
Brand: main color [code], accent [code], font [font], voice [three words].
Sections in order: headline, subhead, three benefits, proof, offer and price, FAQ, one call to action.
Headline: [in customers' words]. Benefits: [1], [2], [3]. Real proof: [only true proof].
Offer: [what they get, price, guarantee if real]. FAQ: [three objections with answers].
Button: [text] linking to [URL].
Rules: no invented testimonials, reviews, logos or numbers. After the code, list everything I need to replace or check.

PROMPT 5: SECOND OPINION (ChatGPT or Claude)
Here's my [offer / landing page / post]: [paste]. Act as a skeptical [type of customer] seeing this for the first time. What's confusing, what don't you believe, and what would stop you from paying [price]? Then rewrite the first line to fix the biggest problem.

sections.example: Illustrative. Ava, 20, wants to sell embroidered hats online for $32. Her Now list: Claude for the idea test and product copy, Perplexity for competitor prices, Notion for one HQ page and CapCut for product videos. All four on free plans. First action today: prompt 1 on the hat idea. Claude flags that she hasn't checked what similar hats sell for, so her second action is prompt 2 in Perplexity. Total spent this month: $0.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Copying the whole stack. Eli's list covers more than one business. Yours needs three or four tools this month.
Paying before the free plan hurts. Upgrade when a free limit blocks real work, not when a tool emails you a discount.
Trusting AI facts. Perplexity shows sources so you can check them. Open them.
Letting AI talk to customers unsupervised. Drafts are fine. Sending without reading isn't.
Using AI video to fake proof. AI visuals are fine for ideas and supporting shots, never for results, reviews or products that don't exist.

resources.title: 30-Day Content Calendar
resources.summary: A 30-day posting plan that fits in under 3 hours a week, with three pillars, one platform and a tracker that shows which format to double down on.
resources.output: Three pillars, one main platform, a 2-hour weekly batching block, a 30-day plan with every post prompted, and a tracker that names your winning format.

sections.heading: Consistency is a planning problem
sections.body:
Posting plans rarely die from a lack of ideas. They die on busy days, when every post starts from a blank screen. This template removes the blank screen. You pick your topics once, film once a week, and let the numbers decide what you make next.

The budget is under 3 hours a week: one 2-hour batching block, about 30 minutes across your posting days to publish and reply, and a 15-minute review. That buys 3 to 5 posts a week on one platform, which is enough. In Buffer's 2025 study of 11.4 million TikTok posts, going from 1 post a week to 2 to 5 gave the biggest jump in views per post, about 17%. Buffer's 2025 Instagram data shows the same shape: 3 to 5 posts a week got about 12% more reach per post than 1 to 2. More posts mostly buy more chances at a breakout.

Eli's proof on this topic: 25M+ views across social, and 100K+ followers built. His method is plain. Be authentic, be consistent, lean into your personal brand, and when a video works, reuse its format until it stops working.

By the end of this page you'll have three pillars, one platform, a batching block on your calendar, 30 days of prompted posts, and a tracker that tells you which format to repeat.

sections.heading: Pick three pillars, one of them you
sections.body:
A pillar is a topic bucket you can pull from for months. Three is enough. More than three and your page looks random. Fewer and you run dry by week 2.

Use this set. Teach: solve one small piece of your customer's problem for free. Proof: show that what you do works. You: what you're learning, building and getting wrong. Eli's audience method starts with authenticity. On his own growth he says: "I leaned heavily into my personal brand." People follow people before they follow businesses, so the You pillar is not optional.
steps: Write your customer's 3 most common problems in their own words. Take 5 minutes. These feed your Teach pillar.
List every piece of proof you have or can create this month: before and afters, results, messages shared with permission. No proof yet? Test something in public and show what happened.
Write your You pillar as one line, for example "a 20-year-old building a sneaker cleaning business between classes."
Stress test each pillar: list 10 post ideas in 10 minutes. If a pillar can't reach 10, widen it one level, from "Jordan 1 creases" to "sneaker care."

Build a grid: 3 pillars down the side, 5 formats across the top. Each cell is a post idea, so one grid gives you 15 posts. Justin Welsh, who built a one-person business on LinkedIn and X, popularized this as a content matrix.
sections.example: A sneaker cleaning side business. Teach: how to get stains and yellowing out at home with what's already under the sink. Proof: before and after clips of real customer pairs, filmed on the same table in the same light. You: a 20-year-old running it between classes, including the pair that got ruined and what changed after. One grid cell, Teach crossed with list of 3: "3 things that ruin white sneakers faster than mud."

sections.heading: Choose one main platform
sections.body:
You have under 3 hours a week. That won't win five platforms. Pick the one where your customer already scrolls and post there first. Copy a post to a second platform only if it takes under 5 minutes, and upload your original file, not a download with another app's watermark. In April 2026 Instagram said watermarked reposts don't count as original, and accounts that mostly repost won't be recommended to people who don't follow them.

The platforms have said what they reward. That tells you what to track.
bullets: Instagram Reels: consumer products, local services, visual results. Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram, said in January 2025 that watch time, likes and sends (shares by DM) matter most for ranking. Likes count slightly more with followers, sends slightly more with people who don't follow you yet.

TikTok: consumer products, younger buyers, personality-led content. TikTok's Creator Rewards Program scores videos on originality, play duration (watch time and finish rate), search value and engagement (TikTok, 2024). Say the words your buyer would search for.

YouTube Shorts: if you want long videos later or your buyers search YouTube. In 2023 YouTube's Shorts product lead said posting more doesn't help on its own, publish time barely matters, and new Shorts get tested on a small seed audience first.
LinkedIn: you sell to businesses or professionals, like a resume review or bookkeeping offer.
X: your buyers are founders, developers or creators who read more than they watch.
Decision rule: if you can't name 3 accounts your customer follows on a platform, it's the wrong platform.
sections.example: Gymshark started in 2012 in Ben Francis's parents' garage. He was 19, delivering pizzas for Pizza Hut, and building it with his friend Lewis Morgan. Francis was a YouTube fan, so instead of spreading across every channel, he handed free clothes to the fitness creators his buyers already watched, and some wore them on camera (Fortune, 2024). The lesson: go where your buyers already pay attention, and show up there first.

sections.heading: Build every post on hook, retain, reward
sections.body:
Alex Hormozi's $100M Leads (2023) gives every piece of content three jobs: hook, retain, reward. Hook gets them to stop. Retain keeps them watching, and his go-to shapes are lists, steps and stories. Reward pays off what the hook promised, fast. Every post in your calendar follows that shape. It's also what pushes up watch time and shares, the signals platforms rank on.

Most of your posts give and only a few ask. Hormozi's rule is to give until they ask. In your calendar, most CTAs ask for a follow, a save or a send, and only a couple ask for a sale.
steps: Hook, first 3 seconds: say the promise, show it in the first frame and put it on screen as text. All three should say the same thing. Hook & Caption Bank has 60 to pick from.
Retain: one idea per post, shaped as a list, steps or a story. Cut every pause. Show progress instead of setup.
Reward: deliver the promise before the end, then give one call to action. If the payoff arrives after 30 seconds, move it earlier.

sections.heading: Batch a week in 2 hours
sections.body:
Posting 3 to 5 times a week doesn't mean filming 3 to 5 times a week. Block one 2-hour slot and make everything at once. Gary Vaynerchuk's "document, don't create" helps here: film what you already do, the work, the lesson, the mistake, instead of inventing a show. Edit on your phone in CapCut. Its free version is enough to start.

Keep 5 to 10 minutes on each posting day to reply to comments. In Buffer's 2026 engagement report, replying to comments was linked to about 21% more engagement on Instagram.
steps: Minutes 0 to 20, plan: pick 5 cells from your grid. Write 5 hooks per post and keep the best. Pull ideas from last week's comments.
Minutes 20 to 70, film: same spot, same light, back to back. Film each hook 2 ways. For You posts, talk for 10 minutes about your week and cut 2 clips from it.
Minutes 70 to 110, edit in CapCut: cut every pause, add captions, put the hook on screen in the first frame. Aim for 20 to 60 seconds unless the story needs more.
Minutes 110 to 120, caption and schedule in the platform's own scheduler. No scheduler? Set a phone reminder for each posting day.
On Instagram, post the second take of a hook as a trial reel. Trial reels go to people who don't follow you first, so you get a clean hook test for free.
Put the block in your calendar now as a weekly repeating event. A slot you don't schedule is a slot you won't keep.
sections.example: Jordan, 19, tutors high school algebra. Sunday 4 to 6 pm is his batch. In 20 minutes he picks 5 posts from his grid. He films a common sign mistake (Teach, talking head). He films a whiteboard redo of a problem students often miss, with no names or faces (Proof, voiceover). Then he talks for 10 minutes about almost failing calculus and cuts 2 clips from it (You). Everything is edited and scheduled by 6. During the week he spends 10 minutes after each post replying to comments.

sections.heading: Your 30-day calendar
sections.body:
Copy this into Notes, Notion or a Google Doc. Every post is already prompted. Fill the brackets with your own words during your first batch.

Core days are the 3 posts a week you never miss. Bonus days are 2 extra posts you add when the batch went well. Weeks 1 and 2 test two formats, three tries each, and each format gets one try in every pillar, so the pillar doesn't skew the result. Weeks 3 and 4 double down on the winner.

Day 1 is the day after your first batching block. Make today day one: book that block before you leave this page.

Her best post of the month, a 25-second resume redo, gets 12 sends and 4 DMs, and one becomes a paying customer. Month 2 starts with B, plus a carousel as the new test.

sections.heading: Track which format hit
sections.body:
A format is the shape of a post, not its topic. Talking head with a text hook. Voiceover on a before and after. Hands-only demo. List of 3. Day in the life. Log every post 48 hours after it goes live, so you compare like with like.

Judge each post against your own median: the middle value of your last 10 posts' views. Small numbers are normal early. In Buffer's 2025 TikTok data, the median post got roughly 460 to 510 views at every posting frequency.

When a post wins, Eli asks why: "What did this do that other things we did before didn't?" Then he doubles down "until it doesn't work." Do more of what works, not just more.
steps: Mark a post as a hit if it gets at least 2 times your median views, or the best share rate of your month.
Make a format your main format for the next 2 weeks once it hits on 2 of 3 tries.
Cut a format for a month if it misses 3 times in a row.
When your winner drops below your median twice in a row, bring back the runner-up and start a new test.
If views are high but watch time is low, the hook overpromised or the payoff came too late. Keep the hook and fix the middle.
bullets: Instagram: log average watch time, likes per reach and sends per reach, the three numbers Mosseri told creators to check (January 2025). Sends are your best signal for reaching new people.
TikTok: log average watch time, how many people finished the video, shares and new followers.

YouTube Shorts: since March 31, 2025, a view counts every time a Short starts or replays, so log engaged views instead, plus viewed vs swiped away and subscribers gained. In Paddy Galloway's 2023 study of 5,400 Shorts, those under 60% viewed vs swiped away did poorly, and 70% to 90% did very well.
LinkedIn and X: log impressions, comments and profile visits. A comment from a buyer beats 50 likes.
Every platform: log DMs and link clicks. Those are the numbers that turn into customers.

sections.example: Duolingo joined TikTok in February 2021 with a 23-year-old social media manager, Zaria Parvez, in her first job out of college. The account took off after October 2021, when Duo the owl became a regular character: pushy, a bit unhinged, riffing on trending sounds and replying to comments in character. By December 2021 it had about 1.9 million followers, and the team still posted only 3 to 5 times a week, when it had an original idea (Digiday, 2021). Find the format that hits, then reuse it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Posting on four platforms at once. Fix: one platform for 30 days. Repurpose only when it costs under 5 minutes.
Planning 7 posts a week and quitting in week 2. Fix: commit to 3 core days. Add bonus days only after a good batch.
Changing format every post. Fix: two formats, three tries each, before you judge either one.
Pillars that are just your products. Fix: pillars are your customer's problems, your proof, and you.
Deleting flops and reposting them. Fix: leave them up and learn. YouTube has said deleting and reposting to boost views can look like spam (2023).
Staged results or bought followers. Fix: real proof only. Fake proof gets found out, and after that nothing you post is believed.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: $100M Leads by Alex Hormozi (2023): read the chapters on posting free content for hook, retain, reward and why you give value long before you ask.
Show Your Work! by Austin Kleon (2014): how to share your process without bragging. The best short guide to your You pillar.
Hook Point by Brendan Kane (2020): why viewers decide in about 3 seconds whether to keep watching, and why a hook has to deliver substance, not clickbait.
Buffer's 2025 TikTok posting frequency study (search "Buffer how often should you post on TikTok"): the data behind 3 to 5 posts a week, and why the gains come from breakouts.

Then open Hook & Caption Bank to write 5 hooks for each post. When comments and DMs start coming in, Outreach Scripts shows you how to turn them into real conversations without being pushy. sections.heading: A hook is a promise your post has to keep
sections.body:
You get about 3 seconds. In Hook Point (2020), Brendan Kane argues that's how fast people decide whether to keep watching. A hook is a promise: stay, and you get this. The post is the payment. Break the promise and you get one view and lose the follower.

Hooks run on a curiosity gap. The psychologist George Loewenstein (1994) described curiosity as the feeling of noticing a gap between what you know and what you want to know. A good hook opens one specific gap and the post closes it, fast. A gap the post never closes is clickbait, and it teaches people to scroll past you.

The biggest creators work this way. MrBeast's production guide, which leaked in 2024, starts every video with the title and thumbnail, then uses the opening minute to prove the video delivered on that promise. It pays on short-form too: Instagram's Adam Mosseri named watch time as a top three ranking signal, with likes and sends (January 2025).

Inside: 60 fill-in-the-blank hooks across 10 types, each with a filled example, 10 caption templates, 10 calls to action, and a test log built on Eli's rule: do more of what works, not just more.

sections.heading: Write every hook in three layers
sections.body:
Short-form strategist Kallaway calls this the triple hook: on-screen text, spoken line and visual all make the same promise. In his 2026 breakdown of hooks, he says misalignment is the most common mistake he sees from business owners, and that text is the most important layer. Text also works with the sound off.

His test for the hook is four S's: a clear subject, the stakes for the viewer, speed (compress, don't rush) and clarity (only one possible reading). The next 2 to 4 sentences, his lock-in zone, prove the claim with one specific fact.
steps: Write 5 versions of the hook from at least 2 types below. Pick 1 and save the runner-up for a test.
Spoken: say the promise in your first sentence, about 8 to 12 words. No "hey guys", no "so", no intro.
On-screen text: two short lines at most, up for about 3 seconds, a third of the way down so it doesn't cover your face. Use a specific number: "22 days", not "a few weeks".
First frame: show the thing already happening, or move. The dirty sneaker mid-scrub, the before photo, you walking into frame.
Lock-in, the next 5 to 10 seconds: one proof point that the promise is real. A number, a before photo, a screenshot.
Read it out loud. If it sounds like an ad, rewrite it until it sounds like you talking to one friend.
bullets: One promise per post. If the hook promises two things, make two posts.
Only claim what's true. A fake result might get views once. Eli's rule is that trust beats everything else in sales.
sections.example: Misaligned: you say "So this week was crazy", the text reads "Sneaker tips", and the first frame is your ceiling. Aligned: you say "This $3 brush got a yellowed midsole white again", the text reads "$3 fix for yellow midsoles", and the first frame is the shoe mid-scrub. Same footage. Only the hook changed.

sections.heading: Story, mistake and contrarian hooks
sections.body:
Story hooks work because people follow people. Mistake hooks work because nobody wants to repeat one. Contrarian hooks push back on advice your audience hears constantly, so only use one you believe and back up in the post.

Each example comes from a different business, so you can see the pattern travel. Copy the pattern, never the example.
sections.template:
STORY
1. I started [business] with [small amount or resource]. Here's what month one looked like.
   Ex: I started a sneaker cleaning business with $60 and a toothbrush.
2. [Time] ago I [old situation]. Now I [new situation].
   Ex: Six months ago I couldn't edit a video. Now I edit for 4 podcasts.
3. The day I almost quit [thing], [what happened].
   Ex: The day I almost quit making candles, a local shop asked to stock them.
4. My first customer came from [unexpected place].
   Ex: My first resume client came from a comment I left on a Reddit thread.
5. Everyone told me [doubt]. Here's what happened when I tried anyway.
   Ex: Everyone told me college students won't pay for meal prep.
6. This is what [number] weeks of building [business] actually looks like.
   Ex: This is what 8 weeks of building a phone repair business actually looks like.

MISTAKE
7. I wasted [time or money] on [thing] so you don't have to.
   Ex: I wasted $200 on cleaning kits so you don't have to.
8. Stop [common action] if you want [result].
   Ex: Stop washing suede with water if you want it to last.
9. [Number] mistakes I made in my first [timeframe] of [business].
   Ex: 3 mistakes I made in my first month of selling candles.
10. If you're still [common habit], you're losing [result].
    Ex: If you're still pricing by the hour, you're losing your best clients.
11. Don't [action] until you've [done this first].
    Ex: Don't print 500 stickers until you've sold 50.
12. The [mistake] almost every [person] makes with [thing].
    Ex: The mistake almost every new seller makes with shipping costs.

CONTRARIAN (only if you believe it and back it up in the post)
13. Unpopular opinion: you don't need [common belief] to [result].
    Ex: Unpopular opinion: you don't need a camera to start a video editing business.
14. Everyone says [advice]. Here's why I stopped.
    Ex: Everyone says post every day. Here's why I post 3 times a week.
15. [Popular thing] is overrated for [person]. Do this instead.
    Ex: Meal kits are overrated for college students.
16. You don't have a [surface problem] problem. You have a [real problem] problem.
    Ex: You don't have a views problem. You have a first-2-seconds problem.
17. [Thing people fear] isn't the hard part. [Real hard part] is.
    Ex: Getting your first client isn't the hard part. Getting your second one is.
18. The worst advice I got about [topic] was [advice].
    Ex: The worst advice I got about pricing was to start cheap and raise it later.

sections.heading: How-to, list and result hooks
sections.body: How-to and list hooks earn saves because they promise something usable and a clear finish line. Result hooks are your strongest and your riskiest. Use real results only, your own or a customer's shared with permission. No result yet? Use a mistake or experiment hook instead.
sections.template:
HOW-TO
19. How to [result] in [timeframe] without [pain].
    Ex: How to clean white midsoles in 5 minutes without bleach.
20. Here's exactly how I'd [result] if I started today.
    Ex: Here's exactly how I'd get my first editing client if I started today.
21. The [number]-minute fix for [problem].
    Ex: The 2-minute fix for a resume that gets no replies.
22. How I [result] using only [tool or phone].
    Ex: How I film product videos using only my phone and a window.
23. Do this before you [common action].
    Ex: Do this before you send your first invoice.
24. The easiest way to [result] if you're [specific situation].
    Ex: The easiest way to meal prep if you live in a dorm with no stove.

LIST
25. [Number] [things] I tested, ranked from worst to best.
    Ex: 5 sneaker cleaners I tested, ranked from worst to best.
26. [Number] free tools I use every week to [result].
    Ex: 4 free tools I use every week to run my tutoring business.
27. [Number] signs your [thing] is [problem].
    Ex: 3 signs your resume is getting filtered out before a human sees it.
28. [Number] things I wish I knew before [milestone].
    Ex: 3 things I wish I knew before my first market stall.
29. [Number] [things] under [$ amount] that [result].
    Ex: 3 lighting setups under $20 that make phone videos look professional.
30. My [number]-step [process] for [result]. Copy it.
    Ex: My 4-step packing checklist for orders that never arrive broken.

RESULT (real results only: yours, or a customer's shared with permission)
31. This [before] became [after] in [timeframe].
    Ex: This yellowed midsole went white again in 20 minutes.
32. How [customer type] went from [before] to [after].
    Ex: How a nursing student went from 0 interview calls to 3 in two weeks.
33. What [price] gets you with [offer].
    Ex: What $25 gets you with my resume review.
34. [Customer] said "[exact words]." Here's what we did.
    Ex: A client said "I finally get algebra." Here's what we changed.
35. My [first, 10th or 100th] [sale, client or order] and what it taught me.
    Ex: My 10th order and the packing mistake it exposed.
36. Watch this [thing] go from [before] to [after].
    Ex: Watch this $8 thrifted jacket go from stained to resale ready.

sections.heading: Behind-the-scenes, call-out, comparison and experiment hooks
sections.body: Behind-the-scenes hooks build trust by showing the work. Call-out hooks name the viewer, so the right person stops. Comparison hooks promise a verdict, so give one. Experiment hooks open a gap about the outcome, so only use them when you ran the test and will show the real result, good or bad.
sections.template:
BEHIND THE SCENES
37. A day running [business] while [other commitment].
    Ex: A day running a candle business while working a full-time job.
38. What goes into one [product or service] that nobody sees.
    Ex: What goes into one $30 logo that nobody sees.
39. Packing [number] orders for [business]. Come with me.
    Ex: Packing 14 orders for my sticker shop.
40. Here's what my [setup or process] actually looks like.
    Ex: Here's what my $0 editing setup actually looks like.
41. Honest update: week [number] of building [business].
    Ex: Honest update: week 6 of building a meal prep business.
42. The part of [business] I hate, and why I do it anyway.
    Ex: The part of tutoring I hate, and why I do it anyway.

CALL-OUT
43. If you're a [specific person] who [situation], this is for you.
    Ex: If you're a student athlete who hates cooking, this is for you.
44. This is for every [person] who's tired of [pain].
    Ex: This is for every freelancer who's tired of chasing invoices.
45. Do you [common behavior]? Here's what it's doing to [thing].
    Ex: Do you machine-wash your sneakers? Here's what it's doing to the glue.
46. Raise your hand if you've ever [relatable pain].
    Ex: Raise your hand if you've ever bought a planner and quit by February.
47. Only watch this if you [qualifier].
    Ex: Only watch this if you sell something under $50.
48. POV: you [relatable moment].
    Ex: POV: you finally clean the sneakers you've been hiding in your closet.

COMPARISON
49. [Option A] vs [option B]: which one actually [result]?
    Ex: $5 cleaner vs $25 cleaner: which one actually works?
50. I tested [cheap thing] and [expensive thing] for [timeframe]. Here's the verdict.
    Ex: I tested a $12 and a $60 ring light for a week.
51. What [amount] gets you at [place A] vs [place B].
    Ex: What $50 gets you at a local print shop vs online.
52. Beginner [thing] vs pro [thing], same [tool].
    Ex: Beginner lighting vs pro lighting, same phone.
53. [Task] the slow way vs the fast way.
    Ex: Packing orders the slow way vs the fast way.
54. What [customers] expect vs what actually happens.
    Ex: What clients expect from a logo designer vs what actually happens.

EXPERIMENT (only if you ran it, and show the real outcome)
55. I tried [thing] for [timeframe]. Here's what happened.
    Ex: I sold at a farmers market for 4 weekends.
56. Can you [result] with only [constraint]? Let's find out.
    Ex: Can you start a business with only $50?
57. I let [person or group] decide [thing] for my business.
    Ex: I let my followers pick my next candle scent.
58. Testing [popular claim] so you don't have to.
    Ex: Testing the viral toothpaste sneaker trick so you don't have to.
59. Day [number] of [challenge].
    Ex: Day 1 of turning $100 into a real business.
60. I [did something unusual] to get [result]. Was it worth it?
    Ex: I handed out 100 flyers to find tutoring clients.

sections.heading: 10 caption templates
sections.body:
The hook earns the view. The caption keeps the reader and gives one next step. Put the point in the first line. Instagram allows 2,200 characters but shows only about the first 125 in the feed, and TikTok allows 4,000 but shows about 100 (Hootsuite, 2026). On short video, 1 to 3 lines usually do the job.

The first three templates use classic formulas. AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action) is usually credited to adman E. St. Elmo Lewis in the late 1890s. PAS (problem, agitate, solve) and BAB (before, after, bridge) are direct-response staples. The 4 U's check comes from copywriter Michael Masterson's teaching at AWAI.
sections.template:
1. PAS: PROBLEM, AGITATE, SOLVE
[The problem, in your customer's words.]
[Why it's worse than it looks, one specific line.]
[Your fix, in one or two sentences.]
[CTA]

2. BAB: BEFORE, AFTER, BRIDGE
Before: [situation].
After: [situation].
What changed: [the one thing they can copy].
[CTA]

3. AIDA: ATTENTION, INTEREST, DESIRE, ACTION
[Restate the hook in new words.]
[One surprising, specific detail.]
[What it looks like once it's fixed.]
[One CTA.]

4. QUICK LESSON
[Hook restated]. The lesson: [one sentence]. [CTA]

5. THREE TIPS
[Number] things I wish I knew about [topic]:
1) [tip]
2) [tip]
3) [tip]
Which one are you trying first?

6. STORY
[Where you were]. [What happened]. [What you learned]. [Question for the reader]?

7. CUSTOMER WORDS (with permission)
"[Exact customer quote]." That's why we [what you do]. [CTA]

8. BEHIND THE SCENES
What you didn't see: [the hidden work]. That's why [result] takes [time]. [CTA]

9. MYTH VS TRUTH
Myth: [common belief]. Truth: [what you've seen]. Why: [one reason]. [CTA]

10. HONEST OFFER
I help [who] [get result] without [pain]. I have room for [real number] [clients or orders] this month. [CTA]

FIRST-LINE CHECK, THE 4 U'S: is it useful, urgent, unique and ultra-specific? Hit at least 2 before you post.
sections.example: PAS for the sneaker business: "Yellow midsoles make $150 sneakers look ten years old. Most people scrub harder, which spreads the stain into the stitching. A $3 brush and dish soap, 10 minutes, done. Comment CLEAN and I'll DM you the full steps."

sections.heading: 10 calls to action
sections.body:
One CTA per post, matched to one goal, and the label on each line below is its goal. Sends reach new people. Saves signal the post was useful. Comments start conversations. DMs and clicks turn into customers.

127 uses the comment-a-keyword CTA itself: "Comment ROADMAP." ManyChat sends a DM to everyone who comments the word. Meta's developer docs allow an automation one message per comment until the person replies, so send a short note with a button first and the link after they tap. Instagram Teen Accounts only get messages from accounts they follow or are connected with, so say "Follow and comment [KEYWORD]" and keep the link in your bio as a backup.

Deliver exactly what you promised, right away. A keyword that leads to a sales pitch instead of the free thing is bait-and-switch. So is "only 2 spots left" when it isn't true. Both are out of bounds.

Comments also hand you hooks. Duolingo's TikTok team replied to comments in character as Duo, sometimes on video (Digiday, 2021). Reply on video to your best question and open with it.
sections.template:
1. LEADS: Follow and comment [KEYWORD] and I'll DM you [free thing].
2. REACH: Send this to a friend who [situation].
3. SAVES: Save this for the next time you [situation].
4. FOLLOWS: Follow for part 2, where I [what part 2 covers]. (Only when part 2 is already filmed.)
5. SALES CHATS: DM me [KEYWORD] if you want help with [problem].
6. COMMENTS: Which one are you, [A] or [B]? Tell me below.
7. CLICKS: Link in bio to [book, order or get the free guide]. (Use the same words on the link page.)
8. PROOF: Try this today and tell me how it went.
9. TRUST: Drop your [thing] below and I'll give quick feedback on the first [number]. (Then actually do it.)
10. SALES: I have room for [real number] [clients or orders] this month. DM me [KEYWORD] to grab one. (Real capacity only.)

sections.heading: The do-more-of-what-works loop
sections.body:
A bank only helps if you learn from it. Eli's method: when something works, ask "What did this do that other things we did before didn't?" Then double down until it stops working.

Test one thing at a time: the same footage with two hooks beats two random posts. Instagram's trial reels are built for this. They go to people who don't follow you first, and after 24 hours you see views, likes, comments and shares before deciding whether to share with followers.
steps: Once a month, study the top 15 to 20 creators in your niche, 2 or 3 of their best videos from the last 3 to 6 months. That's Kallaway's method. Note the hook pattern, not the words.
Post at least 2 hook types each week so you have a comparison.
Log each post at 48 hours: views, watch time, shares.
Find the winner, the post that clearly beat your median views (the middle of your last 10). Write one reason why: hook type, first frame, topic, length or format.
Double down: write 3 new hooks that keep the winning element and change the topic. Retire a hook type that misses 3 times in a row and retry it next month.
bullets: High views, low watch time: the hook overpromised or the payoff came late. Keep the hook, move the payoff earlier.
Low views, good watch time: the first frame and line aren't stopping the scroll. Keep the body, rewrite the hook.
Good watch time, few shares: fine but not worth sending. Add one surprising, specific detail.
Lots of comments, no DMs: your CTA asks for opinions, not action. Switch to a keyword or DM CTA.

sections.example: Sam, 20, cleans sneakers for $30 a pair. He posts one before and after twice as Instagram trial reels with different hooks. Mistake: "Stop scrubbing yellow midsoles with bleach." Result: "This yellowed midsole went white again in 20 minutes." After 24 hours the mistake version has 380 views and 3 sends. The result version has 1,150 views and 19 sends. He shares the winner with his followers and writes 3 remixes with the same before shot and hook structure. Next week's test: result hook vs comparison hook.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Clickbait the post doesn't pay off. Fix: if the post can't deliver, change the hook, not the facts.
A hook that needs context, like "So yesterday..." Fix: start mid-action with the payoff named.
Text, frame and voice saying three different things. Fix: one promise, matched in all three layers.
Copying a creator's exact line. Fix: borrow the pattern, fill it with your customer's words and your real numbers.
Three CTAs in one post. Fix: one ask per post.
Judging a hook type on one post. Fix: give it 3 tries before you decide.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: $100M Leads by Alex Hormozi (2023): read the chapters on posting free content for hook, retain, reward and how to give value before you ask.
Hook Point by Brendan Kane (2020): why viewers decide in about 3 seconds whether to keep watching, and why a real hook delivers substance instead of clickbait.
Made to Stick by Chip Heath and Dan Heath (2007): the Unexpected chapter shows how to open a curiosity gap and close it.
The Psychology of Curiosity by George Loewenstein (Psychological Bulletin, 1994): the original information-gap research, if you want the science behind hooks.

sections.heading: Your output and next step
sections.body:
Before you close this page: write 10 hooks from at least 6 types, write your best one in three layers, fill 3 caption templates and set your keyword CTA.

Then put the hooks into your posting days in the 30-Day Content Calendar. When keyword DMs arrive, Outreach Scripts shows you how to reply and start a real conversation. Track how many DMs become customers in the Founder KPI Dashboard. Want a week of posts with the hooks written for you? Run the Content & Distribution Planner.
