resources.aiPrompt: Check that each hook names a specific person, problem, number, tool or timeframe from the member's niche instead of generic words like "tips" or "results", and that the 10 hooks span at least 6 types. Flag any hook that claims a result, number or story the member hasn't shown they have, and any curiosity hook the post can't pay off; tell them to swap it for a mistake or experiment hook. Check that the three-layer hook makes the same promise in the first frame, the on-screen text and the spoken line, and that the spoken line has no intro and runs about 12 words or fewer. Check that the CTA asks for one action, delivers something real right away, and uses no fake scarcity. Check that the test plan changes one variable and names the number that picks the winner. Then send them to the 30-Day Content Calendar to schedule the hooks, or to Outreach Scripts if their CTA drives DMs.

resources.title: Outreach Scripts
resources.summary: Copy-paste scripts for warm, cold, referral, follow-up, inbound and objection messages, plus the volume and tracking rules that get replies.
resources.output: A 50-name list, your first 10 messages sent, scripts for every reply you get, answers to the 5 common objections and a tracker with follow-up dates.

sections.heading: Trust first, then volume
sections.body:
Your first customers come from people who already trust you, then from the people they trust. Strangers come later. Alex Hormozi's $100M Leads names four ways to get leads: warm outreach, free content, cold outreach and paid ads. Warm outreach goes first. It's free, and people who know you reply.

Eli's rule: "Trust beats everything else in sales." His sales record: #3 in the country on a national vendor sales list of 6,000+ agents (2025); top 25 in his first 6 months (2024). His habit is to talk to everyone, everywhere, every time. He calls it his networking glitch hack.

Inside: 22 scripts for warm, cold, referral, follow-up, inbound and booking messages, replies to the 5 objections you will hear, how much to send, and a tracker. The rule under all of it: be specific, be brief, ask permission and take no for an answer.
steps: Write 50 names before you write a message: phone contacts, DMs, followers who reply, teams, clubs, old coworkers and past customers.
Tag each one B (might buy), K (knows buyers) or F (will give honest feedback).
Send 10 messages today and log each one with a follow-up date 3 days out.

sections.heading: The rules every message follows
sections.body:
Good outreach reads like a text from a person, not a campaign. Hormozi's opener is ACA: acknowledge something real about them, compliment it honestly, then ask a question. Josh Braun teaches asking permission instead of pushing for time on a calendar, so saying no feels safe. Chris Voss, a former FBI hostage negotiator, shows in Never Split the Difference that people answer "no" questions more easily than "yes" traps. Naming what someone feels gets them talking.

Cold is a different game from warm. Platforms filter strangers, and the law covers commercial email. Read the cold section before you send.
bullets: Keep it under 75 words. If it needs scrolling on a phone, cut it.
Open with them: a real detail you noticed, not "hope you're well".
Make one ask per message: feedback, a referral or a yes. Never all three.
Ask before you send a link or a pitch: "Want me to send it?" or "Open to a quick look?"
Poke the bear, Josh Braun's name for a question that helps someone notice a gap: "How are you getting new clients right now? Is it as steady as you'd like?"
When people go quiet, ask a no-oriented question: "Is it a bad idea to..." or "Have you given up on..."
Label instead of arguing: "It sounds like timing is the real issue."
Rewrite the first line for every person, and take no for an answer. Never cold-message anyone under 18.

sections.heading: Warm scripts: people who know you
sections.body: Warm outreach works because they already know you're real. Hormozi's twist is to ask who they know instead of asking them to buy. People who have the problem tend to raise their hand anyway, and nobody feels cornered.
sections.template:
WARM 1:1 (acknowledge, compliment, ask)
Hey [name], [acknowledge something real: saw you started at (place) / your team won Saturday]. [Honest, specific compliment]. Random question: I just started [business], helping [who] with [problem]. Do you know anyone dealing with that right now?

WARM DIRECT OFFER (only if they told you about the problem before)
Hey [name], you mentioned [problem they told you about] a while back. I'm now doing [service] for [who], and I'm taking my first [a real number] at [intro price or bonus] through [date]. Is that still a thing for you, or did you sort it out?

WARM ANNOUNCEMENT (your story, a post, or a group chat you're already in)
Some news: I started [business]. I help [who] [get result] in [timeframe]. I'm taking [a real number] [clients / orders] this month at [intro price] while I build my first reviews. If that's you or someone you know, reply or DM me "[KEYWORD]".

REFERRAL ASK (right after a customer says something good)
So glad [result] worked out, [name]. Who's one person you know dealing with [problem]? If it helps, here's a text you can forward: "I used [your name] for [service] and [result]. Thought of you: [link or handle]."

RE-ENGAGE A PAST CUSTOMER (30 to 90 days after delivery)
Hey [name], it's been [time] since [what you did for them]. How's [result] holding up? I'm opening [new offer / next batch] on [date] and wanted to offer it to past customers first. Want the details?
sections.example: Illustrative: "Hey Marcus, saw your sister's graduation pics, congrats to your whole family. Random question: I just started a lawn care business this spring, mowing and edging for families around Westwood. Do you know anyone whose yard has gotten out of hand?" Marcus replied that his parents did, and that turned into a weekly client. One honest first line did more than a perfect pitch.

sections.heading: Cold scripts: strangers, done right
sections.body:
Cold works when it's clearly written for one person and offers help before it asks. Paul Graham's essay Do Things That Don't Scale tells how Stripe's founders, the Collison brothers, handled "I'll try it." They asked for the person's laptop and set Stripe up on the spot. Airbnb's founders went door to door in New York, signing up hosts and helping them improve their listings. Your version: show up with the help already in hand.

Check the platform before you send. On Instagram, a message to someone who doesn't follow you usually lands in their message requests, so your first line has to earn the open. Instagram's Teen Accounts also limit who can contact under-18s by default, one more reason to reach teens through their parents. LinkedIn limits the length of a connection note, so keep it to two short sentences.

Cold email to US inboxes falls under the CAN-SPAM Act. Use an honest sender and subject line, and say it's an ad when it is. Include a valid postal address (a registered P.O. box counts) and a working opt-out you honor within 10 business days. The FTC's guide, CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business, has the details. Canada's anti-spam law (CASL) and the EU and UK rules (GDPR, and PECR in the UK) set stricter consent rules for marketing messages. Check the official guidance before you email anyone there. This isn't legal advice.
sections.template:
COLD DM: LOCAL BUSINESS (Instagram or Facebook, owner or business account)
Hey [name], [specific thing you noticed: the new fall menu / the line out the door Saturday]. I'm [your name], I [do thing] for [type of business] in [town]. I noticed [one small, fixable issue, e.g. your last 3 reels have no captions]. Mind if I send you a quick fix? Free, no strings.

COLD EMAIL (to a business address)
Subject: [their business]'s [specific thing]
Hi [name],
I [noticed / tried / read] [specific detail about their business]. [One-line question about a likely problem, e.g. "Are online orders still coming in by phone?"]
I help [type of business] [result] in [timeframe]. [Only if real: For (similar business), that meant (honest result).]
Open to a 10-minute call to see if it fits? If not, no worries at all.
[Your name] | [Business] | [Postal address]
Not interested? Reply "no" and I won't email again.

LINKEDIN CONNECTION NOTE (two short sentences; LinkedIn limits the length)
Hi [name], [specific thing: your post on (topic) / we both went to (school)]. I help [who] with [problem]. Would love to connect and hear how you handle [topic].

AFTER THEY REPLY WITH THE PROBLEM
That makes sense. It sounds like [label their situation in their words]. That's exactly what I help with: [one-line offer]. Want me to show you how it would work for you?
bullets: Message adults and businesses only. Sell to parents, never cold to a minor.
Send no link in the first message. Earn the reply first.
If they don't describe a problem, don't pitch. Thank them and move on.

sections.heading: Follow-ups and closing the loop
sections.body:
Most replies come after a follow-up, because people are busy, not because they said no. Send 3 touches, each adding something new, then close the loop and stop.

Touch 3 uses a Voss-style no-oriented question. It works because answering "no, I haven't" feels safe. Use it once, kindly. If it reads like a guilt trip in your voice, skip to closing the loop.

A "no", a "stop" or a block ends it the first time. Mark it in your tracker and never message that person about it again.
sections.template:
TOUCH 1 (day 3): BUMP WITH CONTEXT
Hey [name], floating this back up in case it got buried. Short version: [one-line offer]. No pressure either way.

TOUCH 2 (day 7): ADD SOMETHING USEFUL
Hey [name], saw [relevant thing] and thought of you: [one tip, idea or free resource]. Still happy to help with [problem] if it's useful.

TOUCH 3 (day 14): NO-ORIENTED QUESTION
Hey [name], have you given up on [fixing problem] for now?

CLOSE THE LOOP (day 21, last message)
Hey [name], I'll stop filling your inbox. If [problem] becomes a priority, I'm here. Thanks for reading these.

sections.heading: Inbound replies and booking the call
sections.body:
When someone reaches out first, reply the same day. Ask one question before you quote a price so the offer fits their situation. Then give one easy next step: a booking link (Eli's stack uses Calendly) or two times to pick from.

Eli's offer rule: "When selling cost, always frame it as the lowest possible number, when value the highest." Make the recap so clear and fair that saying yes feels obvious. Once a call is booked, The Sales Conversation covers what to say on it.
sections.template:
INBOUND: FIRST REPLY (same day)
Hey [name], thanks for reaching out. So I can actually help: what's going on with [problem] right now, and what have you tried so far?

INBOUND: AFTER THEY EXPLAIN
Got it. It sounds like [label their situation]. That's exactly what I help with. The fastest way to see if it fits is a 15-minute call. Grab a time here: [booking link], or send me two times that work.

BOOKING CONFIRMATION
You're booked for [day, time]. I'll bring [one thing you'll prepare, e.g. 3 ideas for your page]. If anything changes, just reply here.

AFTER THE CALL: OFFER RECAP
Great talking, [name]. What I heard: [their problem in their words]. What I'll do: [deliverable] by [date]. Price: [price]. If you're in, reply YES and I'll send [payment link / next step]. If it's a no, that's completely fine too.
sections.example: Illustrative, on LinkedIn: "Got it, you've applied to 40 roles and heard back from 2. That's exactly what I help with. I'll rewrite your resume for one target role and send it back in 48 hours for $49, less than $2 a day for a month of better applications. If you don't get a single interview from your next 15 applications, I'll redo it free." The price is framed small, the outcome is framed big, and the guarantee is one the seller can keep.

sections.heading: Replies to the 5 objections you will hear
sections.body: Objections are questions in disguise. Don't argue. Label what you heard, ask one question and respect the answer. If the honest answer is that your offer isn't right for them, say so. Eli's rule: "Solve problems don't sell products."
sections.template:
"IT'S TOO EXPENSIVE"
Totally fair. It sounds like the price feels high for what you'd get. Can I ask what you expected to pay? [If you have a smaller version:] I also do [smaller option] for [lower price]. [If not:] No worries, it might not be the right fit right now.

"I NEED TO THINK ABOUT IT"
Of course. Usually that means one thing doesn't sit right yet. Is it the price, the timing, or whether it'll work for you? Happy to answer whichever it is.

"NOT RIGHT NOW"
Makes sense. Would it be a bad idea for me to check back in [month]? If anything changes before then, just reply here.

"I ALREADY HAVE SOMEONE" / "I DO IT MYSELF"
Sounds like you've got it covered. Out of curiosity, if you could change one thing about how it's going, what would it be? [If they name something you fix:] That's exactly what I help with. Want to see how? [If not:] Glad it's working. I'll leave you to it.

"IS THIS LEGIT?" / "SEND ME MORE INFO"
Fair question, you should ask it. So I send the right thing: what matters most to you, [result A] or [result B]? Here's my page: [link]. [Only if real: here's what (customer) said.] Happy to do a quick call so you can see who you're dealing with.

sections.heading: Track it and set your volume
sections.body:
Outreach dies without tracking. You forget who you messaged, and follow-ups never happen. Use a sheet, Notion or Attio, and pick one tonight.

Volume decides results more than wording does. Hormozi's Rule of 100 is 100 outreach actions a day, every day, for 100 days. With under 3 hours a week, aim for about 50 new messages a week plus follow-ups. That's 10 a day on 5 days, about 20 minutes each, or the same 50 in two or three longer blocks.

Judge cold and warm separately. Cold reply rates run far lower, so a quiet week of cold messages is normal and a quiet week of warm ones is a signal.
bullets: Under 2 replies per 20 warm messages: your first line is the problem. Make it more personal.
Replies but no calls or sales: your offer is the problem. Go back to The One-Page Offer.
Under 3 replies after 100 cold messages: change who you message before you change the words.
One script beats the others two weeks in a row: make it your default and test a new first line against it.
sections.example: Illustrative: Ava, 20, posts for local cafes and salons at $150 a month. Week 1, she sends 50 warm ACA messages: 21 reply, 6 name a business owner, and her aunt's salon books a call. Week 2, she sends 40 cold DMs to cafes, each pointing out one fixable thing, like reels with no captions: 5 reply. Follow-ups add 4 more replies. She books 5 calls and signs 2 clients. Her most common objection is "I do it myself", and the "change one thing" reply turns one of those into client 3. Warm replies beat cold more than 3 to 1, so warm stays her main channel and cold tests one new neighborhood a week.

OUTREACH TRACKER (one row per person)
Name | Warm or cold | B / K / F | Date sent | Script used | Replied? | Next touch date | Stage | Outcome

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Pitching in the first line. Ask about their situation first.
Writing a paragraph. Stay under 75 words with one ask.
Sending a link cold. Ask permission, then send it.
Following up with "just checking in". Add something new every touch.
Arguing with objections. Label it, ask one question, accept the answer.

Buying a bot to blast DMs. Platform rules ban spam and unauthorized automation. Automate only replies to people who reached out first, like a ManyChat keyword reply. Even then, Meta allows one private reply to a comment, and more only after the person answers.
No tracker. Log every send the same day with a follow-up date.

sections.heading: Go deeper
bullets: $100M Leads by Alex Hormozi: read the warm and cold outreach chapters for the Core Four and how much outreach it really takes.
Never Split the Difference by Chris Voss with Tahl Raz: take labels, mirrors and no-oriented questions for objections and follow-ups.
Do Things That Don't Scale by Paul Graham: a short essay on recruiting your first users by hand. Read it before your first cold message.
Million Dollar Weekend by Noah Kagan: practice asking for things until hearing no stops scaring you.

sections.heading: Your next step
sections.body: Send your first 10 messages today and log them. Still not sure who has the problem? Run Validation Interview Scripts first. Replies but no yeses? Tighten The One-Page Offer. Need a page to send people to? Use the Landing Page Brief. Track sends, replies and sales each week in the Founder KPI Dashboard. Launching something? Pair these scripts with the First Launch Checklist and the Launch Checklist Generator.

resources.aiPrompt: Check that the warm list has at least 20 real names, each with how they know them and a B, K or F tag; flag vague entries like "friends from school" or "my followers". Check the first message is under 75 words, opens with a specific detail about that person, makes one ask, asks permission before any link and contains no fake scarcity, guilt or invented results; if it opens with a pitch, rewrite it with acknowledge, compliment, ask. Confirm the cold target is adults or businesses, never minors, and that any cold email plan includes an opt-out and a postal address under CAN-SPAM, without giving legal advice. Check the objection reply labels the concern, asks one question and accepts a no rather than pushing. Check there is a daily send number with a time slot and follow-ups on about day 3, 7 and 14; if volume is under 5 a day, push for 10. If they have replies but no yeses, send them to The One-Page Offer; if they still can't name who has the problem, send them to Validation Interview Scripts.

resources.title: Founder KPI Dashboard
resources.summary: Track five results and two inputs you control each week, find the step where people drop off, and make one kill, pause or double-down call.
resources.output: A weekly scorecard: five results, two lead measures with targets, the conversion rate at every step, your one metric for the month, and one written decision for next week.

sections.heading: Track what pays you, not what flatters you
sections.body:
Followers, likes and views feel like progress. They can climb for months while sales sit at zero.

This dashboard tracks the chain that pays you: reach, visits, leads, sales and revenue. It divides each step by the one before it, so you see exactly where people drop off. Fix that leak before you pour more people into the top.

Next to those results, you track two inputs you control: posts published and outreach sent. Results show up late. Inputs you can change by tomorrow. When results drop, check your inputs before you change your strategy.

Eli's rule: do more of what works, not just more in general. You can't do that until you know what works. The rest of this page covers where to pull each number, how to pick your lead measures and your one metric for the month, and what each rate means. Then you make the weekly kill, pause or double-down call. Ten minutes every Monday.

sections.heading: Fill in last week first
sections.body:
Enter last week in the dashboard before you read on. Guesses are fine for week one. Write down where each number came from, so next week takes half the time.

If a number is zero, enter zero. A zero is information. It tells you exactly where to look.
steps: Count posts published: everything that went live last week, on every platform. This is a lead measure, so log it next to its weekly target.
Count outreach sent: DMs, emails or calls you started with potential buyers. Count messages actually sent, not people you meant to message. This is your other lead measure.
Pull reach: total views or impressions from your content, ads or flyers, from each platform's analytics or insights tab.
Pull visits: profile visits plus website visitors. Your store or site dashboard shows visitors.
Count leads: everyone who raised a hand. DMs asking to buy, form fills, booked calls and replies to your outreach. Note how many came from outreach.
Pull sales: paying orders or customers, from your store or payment app, not your memory.
Pull revenue: money in from those sales, before costs. It is not profit.
sections.template:
NUMBER SOURCES (fill once, reuse every week)
Posts published: [where you count them]
Outreach sent: [e.g. a DM list in Notion, your sent folder]
Reach: [e.g. TikTok analytics, last 7 days]
Visits: [e.g. Instagram profile visits + store visitors]
Leads: [e.g. DMs asking price + form fills + outreach replies]
Sales: [e.g. store orders]
Revenue: [e.g. store total sales]
Pulled every: [day and time, e.g. Monday 8am]

sections.heading: Pick two lead measures you control
sections.body:
Revenue is a lag measure. By the time you see it, the week is over. The 4 Disciplines of Execution (Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling, 2012) says to steer by lead measures instead. A lead measure predicts the result, and you can directly control it. For a new founder, the two that matter most are usually posts published and outreach sent.

Picking the right input is a skill. In Working Backwards (2021), Colin Bryar and Bill Carr describe an Amazon team that first tracked how many new product pages it added. The count went up, but plenty of the new pages were for products few people wanted. The team kept changing the input until it tracked something customers felt: whether the products they looked at were actually in stock. Pick lead measures that move sales, not just activity.

Set a weekly target for each one that you can hit 4 weeks out of 5. Then hit it.
bullets: Strong: 20 DMs a week to past buyers and warm contacts. You control it, and replies follow it.
Strong: 4 posts a week in your best-performing format. You control it, and reach follows it.
Weak: 'go viral' or 'hit 1,000 followers'. Those are results. You can't do them on a Tuesday.
If you hit a lead measure 3 weeks running and results don't move, the measure is wrong. Swap it.

sections.heading: Choose one metric that matters this month
sections.body:
Lean Analytics (Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz, 2013) argues for One Metric That Matters: the single number that best shows whether your current stage is working. It changes as you grow. Dave McClure's pirate metrics (2007) lay out the stages in order: acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue.

Croll and Yoskovitz also say a good metric is a rate or ratio you can compare over time, and one that changes what you do. Follower count fails that test. Leads to sales passes. Pick yours by stage.
bullets: No sales yet: leads per week. Your job is conversations. Everything else waits.
First sales, under 10 customers: leads to sales. Learn what makes people say yes.
Steady sales: revenue per sale, or repeat buyers. Get more from the customers you have before chasing new ones.
Paying for traffic: cost per sale against revenue per sale. Run the Launch Budget Calculator before you spend.

sections.heading: What each conversion rate tells you
sections.body:
The dashboard divides each step by the one before it. A big number followed by a weak rate is a leak. More reach on a leaky profile just means more people leaving.

If two steps look weak, fix the one closest to the sale first. It's usually the cheaper fix, and every gain there flows straight into sales.

Treat outside benchmarks as a rough sense of scale, not a target. One of the few solid ones: across industries, the median landing page converts about 6.6 percent of visitors into its goal, such as a signup or a sale (Unbounce, Q4 2024 data). That's for dedicated pages, not social profiles. Your numbers are small and your market is specific, so your own trend beats any average.
bullets: Reach to visits (visits divided by reach): is your content making people curious about you? If it's low, your hooks get views but your profile doesn't pull people in. Fix your bio, pinned posts and the first line of your site.

Visits to leads (inbound leads divided by visits): when people look closer, do they raise a hand? If it's low, the offer or the next step is unclear. Use The One-Page Offer and the Landing Page Brief.

Leads to sales (sales divided by leads): when people talk to you, do they buy? If it's low, it's usually trust, price framing or a fuzzy offer, not traffic. Reread your DMs and use the Outreach Scripts.
Revenue per sale (revenue divided by sales): what each customer is worth. If it's low, look at bundles, an add-on or pricing tied to the customer's ROI. Use the Pricing Worksheet.
sections.example: Illustrative: Sam, 19, sells print-on-demand hoodies. Week 1: 12,000 views, 300 profile visits, 6 DMs, 3 sales, $105. Reach to visits is 2.5 percent, visits to leads 2 percent, leads to sales 50 percent, $35 per sale. Six leads is too few to trust that 50 percent, but the shape is clear: people who talk to Sam buy, and people who look at the profile leave. The profile is the step closest to the sale with a real leak, and a new bio costs nothing. The fix goes there, not into more posts.

sections.heading: Read three weeks, not one day
sections.body:
One good day means nothing. One week is a data point. Three weeks is a trend. Small numbers swing hard: with 5 leads, one extra sale moves your close rate by 20 points. Until a step has at least 100 visits or 10 leads behind it, read the counts, not the percentage.

When something works, Eli's question is why. What did this do that everything before it didn't? Then do more of exactly that until it stops working. Your inputs help you find the answer.
bullets: Inputs down, results down: you did less. Get back to your targets before you change the strategy.
Inputs on target, results flat: the volume is there and the message isn't. Change one thing: the hook, the offer or who you message.
Inputs on target, results up: double down. Keep the format, channel and message, and add a little volume.
Results up, inputs flat: something other than volume worked, like one post or one referral. Find it and write down why.
Reach up, everything else flat: you found a hook, but it pulls in the wrong people or your next step is unclear.

sections.heading: Kill, pause or double down
sections.body:
List what you spent time on last week, match each activity to the numbers, and make one call per activity. Product-market fit, in Eli's words, is when people want to pay for your product without you needing to sell it to them. Until then, these weekly calls are how you find your way to it.

Airbnb's founders made this kind of call early. Growth had stalled, and when they studied their New York listings, the photos were poor. So they went to New York and photographed hosts' homes themselves, and revenue there rose soon after. They fixed the one leaking step instead of buying more traffic.
bullets: Double down: it moved a number you care about 2 weeks or more in a row. Do more of exactly that: same format, same channel, same message.
Pause: it hasn't moved anything yet, but you've run it fewer than 3 times, or you changed too much at once. Run it cleanly once more, then decide.
Kill: you gave it at least 3 clean runs and leads and sales didn't move. Stop. With under 3 hours a week, time is your scarcest input.
sections.example: Illustrative, start to finish: Sam's metric for the month is visits to leads, from 2 to 5 percent. Lead measures: 4 posts and 20 DMs to past buyers a week. In week 2, Sam rewrites the bio and pins a post with the 3 best designs and 'DM DROP to order'. Inputs: both targets hit. Results: 280 visits, 14 inbound DMs (5 percent), 5 replies from the 20 outreach DMs, 7 sales, $245. Calls: double down on the pinned post, pause posting every day, kill the hashtag research, which never moved a number. Next test: a second pinned post that shows prices. Sam changes only that one thing in week 3.

sections.heading: Your 10-minute Monday
sections.body:
Same day, same time, same sources. The EOS Scorecard from Gino Wickman's Traction keeps 5 to 15 weekly numbers, each with an owner and a goal, and shows the last 13 weeks on one page. You're a team of one, so you own every number. Keep each week's scorecard so you can see the trend.

Then carry the decision into your Weekly CEO Review, where it becomes next week's top three.
steps: Pull last week's numbers from your sources list. 3 minutes.
Enter them in the dashboard and mark each lead measure hit or missed against its target. 2 minutes.
Find the rate that dropped most since last week, using only steps with enough data. If nothing dropped, take the weak step closest to the sale. 2 minutes.
Write one kill, one pause, one double down and one test for next week. 3 minutes.
Put the test on your calendar. Once the habit sticks, automate the number pull with the weekly metrics email in the Automation Starter Pack.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Tracking vanity numbers. Followers and likes don't pay. Track the chain that ends in revenue.
Too many numbers. Five results and two inputs is enough. Add one only when a decision needs it.
Changing three things in one week. You won't know which one worked. One test at a time.
Judging a rate on tiny numbers. Under 100 visits or 10 leads, read counts, not percentages.
Different sources every week. Pull each number from the same place, on the same day.
Counting revenue as profit. Revenue is money in. Costs come out after.
Tracking without deciding. If Monday ends without a kill, pause or double down, you just took notes.

sections.heading: Go deeper
sections.body: Next: take this week's decision into the Weekly CEO Review. If your leak is reach, work through the 30-Day Content Calendar and the Hook & Caption Bank. If you're about to pay for traffic, run the Launch Budget Calculator first.
bullets: Lean Analytics by Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz (2013): One Metric That Matters, and what to track at each stage.
The 4 Disciplines of Execution by Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling (2012): lead versus lag measures, and a scoreboard you check every week.
Traction by Gino Wickman: the EOS Scorecard, one page of weekly numbers with an owner and a goal for each.
Startup Metrics for Pirates by Dave McClure (2007): the AARRR funnel in one short talk. Search the slides by name.
Working Backwards by Colin Bryar and Bill Carr (2021): how Amazon picks inputs it controls and reviews them every week.

If a step has fewer than 100 visits or 10 leads behind it, tell them the rate is too noisy to judge and to read counts instead. resources.title: Weekly CEO Review
resources.summary: A 30-minute weekly review that pulls you out of the busywork, scores the week and decides what next week is for. Plus a 90-day version.
resources.output: A finished weekly review: numbers, last week's promises checked, what worked and why, one cut, one handoff, next week's ONE thing and top three on your calendar, plus your 90-day priorities.

sections.heading: Thirty minutes a week as the CEO
sections.body:
Eli's rule: get to working on the business, not in it, as fast as you can. Nothing in your week forces that. DMs, orders and posts fill every hour you give them. So you need one block a week where you stop doing the work and decide what the work should be.

Book it before you read further: a recurring 30 minutes, same day and time, phone on do not disturb. Sunday evening or Monday morning works for most people.

This review borrows from three weekly systems: David Allen's GTD weekly review, the weekly session from The 4 Disciplines of Execution, and the EOS Level 10 meeting, cut down for a team of one. Below you get the agenda, a rule for judging what worked, the weekly template, a 10-minute version for bad weeks, and a 90-day review that sets the priorities your weeks serve.

sections.heading: The 30-minute agenda
sections.body: Each part has a time box. Stick to it. The point is decisions, not a journal entry. If you only finish half, finish the plan step.
steps: Get clear (5 minutes): empty your DMs, notes app, screenshots and inbox onto one list. Nothing stays in your head.
Score (5 minutes): enter last week in the Founder KPI Dashboard. Mark each lead measure hit or missed.
Account (3 minutes): look at last week's top three. Done or not done, with one honest reason for each miss.
Learn (5 minutes): name what worked and why, and whether it was a good decision or good luck.
Cut and hand off (5 minutes): pick one thing to kill or pause and one task to delegate or automate.
Plan (5 minutes): pick next week's ONE thing, then two more. Put all three on your calendar.
Perspective (2 minutes, optional): step back and check what matters more than the business.

sections.heading: Get clear, then score the week
sections.body:
David Allen splits his weekly review into three moves: get clear, get current, get creative. Clear means every loose note, message and idea lands on one list. Current means you check your calendar and lists so nothing is stale. Creative means you look at your someday ideas with fresh eyes. For you, creative gets one minute. Park new ideas on a someday list. A new idea earns a slot only if it beats your current ONE thing.

Then score. Numbers come first because feelings lie. A week that felt busy can be a week where nothing moved. A week that felt slow can be the week you got your first referral.

The weekly session in The 4 Disciplines of Execution runs in three beats: account for last week's commitments, review the scoreboard, plan new commitments. The accounting is the part people skip. Write done or not done next to each of last week's top three. If the same item misses twice, it's too big, or it isn't really a priority.

sections.heading: Judge the decision, not just the result
sections.body:
When something works, Eli's question is why: what did this do that the things before it didn't? Then double down until it stops working. That only helps if your why is right.

Annie Duke, a former professional poker player, names the trap in Thinking in Bets (2018): resulting, which means judging a decision only by how it turned out. Her lead example is Pete Carroll's pass call near the end of Super Bowl XLIX. It was intercepted, and it was widely called the worst call in Super Bowl history. Duke walks through why it was a reasonable call with a bad outcome.

One viral post can be luck. One flop can be a good bet that missed. Before you double down or kill something, sort it into one of four boxes.
bullets: Good decision, good result: you earned it. Write down what you did so you can repeat it.
Good decision, bad result: bad luck or too few tries. Run it again before you kill it.
Bad decision, good result: luck. Don't build next week on it.
Bad decision, bad result: the lesson is in your process. Change how you decide, not just the tactic.
sections.template:
DECISION LOG (one entry per big call)
Date: [ ]
Decision: [what you chose]
What you knew at the time: [ ]
What you expected: [a number and a date, e.g. 5 leads by Friday]
What happened: [ ]
Decision or luck: [good call / bad call / too early to tell]
Would you make it again with the same information? [yes / no, because ]

sections.heading: Plan next week: one thing, then three
sections.body:
Gary Keller's The ONE Thing (2013, with Jay Papasan) gives you the filter: ask which one thing you could do that would make everything else easier or unnecessary. That's priority one. It gets the first time block of your week, before anything else.

Then add two more. Each one should be specific, finishable in a week and tied to a number. 'Grow on TikTok' isn't a priority. 'Post 4 before-and-after clips and reply to every comment within a day' is.

Put all three on your calendar before you close the review. A priority without a time slot is a wish. If they don't fit in your hours, that's your answer: cut one, or hand something off.
sections.example: Illustrative: Ava, 19, edits short-form clips for podcasters. Scoreboard: 40 outreach DMs (target 40, hit), 3 posts (target 4, missed), 6 leads, 2 sales, $300. Account: 2 of 3 priorities done. The portfolio page slipped because she spent 2 hours redesigning her logo. Learn: a before-and-after clip drove 4 of the 6 leads. Good decision, not luck: it shows the result in the first second, and her last two before-and-afters also beat her average. Cut: logo work. Hand off: caption drafts to Claude, using her hook bank. ONE thing: 40 DMs to podcasters with the before-and-after attached, because more conversations make every other number easier. Top three on the calendar: the DMs (Monday and Wednesday, 45 minutes each), 2 more before-and-after clips (Thursday), portfolio page live (Saturday, 30 minutes).

sections.heading: The weekly template
sections.body: Copy this into Notion, Google Docs or your notes app. Duplicate it every week so you can look back at the last 13 reviews when you do your 90-day review.

sections.heading: The 10-minute version for bad weeks
sections.body: Exams, a sick week, a family thing. Skipping the review is how one bad week turns into a lost month. On a week like that, do this version instead: rough numbers, three questions, one calendar block. Ten minutes.

sections.heading: The 90-day review
sections.body:
Weeks need a direction. Once a quarter, take 60 to 90 minutes and set it. EOS calls quarterly priorities Rocks, and keeps them few. The 4 Disciplines of Execution writes each goal as from X to Y by when, which forces a number and a date. With under 3 hours a week, set 1 priority for the quarter, 2 at most.

Stepping away to think is a habit at the top, too. Bill Gates has taken Think Weeks for decades: time away, alone, to read and think about where his work should go. Your version is one long block every 90 days. Reread your last 13 weekly reviews first. Patterns you can't see week to week show up there.

sections.heading: Perspective check (optional)
sections.body: Two minutes, and it's yours to use or skip. The numbers tell you how the business did. These questions ask how you did, because a business that costs you your people and your integrity isn't worth the revenue.
bullets: Did you keep your commitments to the people closest to you this week?
Did the business leave room for anything else this week?
Did you do business with integrity: no shortcuts, no promises you couldn't keep?
Who helped you this week, and have you thanked them? No one is self-made.
Are you still building for the reason you started?
If faith is part of your life, sit with Eli's principle for a minute: 'Success will never satisfy. Only a relationship with God can do that.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Skipping after one busy week. A busy week is when you need it most. Do the 10-minute version.
Turning it into a journal. If you finish without a cut, a handoff and three calendar blocks, it wasn't a review.
Reviewing feelings instead of numbers. Fill the scoreboard before you write a word.
Ten priorities. Three is the cap, and the ONE thing goes first.
Judging by results only. One viral post isn't a strategy and one flop isn't a verdict. Sort it into the four boxes.
Never cutting anything. If nothing comes off the list, next week will be as crowded as this one.
Never looking back. Reread your old reviews every 90 days. That's where the patterns are.

sections.heading: Go deeper
sections.body: Next in the library: the Founder KPI Dashboard feeds your scoreboard. Does the same task show up under hand off two weeks in a row? Work through Delegate Your First Task, then set it up with the Automation Starter Pack or ask the Workflow Recommender. If your top three are mostly content, plan them with the 30-Day Content Calendar.
bullets: Getting Things Done by David Allen: read how he runs the weekly review, the source of get clear, get current, get creative.
The 4 Disciplines of Execution by Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling (2012): the weekly session and from X to Y by when.
Traction by Gino Wickman: the Level 10 meeting and quarterly Rocks, built for teams but easy to shrink.
The ONE Thing by Gary Keller with Jay Papasan (2013): the focusing question and how to protect a time block.
Thinking in Bets by Annie Duke (2018): resulting, and how to judge decisions when luck is involved.

resources.aiPrompt: Check the scoreboard first: it needs real numbers for the five results and the lead measures against target, not 'good week'; if numbers are missing, ask for them and point to the Founder KPI Dashboard. Check that every one of last week's top three is marked done or not done with an honest reason, and flag the same miss two weeks running as a sign the item is too big or not a real priority. In what worked, flag answers that only describe ('the reel did well') without a reason, ask for the number that moved, and ask whether it was a good decision or luck, using Annie Duke's idea of resulting. Check something real was cut and one specific task was named with who or what will run it; if the same task shows up again, send them to Delegate Your First Task. Check the ONE thing passes Keller's test (it makes the other priorities easier or unnecessary) and that all three priorities are finishable in a week, tied to a number and given a calendar slot; rewrite one vague item such as 'grow on TikTok' into a specific one. Treat the perspective check as optional: never judge or push on faith, and if they wrote something personal, respond briefly and kindly.
